title: MEDuSA
text:
Introduction
Imagine a reinforcement-learning task in which participants decide when to respond and then receive feedback. Choice deliberation varies in duration from trial to trial, while feedback triggers a phasic prediction error. Because hemodynamic responses span 15–30 seconds, BOLD signals evoked by cues, variable-duration decisions, and feedback overlap substantially even when the underlying neural processes are distinct. Depending on the scientific question, an investigator may want to test:
Michael Hallquist’s 2022 MEDuSA Quant Talk introduced the clock-task motivation for placing deconvolution, event alignment, and multilevel modeling into a unified sequence. This book documents how the standalone medusa R package implements that framework end to end—walking through the statistical logic, modeling choices, and practical diagnostics at each stage.

title: MEDuSA
section: Why use MEDuSA—and how does the pipeline fit together?
text:
Why use MEDuSA—and how does the pipeline fit together?
Common fMRI analysis strategies each address part of the problem:

Condition-level task GLMs test prespecified canonical BOLD predictors efficiently, while collapsing trial-to-trial variability unless parametric modulators are specified for one model at a time.
Finite impulse response (FIR) models relax HRF shape assumptions for condition averages, while becoming difficult to estimate under rapid jittered trial-by-trial modulation and variable reaction-time intervals.
Single-trial GLMs (LSS / LSA) estimate one scalar amplitude per event under an assumed HRF, rather than a continuous event-locked trajectory across lags with cross-fitted vascular timing.
Blind deconvolution (deconvolve_nlreg(), deconvolve_reglin()) reconstructs continuous time series without event timestamps, leaving neurovascular delay, task-free noise scaling, and trial-level error covariances unanchored.

For a side-by-side simulation comparing Parametric GLM, Condition-Modulated FIR, LSS beta-series, and MEDuSA across single-phase, rapid multi-phase RL, and biphasic neural regimes, see Conceptual foundations §5.
MEDuSA combines out-of-sample event-informed neurovascular identification with continuous regularized linear deconvolution and operator-propagated trial inference. Because every linear transformation from raw BOLD to trial readouts is retained explicitly, downstream epoch regressions, parcel aggregations, multilevel models, and connectivity estimators carry both the resolution matrix (how neighboring events and lags mix in expectation) and the propagated error covariance (how observation noise varies and correlates across trials, lags, and parcels).

title: MEDuSA
section: How to read this book
text:
How to read this book

Begin with Conceptual foundations for the unifying measurement-and-structural framework (\(y \to \widehat{a} \to \widehat{z}\), including the end-to-end data-flow schematic and notation and S3 object map) and A worked analysis for an executable 12-participant walkthrough from simulated BOLD matrices to group inference.
Read the chapters in The MEDuSA pipeline (Steps 0–6), accompanied by the Visual QC and Troubleshooting Gallery. Each stepwise chapter opens with a thumbnail Overview and clean Goals, Inputs, and Outputs tables, walks step by step through each Substep and Choice Point from simple intuition to the full estimator, summarizes Recommended Settings, and closes with Practical Considerations, Diagnostics, and Scope.
Explore Spatial Graph Pooling: Voxelwise and Parcel-Wise NIfTI Workflows for an MNI152 cortical-ribbon walkthrough comparing geodesic bilateral graph pooling, SNR-stratified deconvolution, voxelwise Graph-EB mapping (write_nifti_ts()), and parcel-wise panel backprojection (backproject_medusa()) visualized with ggbrain.
Consult Measurement models and evidence for deeper derivations of method-of-moments (M-MOM) standard-error propagation, latent connectivity measurement models, multi-lag calibration, autocorrelation estimation, and validation benchmarks.

All code examples, figures, and diagnostic tables in this book are generated directly from the standalone medusa package (library(medusa)). See Reproduction and references for instructions on re-running the simulations and rendering the book from book/.

title: Conceptual Foundations
text:
1. Express BOLD through a linear neurovascular forward model
Many task-fMRI studies aim to relate fast, trial-specific cognitive processes—such as reward prediction errors, choice conflict, or deliberation effort—to neural dynamics across brain regions and participants. Because the hemodynamic response blurs neural activity across 15–30 seconds and scanner observations carry serial and spatial noise, trial-level neural responses are not observed directly. Instead, they are estimated from noisy, overlapping BOLD time series and then entered into second-stage models across trials and participants.
A central insight from two-step latent-variable and multilevel measurement-error modeling (Croon, 2002; Fuller, 1987; Skrondal & Laake, 2001; Vig & Hallquist, 2026) guides the design of MEDuSA: separating signal estimation from downstream structural inference works cleanly when the first stage places estimates on an unshrunk, additive-error scale and carries unit-specific error covariances into the second stage. The six subsections below develop how MEDuSA implements this principle from a single run’s forward model to population inference, method selection, and unified notation.
Figure 1.1 provides a bird’s-eye map of how data objects, linear operators, and propagated noise covariances travel through the package—and why the pipeline branches at the end according to whether deconvolved neural activity serves as a regression outcome (Step 5) or a noisy predictor (Step 6). (For visual examples of what happens when an assumption along any of these tracks is violated, see the Visual QC and Troubleshooting Gallery.)
Consider a single fMRI run and voxel (or parcel) observed at \(T\) acquisition times. Let \(a \in \mathbb{R}^T\) denote latent neural activity on the acquisition grid, \(H(h)\) denote time-invariant causal convolution with the local hemodynamic response function \(h\) (a Toeplitz matrix whose columns shift \(h\) forward volume by volume), \(Z\) collect low-frequency drift and nuisance terms, and \(\varepsilon\) denote zero-mean serial observation noise with covariance \(\Sigma\):
\[
y = H(h)a + Z\gamma + \varepsilon,
\qquad \mathbb{E}(\varepsilon) = 0, \quad \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon) = \Sigma.
\]
As Figure 1.2 illustrates, each brief or sustained neural event influences BOLD across many subsequent volumes, so nearby events overlap substantially in the recorded signal. Step 1 (estimate_crossrun_hrf()) identifies \(h\) out of sample from the participant’s other runs and estimates \(\Sigma\) on task-adjusted residuals. Step 2 (deconvolve_crossrun_hrf()) then reconstructs continuous activity on the acquisition grid via smoothness-penalized generalized least squares:
\[
\widehat{a} = \arg\min_a (y - Ha)^\top \Sigma^{-1}(y - Ha) + \lambda \|Pa\|^2.
\]
With nuisance projection absorbed into the whitened solve, the deconvolved series is a known linear transformation of the BOLD vector, \(\widehat{a} = D y\). Larger values of \(\lambda\) suppress high-frequency noise while modestly broadening peaks; smaller values preserve rapid transitions at the cost of higher variance.

title: Conceptual Foundations
section: 2. Write the exact trial-readout measurement model
text:
2. Write the exact trial-readout measurement model
To move from continuous activity \(\widehat{a}\) to event-locked trial quantities, suppose an investigator samples \(\widehat{a}\) around target events using a local time-averaging matrix \(S\) (symmetric kernel quadrature—for instance, a triangle window centered at feedback onset). If the true event-related neural amplitudes are \(\theta\) with forward BOLD design \(F\theta\) (\(y = F\theta + \varepsilon\) after nuisance removal), the raw trial readout \(\widehat{z}_{\text{raw}} = S\widehat{a} = SD y\) can be written by adding and subtracting \(\theta\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{z}_{\text{raw}} &= SD(F\theta + \varepsilon) \\
&= K_{\text{raw}}\theta + SD\varepsilon \\
&= \theta - (I - K_{\text{raw}})\theta + SD\varepsilon,
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(K_{\text{raw}} = SDF\) is the raw trial resolution matrix.
Notice the direct parallel to Empirical Bayes random-effect predictions in multilevel models (Vig & Hallquist, 2026): the estimation error \(\widehat{z}_{\text{raw}} - \theta\) contains two distinct components. The first, \(-(I - K_{\text{raw}})\theta\), is systematic regularization attenuation (\([K_{\text{raw}}]_{ii} < 1\)) and spillover from neighboring cues or trials (\([K_{\text{raw}}]_{ij} \neq 0\)), which depends on the signal itself. The second, \(SD\varepsilon\), is conditionally mean-zero observation noise propagated through deconvolution and readout.

title: Conceptual Foundations
section: 3. Invert event mixing to recover an additive-error scale
text:
3. Invert event mixing to recover an additive-error scale
If raw readouts were passed directly into trial regressions, regularization shrinkage would attenuate amplitudes while spillover from preceding cues or rapid neighboring trials could confound slopes. In Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()), MEDuSA subtracts non-target spillover and applies a regularized inverse of the target mixing matrix (mirroring the inverse-shrinkage step in REPAIR) to form the composite epoch operator \(B\):
\[
\widehat{z} = B y \approx \theta + e,
\qquad \mathbb{E}(e \mid \theta) = 0,
\qquad \Omega = \operatorname{Cov}(e \mid B) = B \Sigma B^\top.
\]
Removing systematic mixing places decon_demixed (\(\widehat{z}\)) on a classical additive measurement-error scale: target amplitude plus zero-mean propagated error with known trial-by-trial covariance \(\Omega\) (whose diagonal square roots are se_demixed). When a small ridge term is retained in \(B\) to stabilize very rapid inter-stimulus intervals, Step 3 applies the matching post-demixing resolution map \(M_{\text{post}}\) to centered within-run covariates so both sides of a trial regression share identical coordinates. Step 4 then extends this exact operator across voxels within each anatomical parcel using task-free noise innovations to account for spatial error correlation.

title: Conceptual Foundations
section: 4. Match downstream inference to the structural role of the neural variable
text:
4. Match downstream inference to the structural role of the neural variable
Once trial readouts \(\widehat{z}\) are expressed as latent signal plus additive error \(e\) with known variance \(s_i^2 = \Omega_{ii}\), how measurement error affects group inference depends on which side of the structural equation \(\widehat{z}\) occupies (Skrondal & Laake, 2001; Vig & Hallquist, 2026):

Neural activity as the outcome (Neural ~ Behavior, Step 5): When error-free task or behavioral variables predict decon_demixed, additive zero-mean error \(e_i\) enters the regression residual without biasing fixed-effect slope estimates. However, error precision varies across trials, runs, and participants. Step 5 (mixed_by() and medusa_multilag_infer()) pairs participant random slopes—treating participants as the independent unit of population replication—with composite inverse-variance weights \((\widehat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_i^2)^{-1}\) (precision_weight_cohort) and cross-lag covariance matrices so standard errors, simultaneous bands, and window contrasts remain calibrated.
Neural activity as a predictor (Target ~ Seed * Task or Behavior ~ Seed, Step 6): When a noisy parcel readout moves to the right-hand side as a predictor (\(\widehat{z}_{S,i} = \theta_{S,i} + u_i\) predicting \(\widehat{z}_{T,i} = \theta_{T,i} + v_i\)), trial error \(u_i\) inflates the predictor variance \(X^\top X\) (attenuating slopes toward zero) and any shared scanner or physiological noise \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i) \neq 0\) between seed and target shifts \(X^\top Y\). Step 6 (decon_connectivity_repair()) subtracts per-trial predictor error covariance blocks \(\Psi_i\) and task-free cross-parcel noise covariances from the sample cross-products while guarding against unstable small denominators in low-reliability scans (Modified Method of Moments with Step-up Regularization, M-MOMS, medusa_fit_mmom()), before pooling participant slopes at the group level.

title: Conceptual Foundations
section: 5. When does MEDuSA agree with—or outperform—GLM, FIR, and LSS beta-series?
text:
5. When does MEDuSA agree with—or outperform—GLM, FIR, and LSS beta-series?
Before committing to a full deconvolution pipeline, a practical question is when MEDuSA yields the same answer as simpler fMRI estimators—and when its extra machinery materially improves inference. To make that comparison concrete, assets/compare_glm_fir_lss_medusa.R evaluates four widely used methods on identical 16-participant, 3-run BOLD cohorts (\(\text{TR} = 1.0\text{ s}\), 6 voxels per parcel, shared + voxel-specific \(\text{AR}(1)\) noise, population feedback RPE slope \(\beta = 0.50\)):

Parametric Canonical GLM: Standard run-wise prewhitened general linear model convolving feedback and centered rpe (plus cue and decision boxcars when present) with a canonical \(6.0\text{ s}\) two-gamma HRF, followed by a group random-effects \(t\)-test.
LSS Single-Trial Beta-Series (Mumford et al., 2012): Separate prewhitened canonical-HRF GLM for every feedback trial (one column for the target trial, one column summing all other feedback trials, plus cue/decision regressors), followed by a multilevel model (beta_lss ~ rpe_within + (1 + rpe_within || id) + (1 | id:run)).
Condition-Modulated FIR: Prewhitened finite impulse response basis (\(-2\) to \(+14\text{ s}\)) for both the feedback main effect and rpe modulation, summarizing the peak-scaled canonical BOLD window (\(+4\) to \(+6\text{ s}\)) across participants alongside the full BOLD-time curve.
MEDuSA: Out-of-sample parcel HRF cross-fitting (estimate_crossrun_hrf()), event-informed slope-and-curvature-penalized deconvolution (deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(), penalty = "sobolev"), de-mixed parcel epoch extraction (decon_epoch_regression()), and cohort-weighted multilevel / trajectory inference (mixed_by() and medusa_multilag_infer()).

Figure 1.3 and Table 1.1 compare all four estimators across three progressively more demanding task regimes:

Regime 1 — Well-spaced single-phase events with a canonical HRF (7.5–10.5 s ITI): When isolated impulses evoke a canonical \(6.0\text{ s}\) hemodynamic response, all four estimators converge on nearly identical, well-calibrated group slopes (0.478 to 0.474). When classical GLM assumptions hold, MEDuSA introduces no bias or efficiency loss.
Regime 2 — Rapid multi-phase RL trials (Cue -> variable-RT Decision -> Feedback) in a fast-HRF region (3.0 s peak): Here expected value at cue correlates negatively with signed rpe at feedback, deliberation varies in reaction time, and the local vasculature peaks 3 seconds earlier than the canonical template (as often observed in striatum, thalamus, and insula). Canonical-HRF Parametric GLM (0.191) and LSS (0.169) suffer substantial vascular-mismatch attenuation and cue bleed, while a canonical \(4\text{--}6\text{ s}\) FIR peak window (0.284) partially misses the early hemodynamic peak. By learning the \(3.0\text{ s}\) HRF out of sample and de-mixing cue and variable-duration decision intervals, MEDuSA recovers the generating onset slope (0.542).
Regime 3 — Biphasic neural trajectory (+0.50 early phasic burst at 0–1.0 s, -0.45 late regulatory dip at 1.6–3.6 s): Single-scalar GLM (-0.007) and LSS (0.014) project the entire peri-event trajectory onto one basis function, integrating across opposing early and late lobes so the two phases largely cancel. Condition-modulated FIR (Figure 1.3, Panel C) captures the biphasic wave only in delayed, vascularly smeared BOLD time (\(+2\) to \(+12\text{ s}\)) without trial-level readouts. MEDuSA (Figure 1.3, Panel B) resolves both the early positive burst and the late negative dip directly on neural event time, with simultaneous Max-|T| bands and a late_minus_early window contrast (-0.316, \(\text{SE} = 0.033\)).







Figure 1.3: Head-to-head comparison of Parametric Canonical GLM, LSS Single-Trial Beta-Series (Mumford et al., 2012), Condition-Modulated FIR, and MEDuSA across 16-participant multi-run cohorts (assets/compare_glm_fir_lss_medusa.R). (A) Population onset RPE slope recovery (95% CI; dashed line = +0.50 truth) across three task regimes. (B) Regime 3 biphasic trajectory recovered by medusa_multilag_infer() on neural event time with simultaneous 95% Max-|T| bands vs. scalar LSS cancellation. (C) The same Regime 3 signal viewed through condition-modulated FIR in delayed BOLD time.

Scientific question & task regime
When GLM / LSS / FIR suffices
When MEDuSA provides a clear advantage




Single-phase, well-spaced events (\(\text{ITI} \ge 8\text{ s}\)) in cortical regions near canonical HRF timing, testing one scalar modulator
Parametric GLM and LSS recover nearly identical population slopes with minimal setup.
Useful mainly if trial-specific precision weights (se_demixed) or downstream M-MOMS connectivity (Step 6) are needed.


Multi-phase cognitive tasks (cue \(\to\) variable-RT decision \(\to\) feedback) or subcortical / fast-HRF territories
Canonical GLM and LSS attenuate effects when regional HRFs peak early/late or correlated trial phases overlap.
Out-of-sample HRF learning (Step 1) + duration-aware (T, O) epoch de-mixing (Step 3) prevent vascular-mismatch loss and neighbor bleed.


Temporally evolving or biphasic dynamics (early phasic salience vs. late sustained regulation, peak latency shifts)
Scalar GLM/LSS integrate opposing lobes; FIR remains in delayed BOLD time without single-trial readouts.
medusa_multilag_infer() (Step 5) estimates neural-time trajectories, simultaneous bands, and window contrasts while retaining trial panels.


Trial-to-trial seed–target connectivity & PPI
LSS beta-series contain unquantified trial estimation error and shared physiological noise that bias Target ~ Seed * Task slopes.
decon_connectivity_repair() (Step 6) propagates per-trial error variances and task-free cross-parcel noise correlations into M-MOMS disattenuation.

title: Conceptual Foundations
section: Practical record-keeping across steps
text:
Practical record-keeping across steps
Throughout the pipeline, latent “activity” is measured in input BOLD units scaled by the chosen HRF normalization convention (normalize = "positive_lobe" under preset = "medusa"), and conditional error propagation treats the learned Step 1–4 operators as fixed while Step 5–6 random-effects models capture between-participant variation. Retaining the full S3 fit objects (hrf_fit, decon, and per-participant epochs lists or .rds/Parquet panels) preserves both the trial table and the operator covariances used by multi-lag and connectivity analyses.

title: A Worked Analysis from BOLD to a Group Claim
text:
1. Estimate participant HRFs, deconvolve runs, and align parcel epochs (Steps 1–4)
Before examining each step in full detail, it is helpful to watch a single scientific question move through the complete MEDuSA pipeline from raw run matrices to population inference. Suppose our primary question is whether signed reward prediction error (RPE) modulates neural activity at feedback onset in a prespecified cortical parcel (Parcel_A), and how that effect evolves over the surrounding seconds.
Our teaching dataset simulates 12 participants, each completing three runs of 20 reinforcement-learning trials (worked/workflow-source.Rmd). Every trial comprises a visual cue, a variable-duration decision interval equal to reaction time, and brief feedback. Two parcels (Parcel_A and Parcel_B) contain three voxels each, and RPE modulates feedback activity in both parcels. (If you are starting from raw BIDS/fMRIPrep directories on disk, see Step 0: Task Design and BIDS/fMRIPrep Ingestion; for a quantitative comparison against canonical GLM, FIR, and LSS beta-series, see Conceptual foundations §5.) Below, we walk through the five core stages of the analysis in execution order and then illustrate two practical data-support and handoff checks.
For each participant, three function calls carry the run-level BOLD matrices and event schedules to a de-mixed, parcel-aggregated trial panel:
library(medusa)

# Step 1: Cross-fit HRFs on non-target runs and estimate own-run AR(p) noise
hrf_fit <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(
  bold, events, tr, candidates, amplitude_model = "trial",
  noise_model = "ar1", evidence = "calibrated"
)

# Step 2: Reconstruct continuous latent activity on an observation-noise scale
dec <- deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(
  bold, hrf_fit, lambda = .1, scaling = "noise_sd", penalty = "sobolev",
  nuisance_mode = "ignore", observation_mask = "fit"
)

# Steps 3 & 4: Aggregate into parcels, de-mix overlapping events, and propagate SEs
epochs <- decon_epoch_regression(
  dec, covariates, target_condition = "feedback", lags = -2:4,
  parcel_groups = parcel_ids, restore_scale = TRUE,
  demix_within_trial = FALSE, tau2_mode = "marginal", return_panel = TRUE
)
(Here lambda = 0.1 is fixed to match the teaching vignette; in empirical studies, leaving lambda = NULL tunes smoothness automatically across runs.)

title: A Worked Analysis from BOLD to a Group Claim
section: 2. Test the planned onset slope across participants (Step 5: mixed_by())
text:
2. Test the planned onset slope across participants (Step 5: mixed_by())
Stacking epochs$panel across all 12 participants and centering RPE within each participant and run (rpe_within) prepares the cohort panel. To test the planned feedback-onset association in Parcel_A (evt_time == 0), we fit a random-slope linear mixed model weighted by precision_weight_cohort:

one <- group_panel[parcel == "Parcel_A" & evt_time == 0]
fit <- mixed_by(
  one, model_formulae = list(
    feedback = decon_demixed ~ rpe_within + (1 + rpe_within || id) + (1 | id:run)
  ),
  weights = "precision_weight_cohort",
  calculate = "parameter_estimates_reml", padjust_by = NULL,
  return_models = TRUE
)

Across all 720 trials and 12 participants, the estimated population feedback-onset slope is 0.574 restored BOLD units per RPE unit (fit status: singular — inspect variance components).

section: 3. Characterize the full lag trajectory and window contrasts (Step 5: medusa_multilag_infer())
text:
3. Characterize the full lag trajectory and window contrasts (Step 5: medusa_multilag_infer())
When the scientific question extends across the entire \(-2\text{ s}\) to \(+4\text{ s}\) peri-event epoch, passing the named subject_epochs list to medusa_multilag_infer() pools participant lag slopes jointly and constructs a simultaneous 95% confidence band covering all seven lags together (Max-|T|):

profile <- medusa_multilag_infer(
  subject_epochs, covariates = "rpe", use_whitened = FALSE,
  trajectory_mode = "none", contrast_source = "unsmoothed",
  tr = tr, n_perm = 1999L, n_boot_latency = 0L, seed = 5420L
)









Figure 2.2: Population RPE slope trajectory around feedback in Parcel A. Orange diamond: true instantaneous feedback effect at lag 0 (zero at non-zero lags). Teal dashed curve: noiseless signal projected through the fitted Step 2–3 operators. Blue curve and ribbon: recovered noisy cohort trajectory and 95% simultaneous Max-|T| band.





Notice why the recovered raw lag curve in Figure 2.2 spans neighboring lags even though the simulated effect occurs instantaneously at \(0\text{ s}\): regularized continuous deconvolution spreads a brief impulse smoothly across adjacent lags (matching the noiseless operator projection, teal dashed line).

section: 4. Test seed-to-target connectivity and PPI (Step 6: decon_connectivity_repair())
text:
4. Test seed-to-target connectivity and PPI (Step 6: decon_connectivity_repair())
Finally, when Parcel_A moves to the right-hand side to test whether its coupling with Parcel_B changes with RPE (Parcel_B ~ Parcel_A + rpe + Parcel_A:rpe), decon_connectivity_repair(..., shared_error = "auto", method = "mmoms") uses per-trial se_demixed^2 and cross-parcel noise correlations to correct predictor measurement error while controlling for the main effect of RPE in both parcels. Because our teaching simulation contains no true PPI modulation, the estimated interaction centers near zero as expected.

title: Step 0: Task Design and BIDS/fMRIPrep Ingestion
text:
Overview
Before hemodynamic estimation (Step 1) or continuous BOLD deconvolution (Step 2) begins, two practical foundations govern how accurately trial-level neural signals can be recovered:
For studies organized in BIDS with fMRIPrep (or BrainGnomes) derivatives, read_fmriprep_subject() assembles all run-level NIfTI matrices, event schedules, nuisance regressors, non-steady-state and motion censoring masks, and parcellation labels into a single "medusa_nifti_ts" bundle ready for Step 1:
library(medusa)

sub01 <- read_fmriprep_subject(
  fmriprep_dir             = "/path/to/derivatives/fmriprep",
  bids_dir                 = "/path/to/bids",
  sub                      = "01",
  task                     = "learn",
  space                    = "MNI152NLin2009cAsym",
  atlas                    = "/path/to/schaefer_200_mni.nii.gz",
  strategy                 = "24p",
  fd_threshold             = 0.5,
  include_non_steady_state = TRUE
)

candidates <- hrf_library(tr = sub01$tr, preset = "medusa")
hrf_fit    <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(sub01, kernel_grid = candidates, pooling = "parcel")
The walkthrough below develops Step 0 across five substeps—from planning run structure and inter-phase jitter (0.1), to ingesting BIDS and fMRIPrep files on an intact acquisition clock (0.2), handling missed or timeout trials (0.3), joining computational model variables safely via event_index (0.4), and denoising motion-contaminated runs with non-aggressive ICA-AROMA and matched nuisance projection (0.5).
crumbs: 3  Step 0: Task Design and BIDS/fMRIPrep Ingestion

title: Step 0: Task Design and BIDS/fMRIPrep Ingestion
text:
Experimental task scheduling: Splitting trials across multiple scanner runs (\(R \ge 3\)) gives Step 1 independent out-of-sample folds for regional HRF estimation, while jittering the intervals between adjacent within-trial phases (such as cue and feedback) makes overlapping neural epochs separable in Step 3.
Clock-aligned derivative ingestion: Preprocessed 4D BOLD volumes, brain masks, fMRIPrep nuisance/censoring tables, and BIDS *_events.tsv schedules must share an exact physical acquisition clock, while real behavioral occurrences such as missed responses or timeouts remain represented in the forward event schedule.









NotePosition in the MEDuSA Pipeline



Task Schedule + BIDS/fMRIPrep Files \(\longrightarrow\) Step 0 (read_fmriprep_subject) \(\longrightarrow\) "medusa_nifti_ts" subject bundle \(\longrightarrow\) Step 1 (estimate_crossrun_hrf)

title: Step 0: Task Design and BIDS/fMRIPrep Ingestion
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 0

Design identifiable multi-run event schedules: Ensure adjacent task phases decouple under hemodynamic blurring and provide independent runs for out-of-sample HRF cross-fitting.
Read 4D NIfTI runs into consistent time × voxel matrices: Verify spatial grid geometry across runs, intersect per-run brain masks (mask_policy = "intersect"), and attach parcel labels or spatial coordinates.
Preserve exact volume timestamps during dummy-scan and motion censoring: Flag initial non-steady-state volumes and high-motion frames in valid_rows rather than deleting time rows, keeping event onset seconds locked to the scanner clock.
Retain complete forward event schedules and trial keys: Keep nuisance task occurrences (such as missed-response timeouts) in events so their BOLD waves are removed rather than absorbed into noise, and link external behavioral or reinforcement-learning (RL) tables through unambiguous event_index keys.



Inputs: What Step 0 Receives and Why



Input
Source & Format
Why It Is Set Up That Way




fmriprep_dir & sub
Root fMRIPrep derivatives directory and subject label (with or without "sub-" prefix)
Automatically discovers *_desc-preproc_bold.nii.gz, per-run *_desc-brain_mask.nii.gz, and *_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv across single-session or multi-session (ses-*) layouts.


bids_dir & task
Raw BIDS root (defaults to dirname(fmriprep_dir) when nested under derivatives/) and task name
Locates matching *_events.tsv schedules and JSON sidecars (RepetitionTime, StartTime), handling run labels consistently across run-1 and run-01 zero-padding conventions.


space, res, & atlas
Template space substring (e.g., "MNI152NLin2009cAsym"), optional resolution tag, and optional 3D integer/labeled NIfTI parcellation
Filters BOLD derivatives when multiple output spaces exist and maps retained gray-matter voxels directly onto parcel_ids for parcel pooling (Step 1 and Step 4).


strategy, fd_threshold, & include_non_steady_state
Confound regression preset ("6p", "24p", "36p", "compcor", "csf_wm", "csf_wm_8p", "24p_csf_wm", "none") and framewise censoring rules
Converts BIDS "n/a" strings on derivative lag columns cleanly to 0, drops linearly dependent nuisance columns per run, and builds logical valid_rows masks without shifting volume timestamps.


aroma, aroma_dir, & aroma_clean_nuisance
Optional ICA-AROMA mode ("none", "nonaggressive", "auto", "aggressive"), optional fMRIPost-AROMA derivatives root, and matched confound projection flag
Discovers fMRIPost-AROMA (*_desc-melodic_mixing.tsv + *_desc-aroma_metrics.tsv) or legacy fMRIPrep AROMA tables, denoises BOLD via Pruim et al. (2015) partial regression, and projects the identical AROMA operator out of $nuisance (Lindquist et al., 2019).


External model covariates (optional)
Trial-level behavioral, RL, or drift-diffusion table keyed by (id, run, event_index) (or extra columns inside *_events.tsv)
Keeps Steps 1–2 blind to downstream hypothesis predictors while supporting exact trial matching in Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()).





Outputs: What Step 0 Produces and Why It Is Set Up That Way
read_fmriprep_subject() (or modular assembly via read_nifti_ts(), read_fmriprep_confounds(), and read_bids_events()) produces an S3 "medusa_nifti_ts" object containing:



Output Component
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




bold
Named list (run1, run2, …) of T_r × V numeric matrices
Reads 4D NIfTI volumes directly into matrices restricted to the shared in-mask voxel set \(V\).


tr, voxel_map, & geometry
Scalar tr (s), V-row coordinate/parcel lookup table, and 3D NIfTI header template
Anchors continuous-to-discrete time mapping and enables instant 3D/4D NIfTI reconstruction via write_nifti_ts() and backproject_medusa().


parcel_ids
Named vector of parcel labels across the \(V\) columns
Supplies spatial_groups / parcel_groups automatically to Steps 1, 3, and 4 when an atlas is provided.


events
Standardized data.frame (run, onset, duration, condition, plus all extra BIDS trial columns)
Normalizes BIDS trial_type to condition, converts "n/a" durations to 0 impulses while retaining numeric covariates, and aligns run names to names(bold).


confounds, nuisance, & valid_rows
"medusa_confounds" object plus per-run nuisance matrices and logical masks (TRUE = keep, FALSE = censor)
Passed automatically when estimate_crossrun_hrf(sub01, ...) is called, with $confounds$summary providing a run-by-run censoring and motion QC table.


aroma (when aroma != "none")
Provenance list (mode, fit_valid, clean_nuisance, and $summary component table)
Audits total, accepted, and rejected MELODIC components per run and confirms whether $nuisance received matched AROMA projection.

title: Step 0: Task Design and BIDS/fMRIPrep Ingestion
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

0.1 Schedule runs and inter-phase jitter for trial-level identifiability
Suppose you are designing—or evaluating an archival dataset for—a multi-phase decision task in which each trial presents a cue followed by feedback. Even before data are collected, two structural features of the schedule determine how well any deconvolution method can separate neural responses:

Within-trial inter-stimulus jitter (ISI): When cue and feedback are separated by a constant short interval on every trial (for example, \(0.8\text{ s}\)) and cue-evoked activity covaries with the feedback predictor (as expected value covaries with reward prediction error), their convolved BOLD waves move nearly in lockstep. Varying the cue-to-feedback interval across trials (for instance, across \(1.0\text{--}4.5\text{ s}\)) breaks that collinearity so Step 3’s (T, O) de-mixing operator can subtract the cue response cleanly without inflating feedback variance.
Multi-run partitioning (\(R\)): Step 1 learns each target run’s HRF from the participant’s other runs (\(s \neq r\)). Holding total trial count fixed at 60 trials, collecting a single continuous run (\(R = 1\)) forces Step 1 to fall back on within-run temporal sub-blocks, whereas collecting \(R = 2\) runs leaves only a single training run per fold—meaning one noisy or motion-contaminated run serves as the sole training set for the cleaner run. Splitting the same 60 trials across \(R \ge 3\) runs ensures every cross-fitting fold pools across at least two runs and unlocks cross-run stability checks.

Figure 3.1 and Table 3.1 illustrate both effects across 20 simulated replications of a two-parcel task (Target_Parcel carries both a cue response and a true \(0.60\) feedback RPE slope; CueOnly_Parcel responds strongly to the correlated cue with zero true feedback effect). Introducing uniform (\(1.0\text{--}4.5\text{ s}\)) or truncated-exponential (\(1.0\text{--}6.0\text{ s}\)) cue–feedback jitter eliminates residual cue-to-feedback bleed in CueOnly_Parcel and reduces feedback slope RMSE, while partitioning 60 trials across \(3\text{--}4\) runs stabilizes HRF peak recovery and downstream slope accuracy when one run exhibits elevated scanner noise.






Figure 3.1: Experimental design feasibility benchmarks across 20 Monte Carlo replications (design_benchmarks.csv): (A) Jittering the within-trial cue-to-feedback ISI decouples overlapping epochs, reducing both target feedback slope RMSE and false cue-to-feedback spillover in a cue-only parcel; (B) For a fixed 60-trial budget when Run 1 has elevated noise, partitioning into \(R \ge 3\) runs stabilizes Step 1 out-of-sample HRF recovery and Step 3 slope estimation.

Choice point — Task design targets and small-parcel thresholds:

Number of runs: Aim for \(R = 3\text{--}5\) task runs per participant with at least \(15\text{--}25\) target trials per run (45–100+ total trials). Single-run and two-run datasets remain fully supported, with \(R \ge 3\) providing the strongest out-of-sample HRF cross-validation.
Within-trial ISI and inter-trial ITI jitter: When adjacent phases within a trial will be analyzed separately, jitter their separation across at least \(1.0\text{--}4.5\text{ s}\) (truncated exponential or uniform) or include a modest fraction (10–20%) of catch/cue-only trials; jitter inter-trial intervals across \(3\text{--}8\text{ s}\) (or longer in slow-trial tasks) so baseline drift and AR(\(p\)) noise remain well separated from task responses.
Tiny subcortical nuclei (min_parcel_voxels): In Step 1, pooling = "parcel" requires at least min_parcel_voxels = 5L voxels per parcel before departing from the canonical reference waveform. When analyzing very small subcortical structures (\(<5\) voxels at \(2\text{--}3\text{ mm}\) isotropic resolution), pass min_parcel_voxels = 2L (or acquire higher spatial resolution) so supported fast vascular timing can be learned.




0.2 Ingest BIDS and fMRIPrep derivatives on an intact acquisition clock
Once fMRIPrep preprocessing completes, each run produces a 4D BOLD NIfTI file, a 3D brain mask, a *_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv table, and a raw BIDS *_events.tsv file whose onset column records event times in seconds from the start of volume 1 (\(t = 0\text{ s}\)).
Calling read_fmriprep_subject() performs four coordinated ingestion steps automatically:

Mask intersection and atlas alignment: Reads all runs’ brain masks, retains voxels present in every run (mask_policy = "intersect" so parcel definitions stay identical across cross-fitting folds), checks 3D affine/dimension agreement against atlas, and extracts the 4D runs directly into T_r × V matrices.
Confound cleaning and rank protection: Parses *_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv under a standard preset (strategy = "6p", "24p", "36p", "24p_csf_wm", or "compcor"), replaces BIDS "n/a" strings on temporal derivative/quadratic lag rows with 0, centers columns, and drops any zero-variance or collinear columns per run.
Clock-preserving frame censoring (valid_rows): Flags fMRIPrep’s non_steady_state_outlier* dummy scans (include_non_steady_state = TRUE) alongside frames exceeding fd_threshold or dvars_threshold by setting valid_rows = FALSE rather than deleting rows from bold.
BIDS event standardization: Reads *_events.tsv, maps trial_type to condition, treats "n/a" durations as 0-second impulses, and coerces numeric trial columns cleanly.

Table 3.2 shows the run-level $confounds$summary table produced by read_fmriprep_subject() on our three-run simulated BIDS/fMRIPrep dataset (240 volumes per run at \(\text{TR} = 1.0\text{ s}\), with 4 initial non-steady-state dummy volumes and 2 two-TR motion spikes per run, yielding 8 censored volumes or 3.3% per run).

Why is censoring initial dummy scans via valid_rows = FALSE preferable to slicing bold <- bold[-(1:4), ] in custom preprocessing scripts? When events.tsv timestamps are measured from volume 1 (\(t = 0\text{ s}\)), physically deleting the first 4 volumes without updating time_offset shifts every retained BOLD sample 4 seconds earlier relative to events$onset. As shown in Figure 3.2 and Table 3.3, keeping the intact 240-volume clock with valid_rows (lag0_beta = 0.644) and physically truncating 4 volumes while declaring time_offset = 4 (lag0_beta = 0.644) produce virtually identical results on the true 0.650 lag-0 RPE slope. By contrast, deleting 4 dummy volumes while leaving time_offset = 0 shifts the entire recovered profile backward by \(-4\text{ s}\), distorting Step 1’s cross-fitted HRF and collapsing the apparent lag-0 slope to 0.033.

Choice point — One-call read_fmriprep_subject() vs. modular readers and confound strategy:

Standard BIDS/fMRIPrep directories: Use read_fmriprep_subject() with include_non_steady_state = TRUE and strategy = "24p" (six rigid-body realignment parameters, their temporal derivatives, and quadratic terms) or "compcor" when anatomical/temporal CompCor components are desired alongside motion terms. When fMRIPost-AROMA or legacy ICA-AROMA mixing matrices are available, setting aroma = "nonaggressive" inside read_fmriprep_subject() (or calling read_fmriprep_aroma() + apply_aroma()) performs partial regression on BOLD and matched nuisance columns simultaneously so downstream confound projection never re-introduces motion variance. Remember that Steps 1–2 already add per-run intercepts, linear trends, and slow < 1/128 Hz cosine drift terms internally, so avoid pre-bandpass-filtering BOLD before MEDuSA.
Fast-TR multiband acquisitions (\(\text{TR} \le 1.0\text{ s}\)): Add motion_bandstop_bpm = c(12, 20) and motion_filter_target = "fd_only" inside read_fmriprep_subject() (or read_fmriprep_confounds()) so respiratory chest-wall modulation does not trigger false FD scrubbing; see Step 1 §1.5.
Custom preprocessing or BrainGnomes pipelines: Assemble the exact same inputs modularly via read_nifti_ts(bold_files, mask = ..., atlas = ...), read_fmriprep_confounds(confound_files, censor_files = ...), and read_bids_events(event_files). If an upstream pipeline already discarded \(k\) initial dummy volumes before writing BOLD NIfTIs while leaving events.tsv anchored to scanner trigger \(t = 0\), pass time_offset = k * tr to Step 1 (or check the BIDS JSON StartTime field).




0.3 Keep missed responses, timeouts, and catch trials in the event schedule
In real cognitive tasks, participants occasionally miss a response deadline or experience a timeout screen (response_time = "n/a", undefined RL choice/RPE). A natural temptation when preparing events for trial-level regression is to filter events.tsv down to valid completed trials before running Step 1.
From the perspective of the forward BOLD model (\(y = Ha + Z\gamma + \varepsilon\)), however, a missed trial is still a physical sensory and cognitive event in the scanner: the cue appeared, a timeout warning or visual change occurred, and salience/error-monitoring cortex responded strongly. Deleting those timestamps from events forces Steps 1–3 to treat large timeout-evoked BOLD waves as unexplained noise:

In Step 1, unmodeled timeout waves inflate residual autocorrelation (\(\hat{\rho}\)).
In Step 2, unmodeled BOLD deflections inflate noise_sd and push automatic cross-validation tuning toward heavier smoothing (lambda), attenuating nearby valid trials.
In Step 3, demix_other_events = TRUE cannot subtract the tail of a preceding timeout wave from the next valid feedback trial if the timeout event was omitted.

Instead, label missed or timeout events as a separate condition in events (for example, trial_type = "missed_feedback" or "timeout"), and keep target_condition = "feedback" in Step 3. Figure 3.3 and Table 3.4 demonstrate the improvement on sub-01 (where 3 of 18 trials per run are timeout trials evoking a strong cortical salience burst): keeping "missed_feedback" in events recovers the exact observation noise (0.029 vs. true 0.030), true AR(1) parameter (0.462 vs. true 0.450), and true lag-0 RPE slope (0.644 vs. 0.650), whereas deleting missed rows from events.tsv inflates estimated noise_sd by 57% and cuts the recovered RPE slope to 0.325.

Choice point — condition_map versus exclude_conditions in read_bids_events():

Use condition_map (or distinct trial_type strings in events.tsv) to group or retain every occurrence that evokes neural/sensory activity—including "missed_feedback", "catch_cue", "instruction_screen", and "button_press"—so Steps 1–3 model and de-mix them cleanly.
Reserve exclude_conditions strictly for non-neural logging markers written into BIDS event files (such as "scanner_trigger", "sync_pulse", or "eyetracker_calibration_flag").




0.4 Join computational model covariates safely via event_index
In cognitive neuroscience workflows, trial-by-trial predictors—such as reinforcement-learning expected values, prediction errors, or drift-diffusion parameters—often live either as extra columns inside *_events.tsv or in a separate behavioral/computational data.table fit outside fMRIPrep. MEDuSA supports both cleanly without risking trial-alignment shifts:

In-table BIDS columns (covariates = "rpe" or ~ rpe + abs(rpe)): Because read_fmriprep_subject() preserves all extra columns in sub01$events (converting "n/a" on non-target or missed rows to NA), passing column names or a one-sided formula to decon_epoch_regression() automatically extracts the rows where condition == target_condition in exact chronological order.
External behavioral / RL model joins via event_index: Every panel returned by decon_epoch_regression() includes two index columns:

trial: sequential counter 1..m_valid indexing only the retained target_condition occurrences within that run.
event_index: the exact integer row position in that run’s events table (1..nrow(events_run)).

Whenever a run contains missed responses or catch trials (for example, 15 valid feedback trials out of 18 task trials, skipping trials 6, 12, and 16), panel$trial runs 1..15 while task trial_number runs 1..18 with gaps. As shown in the bottom row of Table 3.4, mistakenly merging an external RL table on panel$trial == rl_dt$trial_number scrambles every trial pairing after the first missed response (lag0_beta = 0.241, losing 6 trials). Keying external computational tables by (id, run, event_index) (or carrying trial_number inside events.tsv and joining on (id, run, trial_number)) guarantees 1-to-1 alignment:


# Record within-run row position (`event_index`) when building external RL/DDM tables
ev_dt <- data.table::as.data.table(sub01$events)
ev_dt[, event_index := seq_len(.N), by = run]

# After Step 3/4 epoch extraction, join external computational predictors on (id, run, event_index)
panel_merged <- merge(
  epochs$panel,
  rl_model_dt[, .(id, run, event_index, rpe_rl, choice_entropy)],
  by = c("id", "run", "event_index"),
  all.x = FALSE
)




0.5 Denoise motion-contaminated runs with non-aggressive ICA-AROMA
Beginning in fMRIPrep >= 23.1, spatial-ICA motion denoising moved out of fMRIPrep into standalone fMRIPost-AROMA, which writes each run’s full MELODIC time-course matrix (*_desc-melodic_mixing.tsv) and component labels (*_desc-aroma_metrics.tsv; or *_desc-MELODIC_mixing.tsv + *_AROMAnoiseICs.csv in legacy fMRIPrep <= 23.0) while leaving un-denoised *_desc-preproc_bold.nii.gz on disk so downstream pipelines control spatial smoothing and nuisance regression order.
When incorporating ICA-AROMA into task-fMRI deconvolution, two seemingly natural shortcuts introduce substantial distortion:

Pitfall 1 — Aggressive AROMA strips task-correlated neural signal (Pruim et al., 2015): In decision and reinforcement-learning tasks, participants often move slightly in sync with salient task events—pressing a button on choice trials or flinching at unexpected feedback. Appending 30–60 rejected aroma_motion_* columns directly into $nuisance (or projecting rejected components out of BOLD orthogonally without the accepted components) removes all variance shared between head motion and convolved task activity, attenuating downstream trial slopes while consuming dozens of degrees of freedom per run. Non-aggressive ICA-AROMA avoids this by fitting both accepted neural components and rejected motion components jointly to each voxel and subtracting only the unique contribution assigned to the rejected motion components.
Pitfall 2 — Uncleaned physiological confounds re-inject removed motion into BOLD (Lindquist et al., 2019): Even after BOLD is properly cleaned via non-aggressive AROMA, tissue nuisance time series in *_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv (such as csf and white_matter) were extracted from the un-denoised scan and still carry strong motion contamination. If raw, uncleaned csf/white_matter columns are passed into Steps 1–2 (nuisance_mode = "joint"), regressing AROMA-cleaned BOLD onto motion-contaminated confounds projects those removed motion artifacts right back into the BOLD residuals and deconvolved neural series, re-inflating observation noise_sd and trial standard errors.

MEDuSA handles both requirements automatically—either in a single read_fmriprep_subject() call or step by step via read_fmriprep_aroma() and apply_aroma():

# Option A: Turnkey subject ingestion with non-aggressive ICA-AROMA + matched CSF/WM cleaning
# (auto-discovers co-located or sibling `derivatives/fmripost-aroma/` files even when
# fMRIPost-AROMA omits `space-*` entities from mixing/metrics filenames)
sub01_aroma <- read_fmriprep_subject(
  fmriprep_dir             = "/path/to/derivatives/fmriprep",
  bids_dir                 = "/path/to/bids",
  aroma_dir                = "/path/to/derivatives/fmripost-aroma", # optional; auto-discovered when sibling
  sub                      = "01",
  task                     = "learn",
  space                    = "MNI152NLin6Asym",
  atlas                    = "/path/to/schaefer_200_mni6.nii.gz",
  aroma                    = "nonaggressive",
  aroma_clean_nuisance     = TRUE,      # projects identical AROMA operator out of $nuisance
  strategy                 = "csf_wm",  # physiological pairing without redundant 24p motion terms
  fd_threshold             = 0.5,
  include_non_steady_state = TRUE
)
print(sub01_aroma$aroma$summary)

# Option B: Modular assembly on custom NIfTI + confound inputs
aroma      <- read_fmriprep_aroma(mixing_files, bold = ts)
ts_clean   <- apply_aroma(ts, aroma, mode = "nonaggressive")
conf_clean <- read_fmriprep_confounds(
  confound_files, bold = ts_clean, strategy = "csf_wm",
  aroma = aroma, fd_threshold = 0.5     # computes physical FD first, then AROMA-cleans csf/wm
)

Figure 3.4 and Table 3.5 compare all four regimes end to end across Steps 0–3 on a three-run simulated BIDS + fMRIPrep + fMRIPost-AROMA participant (true noise_sd = 0.030, true lag-0 RPE slope = 0.650, 2 accepted neural ICs + 6 rejected motion ICs per run, including one feedback-locked motion component correlated \(r \approx 0.62\) with convolved RPE):

Without AROMA (aroma = "none", csf_wm only): Unremoved motion inflates Step 2 noise_sd more than three-fold (0.097 vs. 0.030) and biases the lag-0 RPE slope upward to 1.018.
Aggressive AROMA (aroma = "aggressive"): Orthogonal removal of the task-correlated motion IC strips shared task variance, attenuating the lag-0 RPE slope by 40% down to 0.393.
Non-aggressive AROMA + uncleaned csf_wm (aroma_clean_nuisance = FALSE): Regressing raw motion-contaminated csf/white_matter columns out of AROMA-cleaned BOLD re-injects pure motion ICs (R2_mot = 0.20 vs. 0.01), inflating Step 2 noise_sd back up to 0.092 and nearly tripling the lag-0 standard error (0.065 vs. 0.024).
Non-aggressive AROMA + matched csf_wm (aroma = "nonaggressive", aroma_clean_nuisance = TRUE): Recovers the generating observation noise (0.030 vs. 0.030) and an unbiased, high-precision lag-0 RPE slope (0.632, \(\text{SE} = 0.024\)).







Figure 3.4: End-to-end impact of ICA-AROMA mode and matched nuisance orthogonalization across Steps 0–3 (aroma_denoising_metrics.csv, true observation noise_sd = 0.030, true lag-0 feedback RPE slope = 0.650): (A) Step 3 recovered peri-event RPE trajectory (-2 to +4 s) under task-correlated head motion; (B) Step 2 observation noise_sd and post-nuisance pure-motion variance (\(R^2_{\text{mot}}\)), showing artifact re-injection when csf_wm confounds are left uncleaned (aroma_clean_nuisance = FALSE; Lindquist et al., 2019); (C) Step 3 lag-0 RPE slope and 95% confidence interval.

Choice point — Pairing aroma, strategy, frame censoring, and BrainGnomes provenance:

Recommended strategy with AROMA: Pair aroma = "nonaggressive" (or aroma = "auto" in mixed cohorts where only some subjects/sessions have AROMA outputs) with strategy = "csf_wm" (mean csf + white_matter; Parkes et al., 2018) or "csf_wm_8p" (adding temporal derivatives and quadratics of csf/white_matter). Avoid pairing AROMA with "24p" or "36p" expansion, whose realignment derivatives largely duplicate the motion subspace already removed by ICA-AROMA while consuming extra degrees of freedom.
Combining AROMA with FD censoring (and fast-TR respiratory filtering): Linear spatial ICA removes continuous head-motion and edge artifacts effectively, whereas abrupt multi-millimeter head jerks cause nonlinear slice-wise spin-history disruptions that no fixed spatial map captures completely. Because read_fmriprep_confounds() evaluates framewise_displacement (including optional fast-TR motion_bandstop_bpm = c(12, 20) notch filtering; Step 1 §1.5) before AROMA projection, keeping fd_threshold = 0.5 (or 0.3 with respiratory filtering) masks severe jerks in valid_rows while aroma_fit_valid = FALSE (default) fits the full-scan MELODIC time series on its native clock (aroma_fit_valid = TRUE optionally restricts the partial regression to valid_rows).
Automatic BrainGnomes provenance protection (desc = "postproc"): When ingesting postprocessed BrainGnomes streams, read_fmriprep_subject() inspects <bold>.json sidecar metadata (inspect_braingnomes_provenance()): it halts with a clear diagnostic if scrub_timepoints physically deleted volumes from the clock, skips duplicate AROMA projection with a warning if apply_aroma already ran upstream, and defaults strategy = "none" when confound_regression was already applied.

title: Step 0: Task Design and BIDS/fMRIPrep Ingestion
section: Recommended Settings
text:
Recommended Settings
For multi-run BIDS + fMRIPrep task studies, ingest each participant with read_fmriprep_subject() (looping over subject IDs in batch scripts) and inspect $confounds$summary (and $aroma$summary when using ICA-AROMA) before launching Step 1:

library(medusa)

# Standard fMRIPrep ingestion (or set aroma = "nonaggressive", strategy = "csf_wm"
# when fMRIPost-AROMA / legacy AROMA outputs are available; see Substep 0.5)
sub_obj <- read_fmriprep_subject(
  fmriprep_dir             = fmriprep_dir,
  bids_dir                 = bids_dir,
  sub                      = sub_id,
  task                     = "learn",
  space                    = "MNI152NLin2009cAsym",
  atlas                    = atlas_nii_path,
  mask_policy              = "intersect",
  aroma                    = "none",     # or "nonaggressive" (paired with strategy = "csf_wm")
  strategy                 = "24p",
  fd_threshold             = 0.5,        # or 0.3 with motion_bandstop_bpm = c(12, 20) for fast TR
  include_non_steady_state = TRUE
)

# Quick pre-flight check before Step 1
print(sub_obj$confounds$summary[, c("run", "n_volumes", "pct_censored", "n_non_steady_state", "mean_fd", "aroma_cleaned")])
table(sub_obj$events$run, sub_obj$events$condition)




Choice Point / Parameter
Recommended Setting
Why




Run structure & phase jitter
\(R \ge 3\) runs; jitter correlated adjacent phases across \(\ge 1.0\text{--}4.5\text{ s}\)
Gives Step 1 \(\ge 2\) independent training runs per cross-fitting fold and decouples adjacent neural phases in Step 3 (T, O) de-mixing.


mask_policy
"intersect"
Guarantees identical voxel/parcel membership across runs within each participant.


include_non_steady_state
TRUE (with intact 4D BOLD volumes)
Masks initial non_steady_state_outlier* dummy frames via valid_rows without shifting event timestamps relative to volume 1.


aroma & aroma_clean_nuisance
"nonaggressive" + TRUE + strategy = "csf_wm" when AROMA exists; "none" + "24p" otherwise
Removes motion ICs via partial regression without stripping task-correlated neural signal (Pruim et al., 2015) or re-injecting motion through uncleaned confounds (Lindquist et al., 2019).


fd_threshold & motion_bandstop_bpm
0.5 (standard TR) or 0.3 + motion_bandstop_bpm = c(12, 20) (fast TR \(\le 1\text{ s}\))
Censors genuine spin-history head jerks on an intact clock without scrubbing normal fast-TR breathing oscillations.


Missed / timeout trials
Retain in events as separate condition ("missed_feedback")
Models evoked salience/visual BOLD waves in Steps 1–2 and subtracts their collateral tail in Step 3 rather than inflating residual noise.


External trial-table joins
Merge on c("id", "run", "event_index") (or trial_number stored in events.tsv)
Prevents silent row shifts between panel$trial (1..m_valid) and task trial_number (1..N_total) when missed trials occur.

title: Step 0: Task Design and BIDS/fMRIPrep Ingestion
section: Practical Considerations, Pre-Flight QC Checklist, and Handoff to Step 1
text:
Practical Considerations, Pre-Flight QC Checklist, and Handoff to Step 1
Before passing sub_obj into estimate_crossrun_hrf() (Step 1):

Screen high-motion runs via $confounds$summary: Runs with pct_censored > 25–30% or very short contiguous unmasked segments (< 15–20 TRs) carry limited effective degrees of freedom; consider excluding severely corrupted individual runs before cross-fitting (retaining the participant if \(\ge 2\) clean runs remain, or falling back to single-run sub-block cross-fitting if 1 clean run remains).
Verify event onset units and bounds: Check range(sub_obj$events$onset) per run. Event times must be in seconds (never TR indices or milliseconds) and fall within \([0, (T_r - 1)\cdot\text{TR} + \text{time\_offset}]\). Events occurring within the final 4–6 seconds of a run before scanner shutoff have truncated causal HRF support and will be gated automatically by Step 3’s min_bold_coverage rule.
Verify condition tables across runs: Confirm via table(sub_obj$events$run, sub_obj$events$condition) that your target_condition appears with consistent spelling in every task run and that missed/timeout occurrences are labeled distinctly rather than dropped.
Scope handoff: Step 0 assembles validated, clock-aligned run matrices, spatial metadata, censoring masks, and complete event schedules without fitting any statistical parameters; out-of-sample HRF identification and \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise estimation begin in Step 1. For side-by-side visual examples of dummy-volume clock shifts and TR-index onset errors, see the Visual QC and Troubleshooting Gallery.



Mathematical & Simulation Details


Non-aggressive ICA-AROMA oblique projector (apply_aroma()): Let \(M \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r \times C}\) denote a run’s MELODIC mixing matrix partitioned into accepted components \(M_{\text{acc}}\) and rejected noise components \(M_{\text{rej}}\) (classification == "rejected"), and let \(\tilde{M} = M - \mathbf{1}\bar{m}_I^\top\) center each component on the fitting frame index set \(I\) (all frames when fit_valid = FALSE, or valid_rows when fit_valid = TRUE). apply_aroma(..., mode = "nonaggressive") solves the SVD-stabilized joint least-squares system \([\mathbf{1}, \tilde{M}][\hat{\mu}^\top; \hat{B}^\top]^\top = Y\) on \(I\) and subtracts only the centered rejected block across all \(T_r\) rows (preserving each voxel’s baseline mean \(\hat{\mu}\) while avoiding intercept shifts when component sample means are nonzero): \[
Y_{\text{nonagg}} = Y - \tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}\hat{B}_{\text{rej}} = P_{\text{aroma}} Y + (I - P_{\text{aroma}})\mathbf{1}\hat{\mu}^\top, \qquad P_{\text{aroma}} = I - \tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}\bigl[(\tilde{M}^\top \tilde{M})^+ \tilde{M}^\top\bigr]_{\text{rej}}.
\] When aroma_clean_nuisance = TRUE, read_fmriprep_confounds() applies the identical partial-regression operator \(P_{\text{aroma}}\) (followed by column re-centering and rank pruning) to the selected nuisance matrix \(Z_r\) so subsequent joint nuisance projection in Steps 1–2 operates strictly within the AROMA-cleaned subspace (Lindquist et al., 2019). By contrast, mode = "aggressive" applies the orthogonal projector \(I - \tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}(\tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}^\top \tilde{M}_{\text{rej}})^+ \tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}^\top\), which strips neural signal proportional to \(\tilde{M}_{\text{rej}}^\top x_{\text{task}} \neq 0\).
Part 1 (Design & Jitter Benchmarks): 20 Monte Carlo replications per condition (TR = 1.0 s, generating HRF peak 3.13 s, AR(1) \(\rho = 0.45\), 6 voxels in Target_Parcel with cue response \(1.2 + 0.45 c_i\) and feedback response \(0.9 + 0.60\,\text{RPE}_i\), 6 voxels in CueOnly_Parcel with cue response \(1.4 + 0.55 c_i\) and zero feedback response, \(\operatorname{Cor}(c_i, \text{RPE}_i) = 0.50\)). Run-structure comparisons hold total trials fixed at 60 (1×60, 2×30, 3×20, 4×15) with elevated noise on Run 1 (2.1× baseline SD) to reflect realistic inter-run scan quality variation.
Part 2 (On-Disk BIDS + fMRIPrep Ingestion): Builds a complete temporary BIDS + fMRIPrep subject directory (3 runs \(\times\) 240 4D NIfTI volumes, 3D masks, 2-parcel atlas.nii.gz, *_bold.json, *_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv with 4 non_steady_state_outlier columns and FD spikes, and *_events.tsv with 18 trials/run including 3 "missed_feedback" timeouts and "n/a" tokens) and ingests it live via read_fmriprep_subject().
Part 3 (On-Disk fMRIPost-AROMA Benchmark): Builds a 3-run BIDS + fMRIPrep (space-MNI152NLin6Asym_res-2) + sibling derivatives/fmripost-aroma/ (*_res-2_desc-melodic_mixing.tsv + *_desc-aroma_metrics.tsv, 2 accepted neural ICs + 6 rejected motion ICs including IC_3 correlated \(r = 0.62\) with convolved feedback RPE, shared physiological csf/white_matter noise contaminated by motion ICs, and AR(1) \(\sigma_{\text{obs}} = 0.030\), \(\rho = 0.45\)) subject and runs all four AROMA/confound regimes end to end through Steps 0–3.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
text:
Overview
In task fMRI, neural events are observed through a regional hemodynamic response function (HRF) that delays and smooths activity over 15–30 seconds, superimposed on serially correlated scanner and physiological noise. Both properties vary across brain territories and scans: sensory and subcortical regions often peak 1–2 seconds earlier than association cortex, while CSF-adjacent cortex exhibits stronger temporal autocorrelation than deep gray matter.
Step 1 (hrf_library() + estimate_crossrun_hrf()) estimates both components before deconvolution begins. To keep vascular shape estimation independent of the noise in the run being deconvolved, Step 1 uses leave-one-run-out cross-fitting: for each target run \(r\), it evaluates a physiological library of candidate HRFs using only the participant’s other runs (\(s \neq r\)), pools shape evidence across parcels or local cortical neighborhoods, and forms a regularized composite HRF that shrinks smoothly back toward a canonical reference where task signal is weak. Holding that cross-fitted HRF fixed, Step 1 then estimates run \(r\)’s own stationary \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise parameters on task-adjusted residuals.
library(medusa)

candidates <- hrf_library(tr = tr, preset = "medusa")
hrf_fit <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(
  bold           = bold,
  events         = events,
  tr             = tr,
  kernel_grid    = candidates,
  spatial_groups = parcel_ids,
  pooling        = "parcel",
  selection_mode = "soft_average"
)
The walkthrough below develops Step 1 across four substeps—from defining a single HRF basis curve (1.1), to cross-run candidate scoring (1.2), spatial evidence pooling (1.3), and post-selection \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise estimation (1.4)—highlighting the modeling choice at each stage.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 1

Estimate regional HRF timing, dispersion, and undershoot out of sample: Learn each target run’s vascular filter from training runs (\(s \neq r\)) so filter selection does not adapt to target-run noise.
Stabilize shape selection in low-SNR regions: Borrow evidence across parcels or geodesic gray-matter neighborhoods and shrink uncertain regions smoothly toward a canonical reference waveform.
Separate hemodynamic shape from serial noise autocorrelation: Fit run-specific \(\text{AR}(p)\) cascade parameters (\(\rho, \psi_1, \dots, \psi_4\)) after projecting out task responses and nuisance drift under the learned HRF.
Bundle forward timing and noise metadata for downstream steps: Record run clocks, observation masks, composite HRFs, and noise parameters in a single "crossrun_hrf" object carried forward into Steps 2–4.



Inputs: What Step 1 Receives and Why



Input
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




bold
Named list of numeric matrices (time × voxel), one per run, or a "medusa_nifti_ts" object from read_nifti_ts() / read_fmriprep_subject()
Keeping runs as separate list elements defines the leave-one-run-out folds (\(s \neq r\)), supports unequal run lengths, and prevents AR filters or HRF convolution tails from crossing run boundaries.


events
Named list of data.frames (onset, optional duration, condition) matching names(bold) (or a combined BIDS event table)
Event timestamps anchor neurovascular delay without needing behavioral or computational trial predictors, keeping downstream hypothesis variables unseen during HRF estimation.


tr & time_offset
Positive scalar TR (s); scalar or per-run acquisition start time (s)
Maps continuous event times in seconds onto discrete acquisition bins with sub-TR fractional interpolation.


kernel_grid
Numeric matrix (L_hrf × K) from hrf_library(), with column 1 as canonical reference
Pre-discretizes normalized candidate HRF waveforms onto the acquisition tr grid for batched evaluation and provides column 1 as a well-defined canonical baseline (fallback_kernel = 1L).


valid_rows & nuisance
Optional per-run logical masks (length == nrow(bold[[r]])) and numeric nuisance matrices (or a "medusa_confounds" object from read_fmriprep_confounds())
Marking censored frames with valid_rows = FALSE keeps every retained volume at its true physical timestamp while excluding high-motion frames from regression and likelihood scoring; nuisance removes motion and physiological drift alongside run intercepts and linear trends.


pooling, spatial_groups, & spatial_graph
pooling = c("voxel", "parcel", "graph"); optional parcel vector or "medusa_spatial_graph" from build_spatial_graph()
Specifies how out-of-sample HRF scores and REML noise parameters borrow strength across space—either within nominal parcels ("parcel"), across local 26-connected geodesic neighborhoods ("graph"), or at single voxels ("voxel").





Outputs: What Step 1 Produces and Why It Is Set Up That Way
estimate_crossrun_hrf() returns an S3 object of class "crossrun_hrf" whose elements map directly to their roles in Steps 2–4:



Output Component
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




selected_kernels
Named list (by target run) of L_hrf × voxel matrices
The realized HRFs used in Step 2. Storing a waveform matrix per run and voxel accommodates leave-one-run-out folds and represents continuous soft_average blends directly.


kernel_weights
Named list of K × voxel unit-sum weight matrices
Records the candidate weights combining columns of kernel_grid into selected_kernels, making composite HRFs transparent and reproducible.


selections
Named list of per-run data.frames (voxel, parcel, kernel_index, status, best_adjusted_partial_r2, selected_task_p, n_compatible_shapes, stability)
Summarizes out-of-sample task fit and compatibility diagnostics, and supplies out-of-sample task SNR metrics to Step 2 for automatic regularization tuning.


noise
Named list of per-run data.frames (voxel, group, rho, psi1–psi4, noise_sd, method, n_voxels)
Stores own-run stationary \(\text{AR}(p)\) cascade parameters separately per run so scanner autocorrelation can vary across scans while grouping matching (HRF, AR) units into shared linear-operator strata.


training_runs & signal_status
Named list of training-run ID vectors; per-run sufficiency summary
Documents cross-fitting provenance confirming which runs trained each target run’s HRF.


specification, spatial, voxel_map, & geometry
Stored events, nuisance, valid_rows, tr, resolved spatial graph, and NIfTI header geometry
Carries timing, censoring masks, neighborhood topology, and volumetric NIfTI coordinates automatically into Steps 2–5.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

1.1 Construct a physiological HRF candidate library
Consider a single brief neural impulse at \(t = 0\). In a vascular territory with impulse response \(h\), that event evokes a delayed, smooth BOLD deflection (Figure 4.2). Rather than estimating unconstrained free FIR parameters on noisy runs, hrf_library() spans plausible neurovascular shapes using a low-dimensional family of two-gamma waveforms varied across peak delay, width (dispersion), and post-stimulus undershoot depth (Figure 4.1), placing the standard canonical shape \((6\text{ s}, 1.0, 6)\) in column 1.






Figure 4.1: Three physiological dimensions spanned by hrf_library(..., preset = "medusa") under positive-lobe normalization: peak delay (left), width/dispersion (middle), and post-stimulus undershoot depth including zero-undershoot subcortical shapes (right).









Figure 4.2: Simulated neural event amplitudes (top) and resulting noisy BOLD signals in a fast-HRF versus slow-HRF parcel (bottom) from the Step 1 demonstration (TR = 0.65 s).



Because deconvolution recovers latent amplitudes relative to the scale of \(h\), candidate waveforms require a shared normalization rule. Under preset = "medusa", each candidate is normalized by its positive-lobe sum (\(\sum_{t: h_t > 0} h_t = 1\)). Compared with signed-sum normalization (\(\sum_t h_t = 1\)), positive-lobe normalization keeps the positive BOLD peak comparable between cortical waveforms with a venous undershoot and subcortical waveforms without one (undershoot_ratio = Inf), so regional undershoot differences do not rescale recovered neural amplitudes.
Choice point — Candidate library (preset): Use hrf_library(tr, preset = "medusa") (~44 evenly spaced 3D candidates spanning \(2.5\text{--}8.0\text{ s}\) delays) as the standard choice across cortical and subcortical studies. Switch to preset = "canonical_27" when restricting strictly to cortical delays (\(4.0\text{--}8.0\text{ s}\)) with a fixed undershoot ratio, or pass a 1-column library (candidates[, 1, drop = FALSE]) when benchmarking against a fixed canonical HRF under matched downstream settings.



1.2 Score candidate HRFs out of sample across runs
Suppose a participant completes \(R = 3\) task runs. If we selected the best-fitting HRF on Run 1 and immediately deconvolved Run 1 with that selected filter, random noise peaks in Run 1 would pull the filter toward themselves and inflate apparent trial effects. Instead, for each target run \(r\), estimate_crossrun_hrf() scores the \(K\) library candidates exclusively on training runs \(s \neq r\) (Figure 4.3). Consequently, even strong synthetic perturbations added to bold$run1 leave Run 1’s learned HRF weights unchanged to machine precision (0; Figure 4.4).






Figure 4.3: Cross-fitting separation in a three-run dataset: candidate HRF evidence for target run \(r\) comes strictly from runs \(s \neq r\), while serial noise parameters are refit on run \(r\) itself.









Figure 4.4: Invariance verification: adding strong synthetic oscillations to target Run 1 leaves its cross-fitted HRF candidate weights completely unchanged.



On each training run \(s \neq r\), MEDuSA whitens usable observations under a first-pass noise filter, projects out nuisance drift, and convolves the event schedule with candidate \(h_m\) to compute degree-of-freedom-adjusted partial \(R^2\) and an effective-DF \(F\)-test (selected_task_p; Figure 4.5).






Figure 4.5: Out-of-sample adjusted partial \(R^2\) surfaces for target Run 1 across the 27-candidate cortical slice (Fast truth: \(4.5\text{ s}, 0.9\); Slow truth: \(7.5\text{ s}, 1.1\); Null: pure \(\text{AR}(3)\) noise). Crosses mark generating parameters.



To build that training regression design without touching external behavioral covariates, MEDuSA needs an assumption about how event amplitudes behave across trials:

Under amplitude_model = "condition", all events of a given condition share one mean amplitude per run. When events evoke a consistent positive (or negative) deflection, this 1-column-per-condition design has maximal degrees of freedom and fast runtime.
Under amplitude_model = "trial", each event receives its own free amplitude (evaluating one condition freed at a time in multi-condition designs to avoid collinearity). This allows regions whose responses fluctuate symmetrically around zero—such as signed prediction-error signals whose mean response is zero—to express strong unsigned trial variance and identify their true HRF (Figure 4.6).







Figure 4.6: Zero-mean alternating trial amplitudes (amplitude_model = "condition" vs. "trial"): freeing trial amplitudes recovers the true \(7.5\text{ s}\) HRF where a condition-mean regressor averages out to zero.



Choice point — Training amplitude model (amplitude_model): Choose "condition" when task events evoke a reliable main-effect activation (e.g., visual cues, motor presses, block transitions). Choose "trial" whenever key regions may encode zero-mean signed fluctuations around baseline without a strong condition-mean offset.



1.3 Pool spatial evidence and form a composite HRF
At the single-voxel level, BOLD noise makes discrete candidate selection jittery across neighboring voxels (Figure 4.7). However, averaging raw BOLD time series across a parcel before scoring HRFs can cancel signals if sub-regions carry opposite task signs. Step 1 resolves this by pooling squared candidate evidence (precision-weighted adjusted partial \(R^2\) profiles) rather than raw time series: voxels with positive and negative task effects both produce positive \(R^2\) peaks at the same vascular delay and reinforce one another cleanly.






Figure 4.7: Voxelwise hard selection vs. parcel-pooled selection across heterogeneous voxel noise levels (0.012 to 0.055). Parcel pooling eliminates noisy single-voxel jumps.



Once pooled candidate scores are combined across training runs, Step 1 converts them into a target-run HRF waveform using two calibrated safeguards:

Task-evidence gating and Empirical-Bayes shrinkage: Regions without calibrated task support across training runs (Null in Figure 4.5 and v17 in Table 4.1) remain at the canonical reference (fallback_prespecified), while regions with moderate task support blend smoothly away from column 1 in proportion to departure confidence.
Soft composite averaging (selection_mode = "soft_average"): Instead of snapping discontinuously to a single grid column ("hard"), compatible candidates near the maximum receive smooth exponential weights scaled by cross-run score uncertainty (Boltzmann-style softmax weights)—interpolating vascular delays smoothly between discrete grid points (Figure 4.8).







Figure 4.8: Generating HRFs, hard-selected library nodes, and soft_average composite HRFs for the Fast and Slow parcels in Run 1.

Choice point — Spatial pooling (pooling) and composite rule (selection_mode): Pair selection_mode = "soft_average" with the spatial pooling mode matched to your representation:

pooling = "parcel" (with spatial_groups = parcel_ids) pools uniformly within predefined ROIs or homogeneous parcels. By default (min_parcel_voxels = 5L), parcels with fewer than 5 voxels retain the canonical fallback waveform to avoid noisy small-parcel switches; lower min_parcel_voxels explicitly (e.g., 2L or 3L) when targeting tiny subcortical nuclei at standard \(2\text{--}3\text{ mm}\) resolution.
pooling = "graph" (with parcel_boundary = "soft") on volumetric "medusa_nifti_ts" inputs builds a 26-connected in-mask geodesic lattice graph (build_spatial_graph()), pooling candidate profiles bilaterally across concordant gray-matter neighbors while stopping at sulcal CSF gaps and functional borders (see Spatial Graph Pooling).
pooling = "voxel" keeps single-voxel HRF fits for task-supported voxels (using parcel fallback on low-SNR voxels when an atlas is attached).




1.4 Refit run-specific \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise covariance on task-adjusted residuals
With each target run’s out-of-sample HRF \(\hat{h}^{(-r)}\) fixed, the final substep estimates run \(r\)’s own serial noise structure. Why wait until after HRF selection to estimate noise? Evoked BOLD waves evolve slowly over time; if residuals were formed under a misspecified canonical HRF (for example, applying a \(6.0\text{ s}\) kernel to a \(4.5\text{ s}\) Fast region), unmodeled task-timing mismatch would leak into the residuals and bias estimated autocorrelation upward.
Using \(\hat{h}^{(-r)}\), estimate_crossrun_hrf() projects out run intercept/trend, user nuisance columns, slow \(<1/128\text{ Hz}\) cosine drift terms (discrete cosine transform, DCT), free-trial responses, and HRF Taylor derivatives, then performs a two-pass pooled REML fit within contiguous unmasked segments of valid_rows[[r]]. Under noise_model = "ar1", this fits a stationary \(\text{AR}(1) \times \text{AR}(q)\) cascade \((1 - \rho B)(1 - \sum_{j=1}^q \psi_j B^j)\varepsilon_t = u_t\) (\(q \le 4\) selected adaptively for multiband sampling rates). As shown in Table 4.2 and Figure 4.9, refitting under the cross-fitted HRF recovers the true \(\text{AR}(3)\) cascade (\(\rho = 0.65, \psi_1 = 0.20, \psi_2 = -0.30\)) accurately across Fast, Slow, and Null parcels and whitens residual autocorrelation across all lags.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
section: Recommended Settings
text:
Recommended Settings
Putting all four substeps together on preprocessed NIfTI/fMRIPrep inputs:

library(medusa)

# 0. Stream preprocessed 4D NIfTI runs + fMRIPrep confounds & BIDS events
#    (or call read_fmriprep_subject() to bundle BOLD, masks, confounds, and events in one call)
ts <- read_nifti_ts(
  niftis = c(run1 = "sub01_run1.nii.gz", run2 = "sub01_run2.nii.gz", run3 = "sub01_run3.nii.gz"),
  mask   = "sub01_mask.nii.gz",
  atlas  = "schaefer200.nii.gz",
  tr     = tr
)
conf <- read_fmriprep_confounds(
  c("sub01_run1_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv",
    "sub01_run2_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv",
    "sub01_run3_desc-confounds_timeseries.tsv"),
  bold                 = ts,
  strategy             = "24p",
  fd_threshold         = 0.3,
  motion_bandstop_bpm  = c(12, 20),   # optional respiratory notch for fast TRs (TR <= 1.0 s)
  motion_filter_target = "fd_only"
)

# 1. Build the 3D physiological HRF manifold (~44 candidates, positive-lobe normalized)
candidates <- hrf_library(tr = ts$tr, preset = "medusa")

# 2. Cross-fit HRF shapes across runs and refit own-run AR(p) noise
hrf_fit <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(
  bold            = ts,
  events          = events,
  kernel_grid     = candidates,
  nuisance        = conf,
  pooling         = "graph",          # or "parcel" for uniform ROI pooling
  parcel_boundary = "soft",
  amplitude_model = "trial",
  noise_model     = "ar1",
  evidence        = "calibrated",
  selection_mode  = "soft_average",
  return_scores   = TRUE
)
