title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
section: Practical Considerations, Special Regimes, and Diagnostics
text:
Practical Considerations, Special Regimes, and Diagnostics

Single-run sessions and resting/baseline runs
When a participant has only a single task run (length(bold) == 1L), estimate_crossrun_hrf() automatically partitions usable observations into contiguous temporal sub-blocks (3 blocks when \(n_{\text{valid}} \ge 120\), 2 halves when \(40 \le n_{\text{valid}} < 120\)), scores candidates on each sub-block against the full causal event design, checks cross-block compatibility, and returns a single continuous HRF for the intact run. Runs with zero task events (such as resting-state scans) are also accepted and receive the canonical reference HRF alongside pure-nuisance \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise estimates.


Respiratory motion filtering for fast-TR censoring
In fast-TR multiband acquisitions (\(\text{TR} = 0.60\text{--}1.0\text{ s}\)), volume realignment resolves normal breathing (\(12\text{--}20\text{ breaths/min} \approx 0.20\text{--}0.33\text{ Hz}\)): chest-wall motion perturbs the \(B_0\) field along the phase-encoding axis and produces rhythmic \(0.25\text{--}0.45\text{ mm}\) fluctuations in raw Power (2012) framewise displacement (FD) even when the head is still (Fair et al., 2020; Gratton et al., 2020). Censoring raw fast-TR FD at \(0.30\text{ mm}\) can fragment valid_rows into short islands and reduce downstream trial retention, whereas simply raising fd_threshold to \(0.60\text{ mm}\) misses genuine sub-millimeter head jerks.
read_fmriprep_confounds() (and read_fmriprep_subject()) addresses this cleanly by applying zero-phase forward-backward frequency filtering (which removes oscillatory respiratory frequencies without shifting movement timing) to the 6 rigid-body realignment parameters before computing FD:

Choice of filter: motion_bandstop_bpm = c(12, 20) applies a narrowband band-stop (notch) filter that removes the breathing frequency band while preserving sharp step displacements on their original millimeter FD scale (pair with standard fd_threshold = 0.30). Alternatively, motion_lowpass_hz = 0.20 applies a smooth low-pass filter (Butterworth; pair with a proportionally lower fd_threshold = 0.15–0.20, following Gratton et al., 2020).
Keeping nuisance regressors unfiltered (motion_filter_target = "fd_only"): Because standard fMRIPrep BOLD volumes retain real respiratory \(B_0\) signal fluctuations, "fd_only" filters motion only for FD censoring while keeping unfiltered 24p/36p regressors in $nuisance so Steps 1–2 project respiratory \(B_0\) variance out of BOLD. (At slower TRs near the Nyquist boundary or on BrainGnomes files that already carry framewise_displacement_filtered, read_fmriprep_confounds() adapts or reuses filtered FD automatically.)
Combining with non-aggressive ICA-AROMA: When fMRIPost-AROMA or legacy ICA-AROMA mixing matrices are available, read_fmriprep_subject(..., aroma = "nonaggressive", strategy = "csf_wm", motion_bandstop_bpm = c(12, 20), fd_threshold = 0.3) computes respiratory-filtered FD on the physical 6-parameter motion estimates before AROMA partial regression so abrupt spin-history jerks are still masked via valid_rows, while avoiding 24/36-parameter collinearity with AROMA components; see Step 0 §0.5.

Figure 4.10, Figure 4.11, and Table 4.3 compare these options on the Step 1 multiband schedule (\(\text{TR} = 0.65\text{ s}\), \(\sim 16\text{ BPM}\) breathing plus two true head jerks of \(0.47\text{ mm}\) and \(1.18\text{ mm}\) in Run 1): both motion_bandstop_bpm = c(12, 20) and motion_lowpass_hz = 0.20 with motion_filter_target = "fd_only" retain 98–99% of volumes and 100% of trials while censoring both true head jerks and recovering the true 0.035 observation noise SD.






Figure 4.10: Fast-TR (\(\text{TR} = 0.65\text{ s}\)) respiratory motion filtering in Run 1 (48–122 s): (A) Unfiltered Power FD vs. zero-phase low-pass (0.20 Hz) and band-stop notch (12–20 BPM) FD across continuous \(\sim 16\text{ BPM}\) breathing and two genuine head jerks; (B) resulting clock-preserving valid_rows masks; (C) Step 2 recovered parcel activity across censoring regimes.









Figure 4.11: End-to-end Steps 1–3 pipeline impact across the five fast-TR censoring regimes (respiratory_fd_metrics.csv): retained acquisition volumes, Step 2 observation noise_sd recovery against generating truth (0.035), Step 3 trial retention after causal BOLD observability gating, and Step 3 lag-0 RPE slope standard error.

Diagnostic checklist and scope handoff to Step 2
Before passing hrf_fit to deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() (Step 2):

Check cross-fitting provenance: Confirm hrf_fit$training_runs lists non-target runs \(s \neq r\) and review hrf_fit$signal_status.
Plot realized waveforms (hrf_fit$selected_kernels): Under soft_average, selections$kernel_index identifies only the top-weight library column, whereas selected_kernels shows the actual composite HRF used in Step 2.
Check hrf_fit$noise for stationarity boundary hits: Widespread \(\hat{\rho} = 0.90\) estimates typically point to unmodeled scanner drift, uncensored motion spikes, or omitted task events (see Pair 1 in the Visual QC Gallery).
Scope boundary: Step 1 estimates the forward neurovascular filter and serial noise structure without modifying bold or evaluating behavioral trial hypotheses; continuous latent signal reconstruction begins in Step 2.



Mathematical Details & Reproduction


Cross-fitted evidence pooling: For candidate \(m\) on training run \(s \neq r\), whitened nuisance-orthogonalized BOLD \(y_{s,\perp}\) is regressed onto whitened candidate design \(X_{s,m,\perp}\) (rank \(d_{s,m}\) over \(m_s\) valid frames), yielding adjusted partial \(R^2_{s,m} = 1 - (1 - R^2_{s,m})\frac{m_s - p_Z}{m_s - p_Z - d_{s,m}}\). Across training runs, scores are weighted by effective degrees of freedom and checked for sign/peak compatibility (stability).
Soft-average shrinkage: Compatible candidates within score_margin receive Boltzmann weights \(w_m \propto \exp(\Delta R^2_m / \tau_{\text{SE}})\) blended with column 1 ((1 - \eta) e_1 + \eta w), where Empirical-Bayes shrinkage \(\eta \in [0, 1]\) approaches 0 as calibrated task \(F\)-statistics weaken toward the evidence_alpha threshold.
Exact gapped covariance: When valid_rows[[r]] masks interior frames, AR estimation restricts lag products strictly within contiguous unmasked runs of frames, while Step 2’s whitener \(W_r\) inverts the exact stationary Toeplitz submatrix \(\Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r]\) on retained timestamps \(I_r\) so multi-TR scrub gaps decay correlation by \(\gamma(|t_a - t_b|)\).
Zero-phase respiratory IIR filtering: For sampling rate \(f_s = 1/\text{TR}\) and stopband \([f_1, f_2] = \text{BPM}/60\) (\(f_0 = (f_1 + f_2)/2\), \(\Delta f = f_2 - f_1\), \(Q = f_0/\Delta f\), \(\omega_0 = 2\pi f_0/f_s\), \(\alpha = \sin\omega_0/(2Q)\)), read_fmriprep_confounds() designs the RBJ biquad notch transfer function \(H(z) = \frac{1 - 2\cos\omega_0 z^{-1} + z^{-2}}{(1 + \alpha) - 2\cos\omega_0 z^{-1} + (1 - \alpha)z^{-2}}\) (or bilinear-warped Butterworth poles for motion_lowpass_hz) and applies forward-backward Direct Form II Transposed filtering (filtfilt) with steady-state initial conditions and reflection padding to all 6 realignment parameters before computing Power (2012) FD.

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
text:
Overview
Given each run’s cross-fitted HRF and serial noise model from Step 1, Step 2 (deconvolve_crossrun_hrf()) reconstructs a continuous latent neural activity time series \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) on the original acquisition grid for every run and voxel. Because hemodynamic convolution smooths rapid neural fluctuations over 15–30 seconds, Step 2 solves a smoothness-penalized, \(\text{AR}(p)\)-whitened generalized least squares (GLS) inverse problem that recovers continuous neural dynamics while controlling high-frequency noise amplification.
The defining feature of MEDuSA’s Step 2 is its event-informed continuous architecture: the latent time series \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) itself is estimated continuously and unconstrained across the entire run, while an auxiliary event-informed GLS regression model calibrates the three quantities that govern inversion quality—(1) task-free observation-noise scaling (scaling = "noise_sd"), (2) neural-safe downweighting of transient scanner glitches (rwls = "auto"), and (3) SNR-stratified cross-run smoothing (lambda_mode = "auto").
library(medusa)

decon <- deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(
  bold        = bold,
  hrf_fit     = hrf_fit,
  scaling     = "noise_sd",
  penalty     = "sobolev",
  lambda_mode = "auto",
  rwls        = "auto"
)
The five substeps below develop this estimator from the basic continuous GLS inverse (2.1), through observation-noise standardization (2.2), adaptive glitch weighting (2.3), and SNR-stratified smoothing (2.4), culminating in a direct comparison between event-informed continuous GLS and blind deconvolution (2.5).

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 2

Recover continuous, unconstrained latent neural time courses: Estimate a time × voxel activity matrix \(\widehat{a}_r\) on the intact acquisition grid via prewhitened penalized GLS.
Standardize voxels and runs by pure observation noise: Estimate marginal observation-noise SD (\(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{marg}}\)) from task-projected GLS residuals (scaling = "noise_sd") so strong task activation does not compress recovered amplitudes.
Downweight transient non-task glitches safely: Attenuate isolated sub-scrubbing motion or RF spikes (rwls = "auto") while leaving genuine high-amplitude neural bursts unclipped.
Adapt regularization (lambda) to regional task SNR: Tune smoothness automatically across runs while grouping voxels from quiet background cortex up to strong task foci so noisier regions receive stronger smoothing (lambda_mode = "auto").
Carry exact linear operator metadata into Steps 3–6: Package activity together with scaling, task-free noise_innovations, frame_weights, and (HRF, AR, lambda) stratum keys so downstream steps de-mix overlapping epochs and propagate analytical standard errors.



Inputs: What Step 2 Receives and Why



Input
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




bold
Named list of time × voxel numeric matrices (or "medusa_nifti_ts" object) matching hrf_fit
Aligns each run’s observations 1-to-1 with its cross-fitted HRFs, valid_rows masks, and \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise parameters from Step 1.


hrf_fit
"crossrun_hrf" S3 object from estimate_crossrun_hrf()
Supplies out-of-sample selected_kernels, own-run noise cascades, out-of-sample task-SNR summaries (selections), events, nuisance, and valid_rows.


scaling
"noise_sd" (recommended), "zscore", "demean", "psc", or "none"
Standardizes each run and voxel before applying the roughness penalty so a shared \(\lambda\) carries a consistent bias–variance meaning across units of differing gain.


penalty
"sobolev" (recommended), "diff2", "diff1", "matern1", or "ridge"
Defines the symmetric positive semi-definite roughness matrix \(P\) governing how rapid fluctuations and baseline drift are penalized.


lambda, lambda_mode, & lambda_grid
NULL (auto-tuned), scalar, or length-\(V\) vector; lambda_mode = c("auto", "global", "stratified")
Controls smoothing strength, tuned automatically across runs over lambda_grid = 10^seq(-2, 1, length.out = 16) either globally or across monotone task-SNR tiers.


rwls, nuisance_mode, & observation_mask
rwls = "auto"; nuisance_mode = "ignore" or "joint"; observation_mask = "fit"
Govern transient glitch weighting, whether Step 1 nuisance columns are projected inside the inverse solve, and exclusion of valid_rows == FALSE frames from the data-fit term.





Outputs: What Step 2 Produces and Why It Is Set Up That Way
deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() returns an S3 "crossrun_decon" object designed to be passed intact into Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()):



Output Component
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




activity
Named list of n_time × n_voxels matrices (with tr, time_offset, and observation_mask attributes)
Retains the full acquisition grid—even across interior censored frames—so event timestamps and continuous diagnostics stay aligned to run seconds.


scaling
Named list of per-run data.frames (voxel, center, scale, noise_sd, lambda, status)
Records the pre-deconvolution divisor (scale), marginal observation-noise SD (noise_sd), and per-voxel penalty (lambda), enabling Step 3 to restore physical BOLD units (restore_scale = TRUE) and propagate exact SEs.


noise_innovations
Named list of n_valid_rows × n_voxels unit-norm task-free whitened residual matrices
Captures spatial error correlations after removing task-evoked BOLD variance, supporting unbiased parcel noise estimation in Step 4 and shared-error connectivity correction in Step 6.


frame_weights
Named list of length-n_valid_rows vectors in \((0, 1]\)
Preserves any adaptive rwls glitch weights so Step 3 reconstructs the exact weighted inverse operator and error covariance.


hrf_fit, settings, voxel_map, & geometry
Embedded crossrun_hrf + tuning tables (lambda_strata, lambda_tuning) + NIfTI metadata
Allows Steps 3–4 to rebuild stratum operators \(D_r\) on the fly without storing gigabytes of dense \(T_r \times m_r\) matrices in memory, and supports direct NIfTI export via write_nifti_ts().

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

2.1 Formulate the continuous prewhitened GLS deconvolution objective
Start with a single run \(r\) and voxel whose centered, standardized usable BOLD observations \(\tilde{y}_{r,o}\) follow the forward convolution model \(\tilde{y}_{r,o} = M_{r,o} H_r a_r + \varepsilon_{r,o}\), where \(H_r\) convolves latent neural activity \(a_r \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r}\) with Step 1’s HRF, \(M_{r,o}\) selects the \(m_r\) unmasked frames (valid_rows[[r]] == TRUE), and \(W_r\) whitens the \(\text{AR}(p)\) error covariance.
Because \(H_r\) acts as a low-pass filter, high-frequency oscillations in \(a_r\) leave convolved BOLD almost unchanged (Figure 5.1). Inverting \(H_r\) with virtually no penalty (lambda = 0.0001) therefore amplifies high-frequency noise dramatically, whereas an overly large penalty (lambda = 3) smooths away phasic peaks (Figure 5.2).






Figure 5.1: High-frequency forward ambiguity: adding rapid alternating neural fluctuations produces virtually identical convolved BOLD.









Figure 5.2: Effect of varying lambda (0.0001, 0.03, 3) on the same noisy BOLD series under the sobolev penalty.



Step 2 estimates \(\widehat{a}_r\) by minimizing the penalized prewhitened GLS objective across the full \(T_r\)-sample run grid: \[
\widehat{a}_r = \arg\min_{a \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r}} \left\| W_r \bigl(\tilde{y}_{r,o} - M_{r,o} H_r a\bigr) \right\|_2^2 + \lambda a^\top P a.
\] Notice that no event timestamps appear inside \(P\) or restrict \(a\): spontaneous inter-trial fluctuations, sustained deliberation plateaus, and brief phasic bursts can occur anywhere on the acquisition clock, and the solution is a linear map \(\widehat{a}_r = D_r \tilde{y}_{r,o}\).






Figure 5.3: Comparison of all five penalty families (ridge, diff1, diff2, matern1, sobolev) on the same run.

Choice point — Roughness penalty (penalty) and nuisance projection (nuisance_mode):

Penalty geometry: penalty = "sobolev" combines a gentle first-difference slope penalty with a strong second-difference curvature penalty (\(0.10 D_1^\top D_1 + 0.90 D_2^\top D_2\), a discrete Sobolev norm) and is recommended as the standard choice. Pure second-difference curvature smoothing ("diff2") leaves global linear ramps unpenalized, whereas pure "ridge" shrinks each time point toward zero without sharing smoothness across neighboring TRs; "sobolev" (and "matern1") gently anchors baseline drift while keeping phasic transitions crisp (Figure 5.3, Table 5.1).
Nuisance handling: Use nuisance_mode = "ignore" when input BOLD has already been detrended or confound-regressed upstream, or switch to nuisance_mode = "joint" when drift and motion regressors passed via hrf_fit remain present in bold and should be projected out inside the whitened inverse (Figure 5.4, top).







Figure 5.4: Joint vs. ignored nuisance handling when drift remains in bold (top) and bridging a masked valid_rows = FALSE artifact window 70–80 s under observation_mask = "fit" (bottom).






2.2 Standardize runs using event-informed marginal noise scaling
Before solving the penalized GLS objective across thousands of voxels, each run and voxel is centered and divided by a reference scale so \(\lambda\) acts comparably everywhere. A common convention in blind deconvolution is whole-run z-scoring (scaling = "zscore"), which divides by total temporal \(\text{SD}(y)\). However, in a strongly task-responsive voxel, \(\text{SD}(y)\) combines background noise and task-evoked BOLD variance—inflating the denominator and compressing recovered neural slopes relative to quieter voxels.
To separate observation noise from task signal without constraining \(\widehat{a}_r\), scaling = "noise_sd" fits an auxiliary event-informed GLS regression containing run drift, user nuisance columns, free per-trial convolved event regressors under Step 1’s HRF, and 1st/2nd HRF Taylor derivatives (absorbing trial-to-trial latency jitter). From the outlier-trimmed, leverage-adjusted residuals of this projection (Winsorized GLS residuals), MEDuSA extracts two quantities:

Uncontaminated marginal observation-noise SD (\(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{marg}}\)): Tracks true background noise uniformly across high-gain, moderate-gain, and null voxels (Figure 5.5 and Table 5.2).
Task-free whitened noise_innovations: Orthonormalized residual series carried forward to measure pure spatial noise correlations in Steps 4 and 6.







Figure 5.5: Comparison of whole-run BOLD SD (zscore), event-informed GLS noise_sd, and true generating observation-noise SD across 8 voxels of varying task gain.

Choice point — Pre-deconvolution scaling (scaling): Specify scaling = "noise_sd" (and pair with restore_scale = TRUE in Step 3 when combining runs onto physical BOLD units). Reserve "zscore" or "demean" for sensitivity comparisons against legacy workflows.



2.3 Guard against transient scanner glitches without clipping neural bursts
Even after binary motion censoring (valid_rows), fMRI runs occasionally contain sub-threshold micro-movements or RF spikes (\(\text{FD} \approx 0.2\text{--}0.3\text{ mm}\)) that would cause oscillatory ringing in an unweighted linear inverse. At the same time, naive outlier downweighting risks mistaking an unusually large, genuine neural response (such as a surprise prediction-error burst) for an artifact.
Under rwls = "auto", Step 2 measures cross-voxel residual energy orthogonal to the modeled [trial HRF, dHRF/dt] task subspace and widens frame tolerance in proportion to the convolved task envelope:

On clean Gaussian runs, a whole-brain tail-energy test calibrated for spatially correlated voxels (via the Liu–Tang–Zhang, 2009 moment approximation) keeps all weights at \(w_t = 1\) so standard unweighted GLS is preserved exactly.
When genuine non-task glitches occur, isolated 1–2 TR spikes are absorbed by adding transient observation-noise variance at only those flagged volumes (\(\Sigma_{\text{AR}} + \operatorname{diag}(\delta^2)\), solved via low-rank Woodbury Sparse Bayesian Learning updates so high-\(\rho\) AR filters do not smear a single-volume spike into neighboring frames), while multi-TR physiological bursts receive smooth innovation-space downweighting—all while keeping \(w_t = 1\) across heavy task-evoked neural bursts.

Choice point — Glitch downweighting (rwls): Leave rwls = "auto" enabled for empirical data; set rwls = "none" only when testing exact unweighted operator identities in synthetic benchmarks.



2.4 Tune smoothing strength (lambda) across task-SNR strata
Choosing \(\lambda\) by ordinary observation-space out-of-sample prediction error—approximated via generalized cross-validation (GCV)—targets BOLD curve fitting rather than downstream trial estimation, and averaging GCV across thousands of task-silent voxels pulls a single global penalty toward oversmoothing.
When lambda = NULL, Step 2 pools prewhitened GCV across usable runs alongside Stage-3 gain-restored trial level/contrast variance and modulation transfer weighted by Step 1’s out-of-sample task SNR (Figure 5.6). Furthermore, on volumetric maps where focal task regions coexist with quiet background cortex, lambda_mode = "auto" stratifies voxels by out-of-sample task SNR and enforces that smoothing never increases as task signal strengthens:

Cross-run false-discovery gate: Combines Step 1 per-run task \(p\)-values across runs (Fisher combination + Benjamini–Hochberg FDR); if no voxels pass \(q \le 0.10\) (e.g., pure-null maps), "auto" collapses safely to one global penalty.
Monotone task-SNR tiers: When focal signal is present, voxels are grouped into a quiet background tier (\(q > 0.20\), graph-stabilized \(R^2 < 0.025\)) and ascending active task-\(R^2\) quantiles (max_lambda_strata = 4L), enforcing \(\lambda_{\text{quiet}} \ge \lambda_{\text{low-SNR}} \ge \dots \ge \lambda_{\text{high-SNR}}\) via a monotone ordering constraint (weighted pool-adjacent-violators, PAVA; see Spatial Graph Pooling).







Figure 5.6: Comparison of raw prewhitened GCV versus MEDuSA’s adaptive task-weighted criterion (top) and the underlying gain-restored level and contrast variance proxies (bottom).



Choice point — Smoothing mode (lambda & lambda_mode): Keep lambda = NULL and lambda_mode = "auto" as the standard choice. Use lambda_mode = "global" (or a fixed scalar lambda) only when holding an identical roughness penalty constant across every voxel in a comparison.



2.5 Why event-informed calibration improves over blind deconvolution
Stepping back across Substeps 2.1–2.4 clarifies how MEDuSA relates to both blind deconvolution (deconvolve_nlreg() / Bush & Cisler, 2013; deconvolve_reglin()) and standard task GLMs:

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
section: Practical Considerations: Operator Resolution, Boundaries, and Handoff to Step 3
text:
Practical Considerations: Operator Resolution, Boundaries, and Handoff to Step 3

Why continuous activity has finite resolution—and why Step 3 handles de-mixing: Under any positive \(\lambda > 0\), the continuous resolution matrix \(R_r = D_r M_{r,o} H_r\) attenuates isolated impulse height (\(R_{tt} < 1\)) and spreads energy smoothly across neighboring TRs and closely spaced events (Figure 5.8, Figure 5.9). Simply dividing \(\widehat{a}_r\) pointwise by \(R_{tt}\) would amplify side-lobe noise everywhere (Figure 5.8, bottom). Instead, diagnose_crossrun_recovery(decon) audits self-gain and neighbor cross-talk on your event schedule, and passing the full decon object to Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()) performs matrix de-mixing and gain restoration specifically at the trial epochs of interest.
Bridging censored gaps (observation_mask = "fit"): Across masked frames (70–80 s in Figure 5.4, bottom), the smoothness penalty interpolates cleanly from surrounding unmasked BOLD without letting artifacts corrupt adjacent trials; Step 3 will automatically check causal BOLD support (obs_frac_tau >= 0.20) so deeply masked events are flagged as NA rather than treated as observed data.
Run-end boundaries (tail_padding = 0L) and HRF timing (Figure 5.10): Appending synthetic zero BOLD frames after the end of a run (tail_padding > 0) pulls genuine late-run activity downward, while a 2-second HRF delay misspecification shifts recovered peaks in the opposite direction—confirming the value of tail_padding = 0L and Step 1’s cross-run HRF estimation. For side-by-side visual diagnostics of over-smoothing gain collapse and uncensored motion-spike ringing, see the Visual QC and Troubleshooting Gallery.







Figure 5.8: Impulse resolution curves \(R_{:,91}\) at weak, moderate, and strong \(\lambda\): raw recovery (top) versus scalar division by diagonal gain (bottom).









Figure 5.9: Event-by-event normalized excess cross-talk matrix from diagnose_crossrun_recovery() across 15 Run 1 events.









Figure 5.10: Sensitivity to run-end zero padding (tail_padding = 33L vs. 0L, top) and a 2-second HRF delay misspecification (bottom).





Mathematical Reference & Reproduction

Let \(I_r \subset \{1, \dots, T_r\}\) index the \(m_r\) valid frames (valid_rows[[r]] == TRUE), \(M_{r,o}\) select rows \(I_r\), \(H_r \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r \times T_r}\) be the causal Toeplitz HRF convolution matrix for stratum kernel \(h\), and \(Z_{r,o}\) be the active nuisance basis ([1, trend, nuisance] under nuisance_mode = "joint", empty under "ignore").

Exact gapped whitening & Woodbury SBL: \(W_r = L_r^{-1}\) is the inverse Cholesky factor of the stationary \(\text{AR}(p)\) correlation submatrix \(\Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r]\). Under rwls_space = "woodbury" with transient variances \(\delta_t^2 = (1 - w_t)/w_t\) on flagged frames \(S\), MEDuSA whitens against \(\Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r] + \operatorname{diag}(\delta^2)\) via a rank-\(|S|\) Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury update in \(O(m_r |S|)\) operations. Orthogonalizing \(Q_Z = \operatorname{orth}(W_r Z_{r,o})\) projects out nuisance terms jointly via \(\tilde{W}_r = (I - Q_Z Q_Z^\top) W_r\).
Linear inverse operator: With \(A_r = \tilde{W}_r M_{r,o} H_r\) and penalty \(P_{\lambda} = \lambda P + \epsilon_{\text{ridge}} I_{T_r}\), the frozen inverse operator is \[
D_r = \bigl(A_r^\top A_r + P_{\lambda}\bigr)^{-1} A_r^\top \tilde{W}_r \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r \times m_r},
\] evaluated across voxel batches via Cholesky solves in C++ (backend = "cpp", agreeing with backend = "r" to 2.71e-14), with restore_scale reproducing demean units to 3.11e-15. Internal R helpers implementing Substeps 2.2–2.4 in R/crossrun_hrf.R are hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd(), hrf_estimate_rwls_weights(), hrf_tune_decon_lambda(), hrf_tune_decon_lambda_stratified(), and hrf_pava_nonincreasing().

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation
text:
Overview
Step 2 produces a continuous deconvolved time series \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) on the acquisition grid, whereas cognitive hypotheses typically concern event-locked trial responses—for example, neural activity across lags \(-2\text{ s}\) to \(+4\text{ s}\) around feedback onset, or sustained deliberation activity across variable reaction times. Because regularized deconvolution smooths slightly across time, simply slicing \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) at event timestamps yields readouts that combine the target trial’s signal with regularization attenuation and spillover from nearby cues or adjacent trials.
Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()) converts continuous deconvolved activity into conditionally unbiased, additive-error trial readouts accompanied by exact propagated measurement uncertainties. Passing the forward event schedule through Step 2’s frozen linear operator \(D_r\), it samples requested peri-event lags via smooth local time-averaging (symmetric kernel quadrature), subtracts spillover from non-target events, inverts target-to-target mixing to restore amplitude gain, and propagates \(\text{AR}(p)\) observation noise through the composite operator to deliver per-trial standard errors (se_demixed), Empirical-Bayes precision weights, and optional within-run decorrelated (*_whitened) variables.
library(medusa)

epochs <- decon_epoch_regression(
  deconvolution       = decon,
  covariates          = covariates,
  events              = events,
  target_condition    = "feedback",
  lags                = seq(-2, 4, by = 1),
  restore_scale       = TRUE,
  whiten_panel        = TRUE,
  return_panel        = TRUE
)
Following the same measurement-model progression used in two-step multilevel inference (Vig & Hallquist, 2026), the four substeps below move from defining the event source and readout kernel (3.1), to writing the epoch measurement model and removing non-target bleed (3.2), inverting target mixing onto an additive-error scale (3.3), and propagating trial error covariances and precision weights (3.4).

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 3

Sample peri-event lag trajectories with explicit duration semantics: Read out continuous activity around each target event across requested lags, supporting brief impulses, fixed windows, and RT-matched sustained intervals ("rate" vs. "integral").
Remove non-target spillover and target-to-target mixing: Use the Step 2 operator \(D_r H_r\) to subtract interfering event bleed (demix_other_events) and invert target cross-talk (demix_target_trials) while matching centered predictors through the post-demixing operator \(M_{\text{post}}\).
Propagate observation-noise covariance analytically to every trial: Compute per-trial measurement standard errors (se_demixed) and lag-1 trial error correlations (error_ac1) directly from the composite linear operator without resampling.
Construct stabilized trial precision weights and optional decorrelated panels: Combine propagated measurement error with Empirical-Bayes biological trial variance (\(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\), stabilized across functionally concordant cortical neighbors on NIfTI maps via "graph_eb") to form cohort-ready weights and decorrelated trial columns.



Inputs: What Step 3 Receives and Why



Input
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




deconvolution
"crossrun_decon" S3 object from deconvolve_crossrun_hrf()
Carries activity together with hrf_fit, scaling, noise_innovations, and frame_weights so Step 3 reconstructs the exact stratum inverse operator \(D_r\) and noise covariance \(\Sigma_r\).


events & target_condition
Run-named list of event data.frames (inherited from hrf_fit by default); character scalar naming target events
Retaining all task events in events while naming target_condition identifies both the target trials to read out and the non-target events (cues, motor responses) whose spillover into target windows should be subtracted.


covariates
NULL (covariate-agnostic panel mode), or numeric matrix/data.frame/formula/column names matching target events
Passing covariates = NULL produces a general-purpose de-mixed panel reusable across many downstream Step 5–6 models; supplying covariates adds within-participant regression tables (coefficients) and paired *_whitened predictor columns.


lags & readout_kernel
Numeric vector of lag offsets in seconds (e.g., seq(-2, 4, by = 1)); "triangle", "linear", "boxcar", or "gaussian"
Evaluates event-locked readouts at arbitrary offsets without resampling BOLD, shifting both the readout window and modeled target source to \(t_i + \tau\).


source_model, trial_durations, & duration_scale
"impulse", "window", or "duration"; optional target durations (s); "rate" or "integral"
Specifies the latent neural waveform represented by each trial amplitude so variable reaction times can be modeled either as firing height ("rate") or time-integrated activity ("integral").


demix_other_events, demix_target_trials, & demix_within_trial
Logical flags + demix_ridge (0.05) & within_trial_ridge (0.06)
Separately control non-target subtraction, trial-to-trial target de-mixing, and optional single-subject cross-lag sharpening.


tau2_shrinkage & spatial_graph
tau2_shrinkage = c("auto", "graph_eb", "eb", "none"); optional "medusa_spatial_graph"
Stabilizes biological trial variance \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) and sandwich residual scales without smoothing trial slopes ("auto" selects bilateral "graph_eb" automatically on voxelwise NIfTI maps).





Outputs: What Step 3 Produces and Why It Is Set Up That Way



Output Component
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




panel
Tidy data.table keyed by run, trial, event_index, onset, evt_time, and voxel/parcel
Primary trial table for Steps 5–6. Stores both trial (1..\(m\) target counter) and event_index (row in events[[r]]) alongside decon_raw, decon_demixed, se_demixed, precision_weight, precision_weight_cohort, error_ac1, tau2_bio, decon_eb, and optional *_whitened columns.


coefficients & summary
Per-unit × lag × term data.frame (beta_raw, beta_corrected, beta_unweighted, beta_weighted, beta_gls, SEs, moderated df, \(t\), \(p\)); lag summary
Places uncorrected (beta_raw) and de-mixed/GLS slopes side by side under the same Step 2 inverse so the impact of operator de-mixing and precision weighting is transparent.


lag_resolution & lag_error_cor
Per-unit \(L \times L\) cross-lag resolution and trial error correlation matrices
Carried forward so medusa_multilag_infer() (Step 5) can apply group-level spectral deblurring, P-spline smoothing, and simultaneous bands across lags.


unit_error_cor & parcel_weights
Empirical-Bayes shrunk unit-by-unit error correlation matrix; voxel weights (when aggregate_by_parcel = TRUE)
Supplies task-free cross-region error correlations (shared_noise_loading in panel) for Step 6 connectivity disattenuation.

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

3.1 Define the event-locked neural source and kernel readout
Consider reading out continuous deconvolved activity \(\widehat{a}_r\) around target event \(i\) at timestamp \(t_i + \tau\). Because \(t_i + \tau\) rarely lands on an exact integer TR, Step 3 forms a row-normalized weight vector \(S_\tau[i, :]\) over nearby acquisition samples (Figure 6.1). While "linear" uses 2-point bracket interpolation, "triangle" (width \(1.5 \times \text{TR}\)) averages 9 symmetrically weighted sub-interval points across adjacent samples (symmetric kernel quadrature)—respecting sub-TR jitter while attenuating high-frequency inverse noise.






Figure 6.1: Acquisition-grid readout weights around an off-grid target timestamp (20.35 s, TR = 1 s) for "linear", "boxcar", "triangle", and "gaussian" kernels.



Alongside the readout window, Step 3 asks a substantive question about source duration: what neural time course does trial \(i\)’s amplitude \(\theta_i\) multiply? Suppose deliberation neural activity stays at a constant firing rate (1.8 units/s) across trials whose reaction times vary from 0.4 to 2.8 s. Because longer deliberation produces larger integrated BOLD deflections, different source models estimate distinct quantities (Figure 6.2):

source_model = "impulse" treats every trial as a brief unit impulse, attributing longer-duration BOLD accumulation to higher amplitude and producing a positive slope against RT (beta = 1.392).
source_model = "duration", duration_scale = "rate" matches both the forward boxcar and midpoint readout window to each trial’s duration [onset + lag, onset + lag + RT], recovering a flat firing-rate slope invariant to RT (beta = 0.015, near true 0.00).
source_model = "duration", duration_scale = "integral" normalizes each forward boxcar to unit area, explicitly estimating time-integrated neural activity (1.8 × duration, recovering slope 1.806 vs. true 1.800).







Figure 6.2: Same simulated constant-rate variable-duration BOLD series analyzed under three source specifications: impulse height (left), duration-matched rate (middle), and duration-integrated neural mass (right).



Choice point — Source model (source_model & duration_scale) and readout_kernel: Pair readout_kernel = "triangle" (readout_width = 1.5 * tr) with source_model = "impulse" for brief phasic events (e.g., feedback delivery). For variable-duration epochs (e.g., choice deliberation), pass source_model = "duration" with trial_durations = rt and choose duration_scale = "rate" to test neural intensity per unit time or "integral" to test cumulative activity.



3.2 Write the epoch measurement model and subtract non-target spillover
Now consider a cue–feedback paradigm where each Cue precedes Feedback by 1–3 seconds. Let \(\theta_T\) denote true target (Feedback) trial amplitudes with forward BOLD design \(G_\tau\), and \(\theta_O\) denote non-target (Cue) amplitudes with forward design \(G_O\). Applying readout \(S_\tau\) to deconvolved activity \(\widehat{a}_r = D_r y_r\) yields a raw trial readout whose conditional expectation contains two distinct terms:
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[\hat{z}_{\text{raw},\tau} \mid \theta_T, \theta_O\bigr]
= \underbrace{(S_\tau D_r G_\tau)\,\theta_T}_{\text{attenuated & mixed targets}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{(S_\tau D_r G_O)\,\theta_O}_{\text{non-target spillover}}.
\]
In simulate_step3.R, a Cue_only voxel responds to cues but has zero true feedback slope (\(\beta = 0\)), while reaction time links cue–feedback spacing to covariate x. Because of the second term above, raw feedback readouts in Cue_only pick up spurious cue spillover (beta_raw = -0.115; Table 6.1).
Enabling demix_other_events = TRUE estimates and subtracts the operator-predicted non-target contribution \((S_\tau D_r G_O) L_{\text{other}} y_r\), forming cleaned readout rows \(S_{\text{clean},\tau}\) before target amplitudes are evaluated (Figure 6.3).






Figure 6.3: Estimated feedback slopes in the null-feedback Cue_only voxel under constant cue amplitude (left) versus trial-varying cue amplitude correlated with x (right), comparing default condition-mean de-mixing (0.05) against joint trial-level de-mixing (0.02).



Choice point — Non-target subtraction (demix_other_events & demix_ridge): Keep demix_other_events = TRUE. At the default demix_ridge = 0.05, non-target subtraction uses a low-variance condition-mean operator (Cue_only slope reduced to -0.006 when cues have constant amplitude; Figure 6.3, left). When an upstream cue is itself strongly modulated trial-by-trial by the same behavioral predictor as your target event, lowering demix_ridge = 0.02 activates joint ridge-stabilized (2nd-order Tikhonov) (T, O) trial de-mixing—reducing correlated cue bleed from 0.488 to 0.074 in trade for modestly wider trial SEs (0.101 vs. 0.070; Figure 6.3, right).



3.3 Invert target-to-target mixing to recover an additive-error readout
After removing non-target spillover, the cleaned readout still reflects Step 2’s regularization blur across target trials, \(K_{\text{clean},\tau} = S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r G_\tau\). Writing this in the exact measurement-model form of Vig & Hallquist (2026) by adding and subtracting \(\theta_T\):
\[
S_{\text{clean},\tau}\widehat{a}_r
= \theta_T - (I - K_{\text{clean},\tau})\theta_T + S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r \varepsilon_r.
\]
Without inverting \(K_{\text{clean},\tau}\), diagonal shrinkage (\([K_{\text{clean},\tau}]_{ii} < 1\)) and neighbor overlap attenuate the true 0.70 feedback slope in Target down to beta_raw = 0.088 (Table 6.1). Enabling demix_target_trials = TRUE applies a ridge-stabilized inverse \(W_\tau\) on run-centered trials (Tikhonov regularization) with diagonal gain restoration \(\tilde{G}_\tau\) (decon_demixed), sharpening the 20×20 target resolution matrix toward the identity (Figure 6.5) and recovering the true 0.70 slope cleanly (Target = 0.705, Noisy_target = 0.673; Figure 6.4, Table 6.1). To ensure any small ridge stabilization in \(W_\tau\) at rapid ISIs never biases trial regressions, centered covariates are multiplied by the matched post-demixing resolution matrix \(M_{\text{post}}\) so predictor and response share identical coordinates.






Figure 6.4: Run-centered trial readouts vs. true injected feedback amplitudes in Target across raw readout, target-only de-mixing, and full cue + target de-mixing.









Figure 6.5: Target-by-target resolution matrix \(K_\tau\) before (Raw target response) and after (Corrected target response) Step 3 regularized de-mixing.

When multiple peri-event lags are requested, adjacent lags within the same trial also share deconvolution smoothness. Setting demix_within_trial = TRUE applies an additional ridge-stabilized cross-lag inverse within each participant, narrowing single-subject lag curves at the cost of larger per-lag SEs (Figure 6.6).






Figure 6.6: Effect of demix_within_trial = TRUE on estimated lag slopes (top) and conditional per-trial measurement SE (bottom).



Choice point — Target and cross-lag de-mixing: Keep demix_target_trials = TRUE in all operator analyses. Leave demix_within_trial = FALSE when passing outputs to medusa_multilag_infer() in Step 5 (which sharpens cross-lag blurring at the group level via spectral deblurring, where SNR is \(\sqrt{N}\) higher), and enable demix_within_trial = TRUE when inspecting descriptive single-subject curves or fitting single-lag models where sharper lag localization is desired.



3.4 Propagate observation-noise covariance and construct trial precision weights
Because every operation from centered BOLD to decon_demixed is captured in the composite linear map \(B_{r,\tau} = \tilde{G}_\tau W_\tau S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r\), the conditional sampling covariance of the de-mixed trial vector is known analytically: \[
\Omega_{r,\tau} = \operatorname{Cov}(e_{r,\tau} \mid B_{r,\tau}) \propto Q_m B_{r,\tau} \Sigma_{\text{obs},r} B_{r,\tau}^\top Q_m.
\] MEDuSA evaluates \(\Omega_{r,\tau}\) in fast factored form without forming dense \(T \times T\) covariance matrices, matching dense matrix multiplication to 6.07e-18 and reproducing 2,500-draw Monte Carlo noise SDs trial by trial (se_demixed; Figure 6.7).






Figure 6.7: Ratio of 2,500-draw Monte Carlo trial SD to analytical se_demixed across all 20 target trials in Run 1.



Trials near run boundaries, scrub gaps, or rapid event clusters naturally have larger measurement error \(s_{ri}^2 = \texttt{se\_demixed}_{ri}^2\). However, trials also vary due to genuine biological trial-to-trial variability \(\tau_{\text{bio}}^2\). Just as composite weights in multilevel moment estimation combine structural disturbance variance with measurement-error variance (Vig & Hallquist, 2026), Step 3 estimates \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) and forms Empirical-Bayes composite precision weights \(w_{ri} \propto (\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{ri}^2)^{-1}\) (precision_weight normalized to mean 1 within unit; precision_weight_cohort left unnormalized for multi-subject models), downweighting high-SE trials smoothly without letting a single low-SE trial dominate (Figure 6.8). When requested (whiten_panel = TRUE), Step 3 also applies a run-mean-preserving symmetric decorrelation transform that removes off-diagonal within-run trial error correlations while keeping each trial aligned as closely as possible to its original ordering (regularized zero-phase component analysis, or ZCA whitening; Figure 6.9).






Figure 6.8: Pure measurement-only inverse-variance weights (precision_weight_op) versus biological-variance-stabilized Empirical-Bayes weights (precision_weight).









Figure 6.9: Within-run total trial correlation matrix \(\Sigma_{\text{tot}}\) before and after symmetric trial decorrelation (whiten_panel = TRUE, regularized ZCA).



Choice point — Variance shrinkage (tau2_shrinkage), physical units (restore_scale), and trial decorrelation (whiten_panel):

Variance stabilization (tau2_shrinkage = "auto"): In single-voxel NIfTI analyses (aggregate_by_parcel = FALSE), raw per-voxel \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{raw}}^2 = \hat{\sigma}_{\text{tot}}^2 - s_{\text{obs}}^2\) has wide sampling variance over 40–80 trials and frequently truncates to zero. "auto" automatically activates edge-preserving neighborhood variance pooling ("graph_eb"), which stabilizes the dimensionless ratio \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{raw}}^2 / s_{\text{obs}}^2\) across functionally concordant cortical neighbors before zero-truncation. To keep neighborhood pooling calibrated, it discounts shared scanner noise between neighbors (via Isserlis’ squared-correlation identity), caps how far isolated focal hotspots can be pulled toward quiet surround voxels (at \(2.5\) standard errors via Efron–Morris limited translation), and borrows residual scale precision across concordant neighbors (Empirical-Bayes variance moderation; Smyth, 2004)—without ever smoothing trial slopes \(\hat{\beta}\) (see Spatial Graph Pooling). In parcel mode (aggregate_by_parcel = TRUE), "auto" defaults to "none", while setting "graph_eb" explicitly builds a 3D parcel-centroid graph for fine parcellations (e.g., Schaefer-400/1000).
Scale restoration & trial decorrelation: Set restore_scale = TRUE whenever pooling runs or participants so decon_demixed and se_demixed return to physical BOLD units, and set whiten_panel = TRUE alongside return_panel = TRUE to export paired *_whitened columns (via regularized ZCA) for rapid-ISI designs.

section: Recommended Settings
text:
Recommended Settings

epochs <- decon_epoch_regression(
  deconvolution       = decon,
  covariates          = covariates,      # or NULL for a covariate-agnostic panel
  events              = events,
  target_condition    = "feedback",
  lags                = seq(-2, 4, by = 1),
  source_model        = "impulse",       # or "duration" + trial_durations for RT intervals
  duration_scale      = "rate",
  readout_kernel      = "triangle",
  readout_width       = 1.5 * tr,
  demix_other_events  = TRUE,
  demix_target_trials = TRUE,
  demix_within_trial  = FALSE,           # FALSE before medusa_multilag_infer(); TRUE for 1-subject curves
  demix_ridge         = 0.05,            # lower to 0.02 if upstream cues covary strongly with covariates
  restore_scale       = TRUE,
  weighting           = "gls",
  tau2_mode           = "auto",
  tau2_shrinkage      = "auto",          # automatic bilateral "graph_eb" on voxelwise NIfTI maps
  parcel_groups       = parcel_ids,      # omit for voxelwise maps; supply to run Step 4 parcel pooling
  whiten_panel        = TRUE,
  return_panel        = TRUE
)

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation
section: Practical Considerations: Descriptive Alignment, Censoring Support, and Scope
text:
Practical Considerations: Descriptive Alignment, Censoring Support, and Scope

When to use descriptive align_medusa_ts() vs. inferential decon_epoch_regression(): When you want descriptive peri-event waveform interpolation without a forward de-mixing model—for example, plotting raw peri-event BOLD averages, inspecting blind deconvolve_nlreg() / deconvolve_reglin() trajectories, or auditing explicit collision rules (overlap_policy = "allow" | "truncate" | "exclude")—use align_medusa_ts() (or evt_align_decon_files() for disk-backed .csv.gz archives). For primary inferential modeling on deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() outputs, use decon_epoch_regression(), which removes neighbor mixing and propagates analytical se_demixed. (Because epochs$panel is already event-aligned, it goes directly to Steps 5–6 without calling align_medusa_ts().)
Causal BOLD observability gating (obs_frac_tau >= 0.20): If at least 80% of the forward HRF energy evoked by a target event at \(t_i + \tau\) falls inside censored frames (valid_rows == FALSE) or past the end of the run, Step 3 records that trial-lag as NA rather than extrapolating from the smoothness penalty (while partial scrubbing inside the HRF window elevates se_demixed; see the Visual QC Gallery). Always inspect retained trial counts across runs and conditions before group modeling.
Scope handoff: Step 3 operates within a single participant. Aggregating voxels into anatomical parcels with spatial noise propagation is covered next in Step 4 (executed inside the same decon_epoch_regression(..., parcel_groups = ...) call), followed by population modeling in Step 5 and connectivity disattenuation in Step 6.



Mathematical Reference & Reproduction

For run \(r\), lag \(\tau\), valid observation frames \(I_r\) (\(m_r\) of \(T_r\) volumes), and frozen Step 2 inverse \(D_r \in \mathbb{R}^{T_r \times m_r}\):

Non-target subtraction: Let \(S_{r,0}\) (build_epoch_readout_matrix()) read out all events at lag 0 and \(G_{r,0}\) be their column-centered forward HRF design. build_other_demix_operator() forms \(L_{\text{other}}\) (condition-mean least squares for demix_ridge >= 0.03, or 2nd-order iterated Tikhonov joint inversion for < 0.03), yielding cleaned target readout rows \(S_{\text{clean},\tau} = S_\tau - (S_\tau D_r G_{r,0,\text{other}}) L_{\text{other}}\).
Target cross-talk & duration baseline invariance: Given uncentered and column-centered target forward designs \((G_{\tau,\text{unc}}, G_\tau)\), solve_duration_demix_operator() row-normalizes \(R_{\text{unc}} = \operatorname{diag}(g_{\text{safe}})^{-1} S_\tau D_r G_{\tau,\text{unc}}\), solves \((R_{\text{unc}}^\top R_{\text{unc}} + \lambda_{\text{demix}} Q_m + 10^{-8} I) W_{\text{unc}} = R_{\text{unc}}^\top \operatorname{diag}(g_{\text{safe}})^{-1}\) (penalizing centered fluctuations \(Q_m = I_m - \frac{1}{m}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top\)), applies a Sherman–Morrison rank-1 centering update to obtain \(W_\tau\), and restores centered diagonal gain \(\tilde{G}_\tau\).
Exact noise propagation & \(M_{\text{post}}\) alignment: The composite linear map from centered run BOLD to de-mixed target trials is \(B_{r,\tau} = \tilde{G}_\tau W_\tau S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r\), with centered trial error covariance \(\Omega_{r,\tau} = \frac{\sigma_{\text{eff}}^2}{1 - 1/m} Q_m B_{r,\tau} C_{\text{obs}} \Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r] C_{\text{obs}}^\top B_{r,\tau}^\top Q_m\) evaluated via compute_ar1_operator_factor(). Centered covariates \(X_{r,c}\) are multiplied by \(M_{\text{post}} = Q_m (\tilde{G}_\tau W_\tau S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r G_\tau) Q_m\) prior to regression and ZCA whitening.
Bilateral Graph-EB variance & scale moderation (tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb"): Defining untruncated \(\hat{\theta}_u = \hat{\tau}_{\text{raw}, u}^2 / s_{\text{obs}, u}^2\) with sampling variance \(v_u \approx \frac{2}{\nu_u}(1 + \max(0, \tilde{\theta}_u))^2\), bilateral weights \(\alpha_{uv}\) combine geodesic distance, Cauchy pilot-jump stopping, and orthogonalized residual sign concordance. Discounting neighbor squared-error correlation \(\rho_{ab}^2\) yields local prior \((\mu_{\text{loc}, u}, \tau_{\text{prior}, u}^2)\), shrinkage \(B_u = v_u / (v_u + \tau_{\text{prior}, u}^2)\), limited-translation posterior \(\theta_u^{\text{EM}} = \hat{\theta}_u + \operatorname{clip}(B_u(\mu_{\text{loc}, u} - \hat{\theta}_u), -2.5\sqrt{v_u}, +2.5\sqrt{v_u})\), and \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}, u}^2 = s_{\text{obs}, u}^2 \max(0, \theta_u^{\text{EM}})\), paired with bilateral Smyth (2004) moderation of sandwich residual scales.

title: Step 4: Parcel Aggregation and Analysis Panels
text:
Overview
Many task-fMRI hypotheses are formulated at the level of anatomical regions or functional parcels rather than single voxels. Combining voxels within a parcel boosts trial-level signal-to-noise ratio substantially, provided aggregation happens at the right point in the pipeline: after each voxel’s run has been deconvolved under its own HRF and \(\text{AR}(p)\) whitener, and before trial-level event de-mixing and precision weighting.
Step 4—executed inside decon_epoch_regression(..., parcel_groups = parcel_ids)—pools continuous deconvolved time series within each parcel using cross-run precision and task-support weights, accumulates exact multi-stratum linear operators when intra-parcel voxels differ in HRF or noise stratum, measures spatial noise correlation directly from Step 2’s task-free noise_innovations, and outputs a tidy participant panel ready to stack across a cohort for Steps 5 and 6.
library(medusa)

ep <- decon_epoch_regression(
  deconvolution    = decon,
  covariates       = covariates,
  events           = events,
  target_condition = "feedback",
  lags             = seq(-2, 4, by = 1),
  parcel_groups    = parcel_ids,
  restore_scale    = TRUE,
  whiten_panel     = TRUE,
  return_panel     = TRUE
)
ep$panel[, id := subject_id]
The walkthrough below develops Step 4 in four substeps: computing SNR-informed voxel weights (4.1), combining mixed intra-parcel operator strata (4.2), propagating spatial noise correlations without task contamination (4.3), and constructing cohort-ready weights and panel columns (4.4).

title: Step 4: Parcel Aggregation and Analysis Panels
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 4

Aggregate voxels using cross-run SNR-optimal weights (parcel_weights): Weight constituent voxels inversely by their cross-run observation-noise variance and upweight voxels with stronger cross-fitted Step 1 task \(R^2\).
Preserve intra-parcel (HRF, AR, lambda) heterogeneity: Combine per-stratum forward and inverse operators (\(\sum_s w_s D_s F_s\)) directly rather than approximating a parcel with a single averaged HRF.
Propagate within- and between-parcel spatial noise correlation accurately: Estimate parcel measurement noise and cross-parcel error correlations from Step 2’s task-free whitened noise_innovations.
Produce a self-contained participant trial panel for cohort inference: Export aligned de-mixed readouts, conditional standard errors, cohort-comparable precision weights, paired within-run decorrelated (*_whitened) variables, and cross-parcel shared-noise loadings.

title: Step 4: Parcel Aggregation and Analysis Panels
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

4.1 Weight voxels within each parcel by cross-run precision and task support
Consider a parcel containing four voxels whose observation-noise SDs range from 0.013 (interior gray matter) to 0.032 (noisy pial edge). An unweighted average gives the noisy edge voxel the same influence as the quietest voxel. Instead, Step 4 forms fixed cross-run voxel weights \(u_v\) normalized to \(\sum_{v \in g} u_v = 1\):
\[
u_v \propto \frac{1 + \overline{R}^2_{\text{cv},v} / \bigl(0.05 + \operatorname{med}(\overline{R}^2_{\text{cv}})\bigr)}{\max\!\bigl(\overline{\sigma}_v^2,\; 0.10\,\operatorname{med}(\overline{\sigma}^2)\bigr)}.
\]
Quieter voxels with stronger cross-fitted Step 1 task \(R^2\) receive higher weight, and if a single voxel becomes invalid in one scan (for instance, partial field-of-view dropout in Run 2), the remaining valid voxels in that run renormalize smoothly to sum to 1 (Figure 7.1).






Figure 7.1: Nominal four-voxel parcel weights in Run 1 (sd = 0.013, 0.018, 0.022, 0.032) and automatic renormalization in Run 2 when Voxel 1 is marked invalid.



Choice point — Parcel panels (parcel_groups) vs. voxelwise Graph-EB mapping: Parcel aggregation is ideal when hypotheses target network ROIs, multi-lag group trajectories (medusa_multilag_infer()), or region-to-region connectivity (decon_connectivity_repair()). When effects may occupy small sub-parcel nuclei (\(< 15\%\) of a parcel) or cross shifted individual functional boundaries, omit parcel_groups to run voxelwise Graph-EB mapping (see Spatial Graph Pooling for a direct benchmark).



4.2 Accumulate exact multi-stratum parcel operators
Suppose voxels inside the same parcel belong to different (HRF, AR, lambda) strata—for example, when Step 1 used pooling = "graph" (separating pial-vein autocorrelation from interior gray matter) and Step 2 used lambda_mode = "auto". Because matrix inversion is nonlinear, deconvolving under a single parcel-averaged HRF \(\bar{h} = \frac{1}{2}(h_4 + h_8)\) differs systematically from averaging voxelwise deconvolved series (16.6% waveform discrepancy in Figure 7.2: \(\frac{1}{2}(D_1 F_1 + D_2 F_2) \neq D(\bar{h})F(\bar{h})\)).
Step 4 preserves exact operator correspondence by first forming the weighted parcel continuous series \(\widehat{a}_{r,g} = \sum_{v \in g} u_v \widehat{a}_{r,v}\) and simultaneously accumulating the exact stratum-weighted forward/inverse operator \(\sum_s w_s D_s F_s\) used in Step 3 de-mixing (Figure 7.2).






Figure 7.2: Exact multi-stratum parcel reconstruction (MEDuSA multi-stratum parcel operator) vs. a single averaged-HRF approximation when a two-voxel parcel mixes 4 s and 8 s HRFs.






4.3 Estimate spatial noise covariance from task-free innovations
To compute valid parcel standard errors (se_demixed), we need the effective observation-noise variance of the weighted parcel combination \(\sum_{v \in g} u_v e_v\). For voxel noise SDs \(\sigma_v\) and spatial noise correlations \(R_{\text{spatial}, uv}\), that variance is
\[
\sigma_{\text{parcel}}^2 = \sum_{u \in g} \sum_{v \in g} u_u u_v \sigma_u \sigma_v R_{\text{spatial}, uv}.
\]
In our 4-voxel example (simulate_step4.R), \(\sigma_{\text{parcel}}\) equals 0.0091 if voxel errors are independent (\(R_{\text{spatial}} = I\)), but rises nearly twofold to 0.0171 if all four voxels share common noise (\(R_{\text{spatial}} = \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top\)). Estimating spatial correlation from second differences of deconvolved activity (\(\Delta^2 \hat{a}\)) conflates shared task-evoked neural responses with shared noise—pegging estimated noise near the 0.0171 ceiling even when true noise is independent (0.00) or negatively correlated (-0.20).
By instead projecting \(u \odot \sigma\) onto Step 2’s task-free whitened noise_innovations (\(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{parcel}} = \|Z_r (u \odot \sigma)\|_2\)), MEDuSA recovers the true spatial noise SD across all four correlation regimes (Figure 7.3, Table 7.1) and matches analytical se_demixed to 9.71e-17. Pooling normalized parcel innovation vectors across runs also yields the cross-parcel error correlation matrix unit_error_cor and its factor representation shared_noise_loading for Step 6.






Figure 7.3: Effective parcel BOLD noise SD across four spatial correlation regimes (-0.20, 0.00, 0.65, 0.95): true oracle spatial SD vs. MEDuSA’s task-free innovation estimator vs. a naive \(\Delta^2\) activity proxy.

4.4 Compute biological trial variance, cohort weights, and panel columns
On the aggregated parcel series, Step 4 estimates biological trial-to-trial variance \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) and builds three complementary sets of panel columns:

Within-person vs. cohort precision weights (Figure 7.4): Both use composite inverse variance \((\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{ri}^2)^{-1}\). precision_weight normalizes to mean 1 within each participant/parcel, whereas precision_weight_cohort retains unnormalized inverse variance so Step 5 mixed_by() appropriately downweights high-noise scans and participants across the cohort.
Empirical-Bayes shrunk readouts (decon_eb, Figure 7.5): Shrinks noisy individual trials toward the run mean using trial reliability \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 / (\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{ri}^2)\) for clean single-trial visualization.
Paired within-run decorrelated columns (whiten_panel = TRUE, Figure 7.6): Applies a run-mean-preserving symmetric decorrelation map (regularized zero-phase component analysis, or ZCA whitening) equally to decon_demixed and supplied covariates on the parcel covariance \(\Sigma_{\text{tot}}\), removing serial trial error correlations while keeping each trial aligned to its original ordering.







Figure 7.4: Relative precision_weight vs. se_demixed under "marginal" and "residual" working trial-variance modes.









Figure 7.5: Empirical-Bayes shrunk trial readouts (decon_eb) vs. decon_demixed colored by reliability_trial (Nearly common parcel, Run 1).









Figure 7.6: Within-run parcel correlation matrix \(\Sigma_{\text{tot}}\) before and after paired regularized ZCA (Nearly common parcel, Run 1).



Choice point — Working trial variance (tau2_mode & tau2_shrinkage) and whiten_panel: Use tau2_mode = "auto" when covariates are supplied at Step 4, or "marginal" when building a covariate-agnostic panel (covariates = NULL) to reuse across multiple behavioral models. Keep tau2_shrinkage = "auto" on standard parcellations (100–200 parcels), or set tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb" on dense 400–1000-parcel atlases to borrow variance precision across 3D parcel centroids.

section: Practical Considerations: Voxel Dropout, Role-Specific Columns, and Handoffs
text:
Practical Considerations: Voxel Dropout, Role-Specific Columns, and Handoffs

Checking run-to-run voxel coverage: When partial FoV clipping drops voxels from a small parcel in one run, renormalization shifts the parcel’s spatial center slightly; inspect decon$scaling[[r]]$status whenever dropout is non-trivial.
Matching panel columns to their statistical role: Mirrors the distinction between unshrunk likelihood-only readouts and shrunken EB predictions (Skrondal & Laake, 2001; Vig & Hallquist, 2026):

Use decon_demixed (with weights = "precision_weight_cohort") for Step 5 outcomes and Step 6 M-MOMS connectivity; reserve decon_eb for plotting stabilized trial values rather than entering it into regressions without accounting for shrinkage (see the Visual QC Gallery for a visual demonstration of decon_eb slope attenuation).
When using ZCA-whitened variables, pair decon_demixed_whitened exclusively with matched <var>_whitened predictors from the same (parcel, evt_time) split.

Cohort storage handoff: Attach id (and session if longitudinal) before combining participants. Saving subject_epochs as .rds or writing panels to Parquet (arrow::write_dataset()) preserves the shared_noise_loading list-column for Step 6 alongside scalable disk streaming for Step 5 mixed_by().



Mathematical Reference & Reproduction


Within-parcel effective noise variance: Let \(Z_r \in \mathbb{R}^{m_r \times V}\) denote Step 2’s column-unit-norm task-projected whitened innovations (colSums(Z_r^2) == 1). For parcel \(g\) with valid voxels \(V_g\), normalized weights \(u_g\), and voxel observation-noise SDs \(\sigma_{r,V_g}\), define \(\zeta_{r,g} = Z_{r,V_g} (u_g \odot \sigma_{r,V_g})\). Because \(\mathbb{E}[Z_{r,i}^\top Z_{r,j}] = R_{\text{spatial},ij}\), \(\|\zeta_{r,g}\|_2^2 = \sum_{i,j \in V_g} u_i u_j \sigma_i \sigma_j \hat{R}_{\text{spatial},ij}\) estimates parcel observation-noise variance without task contamination, bounded into \([0.05\,\sigma_{\text{ind}}^2, \sigma_{\text{ceil}}^2]\).
Cross-parcel shared_noise_loading: Normalizing \(\tilde{z}_{r,g} = \zeta_{r,g} / \|\zeta_{r,g}\|_2\) and pooling \(\tilde{Z}_r^\top \tilde{Z}_r\) across runs (weighted by residual degrees of freedom, adjusted for inter-stratum operator overlap, Empirical-Bayes shrunk on noisy off-diagonals, and projected onto the nearest positive semi-definite correlation matrix) yields unit_error_cor, whose principal factor loadings are stored in panel$shared_noise_loading.

title: Step 5: Group and Trajectory Inference
text:
Overview
Once participant trial panels are assembled in Step 4, Step 5 tests how behavioral or experimental variables relate to deconvolved neural activity across the participant population—and characterizes how those effects unfold over peri-event time. Because neural activity decon_demixed sits on the left-hand side as the outcome (Neural ~ Behavior) on an additive-error scale, conditionally mean-zero measurement noise enters the residual without attenuating fixed-effect slopes, while composite precision weights account for varying reliability across trials, runs, and participants (Skrondal & Laake, 2001; Vig & Hallquist, 2026).
Step 5 provides two complementary modeling pathways plus direct volumetric brain-map export:
library(medusa)

# Pathway A: Split-wise multilevel model across parcels and lags
group_models <- mixed_by(
  group_panel,
  outcomes           = "decon_demixed",
  rhs_model_formulae = ~ value_within + value_mean + (1 + value_within || id) + (1 | id:run),
  split_on           = c("parcel", "evt_time"),
  weights            = "precision_weight_cohort"
)
The four substeps below walk from centering predictors (5.1), through split-wise mixed modeling (5.2), joint multi-lag trajectory inference (5.3), and window contrasts, latency estimation, and brain-map export (5.4).

title: Step 5: Group and Trajectory Inference
text:
Split-wise linear mixed-effects models (mixed_by()): Fits a multilevel formula independently at each (parcel, evt_time) split—in memory or streamed from disk-backed Parquet/.rds datasets—accommodating participant random slopes, nested run intercepts, and rich cross-level interactions.
Joint multi-lag trajectory inference (medusa_multilag_infer()): Models the full lag vector of a (parcel, term) profile jointly using cross-lag resolution and covariance matrices to sharpen blurred lag profiles (spectral deblurring), fit smooth penalized-spline (P-spline) trajectories, and compute simultaneous Max-|T| confidence bands, cluster-enhanced (1D TFCE) tests, planned window contrasts, and peak/latency summaries.
Volumetric NIfTI backprojection (backproject_medusa()): Maps parcel-level group statistics directly onto 3D/4D NIfTI brain volumes for visualization in ggbrain.

title: Step 5: Group and Trajectory Inference
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 5

Separate within-person trial fluctuations from between-person trait differences: Decompose predictors into person/run-centered deviations and person means so cross-sectional differences do not confound phasic trial slopes.
Anchor population inference to participants via random slopes: Model inter-individual slope heterogeneity across independent participants rather than treating repeated trials as independent population draws.
Incorporate heterogeneous trial and scan precision: Weight observations by composite inverse total variance (precision_weight_cohort) across trials, runs, and participants.
Leverage cross-lag covariance for trajectory inference and contrasts: Combine Step 3/4 lag operators with empirical cross-lag slope covariance to compute simultaneous confidence bands, 1D TFCE, window contrasts, and latency intervals.

title: Step 5: Group and Trajectory Inference
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

5.1 Decompose behavioral predictors into within-person and between-person components
A raw trial predictor \(x_{sri}\) (participant \(s\), run \(r\), trial \(i\)) combines phasic trial-to-trial variation around a participant’s mean with stable differences across participants: \[
x_{sri} = \underbrace{(x_{sri} - \bar{x}_s)}_{\text{within-person state } x^W_{sri}} + \underbrace{\bar{x}_s}_{\text{between-person mean}}.
\] Testing whether high-value trials evoke stronger activity than low-value trials within the same person is distinct from comparing participants who experience higher average value overall. In Figure 8.1, the true within-person slope is \(+0.55\) while the between-person slope is \(-0.72\); entering uncentered \(x_{sri}\) estimates a confounded pooled slope of -0.432, whereas decomposing x_within and x_mean recovers 0.521 and -0.731 cleanly.






Figure 8.1: Simulated participant means slope down across people even though the within-participant lines slope up (six representative participants shown).



Compute centered predictors on the behavioral table before merging on (id, run, event_index) so censored fMRI frames in one parcel never alter a participant’s behavioral mean in another:


Show behavioral centering and keyed trial merge
key <- c("id", "run", "event_index")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(trial_behavior[, ..key]))

trial_behavior[, `:=`(
  value_mean     = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
  value_within   = value - mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
  entropy_within = entropy - mean(entropy, na.rm = TRUE)
), by = id]

group_panel <- merge(
  activity_panel,
  trial_behavior[, .(id, run, event_index, value_mean, value_within, entropy_within)],
  by = key, all.x = TRUE
)


Choice point — Centering grain (by = id vs. by = .(id, run)): Center within participant (by = id) when predictor distributions are stationary across runs, or center within each participant-run (by = .(id, run)) when contingencies or block drifts shift across runs and pure within-run trial contrasts are desired.



5.2 Fit participant random-slope mixed models with cohort precision weights
At a single (parcel, evt_time) split, the standard multilevel model expresses de-mixed trial readout \(\widehat{z}_{sri}\) (decon_demixed) as
\[
\widehat{z}_{sri} = \beta_0 + \beta_W x^W_{sri} + \beta_B \bar{x}_s + b_{0s} + b_{Ws} x^W_{sri} + a_{sr} + \varepsilon_{sri},
\]
with participant random intercept and slope \((b_{0s}, b_{Ws})\) ((1 + x_within || id)) and participant-nested run intercept \(a_{sr}\) ((1 | id:run)). In a balanced design with \(S\) participants, \(m\) trials per participant, slope variance \(\sigma_b^2\), and trial residual variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\), the sampling variance of the population slope is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_W) = \frac{\sigma_b^2}{S} + \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{Sm}.
\]
Adding more trials \(m\) sharpens each participant’s slope (\(\sigma_\varepsilon^2 / Sm \to 0\)) while leaving between-participant heterogeneity \(\sigma_b^2 / S\) unchanged. Including the random slope \(b_{Ws}\) reflects that structure: in Figure 8.2 (12 participants, \(\beta_W = 0\), \(\sigma_b > 0\)), random-slope/participant-slope inference holds nominal Type I error at 5.2% at 192 trials per person, whereas trial-row OLS without random slopes reaches 79.8%.






Figure 8.2: Two tests of the same zero population slope across 3,000 replications per trial count (12 participants, nonzero slope heterogeneity). Participant-slope inference stays near 5%, whereas trial-row OLS inflates with trial count.



Simultaneously, conditional residual variance varies across trials and scans because \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{sri}) = \tau_{\text{latent}}^2 + s_{sri}^2\). Passing weights = "precision_weight_cohort" supplies \((\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{sri}^2)^{-1}\) normalized across the full cohort split, allowing noisier runs and participants to carry appropriately wider conditional residual spread (0.191 and 0.396 vs. true 0.194 and 0.403 in Figure 8.3, compared with 0.313 unweighted).






Figure 8.3: Conditional residual spread recovered by weighted vs. unweighted lmer() across a quiet run (SD = 0.194) and a noisy run (SD = 0.403).



Across 3 simulated parcels (Phasic, Sustained, Null) × 8 lags × 2 focal predictors (\(48\) planned tests; Figure 8.4, Figure 8.5), Benjamini–Yekutieli ("BY") adjustment isolates 7 true discoveries around the phasic value_within peak (\(+1\text{ s}\)) and sustained entropy_within plateau (\(+1\) to \(+4\text{ s}\)) while filtering out isolated pointwise fluctuations (9 unadjusted hits).






Figure 8.4: Simulated population slope profiles across three parcels with pointwise 95% Satterthwaite intervals (dashed lines mark generating truth).









Figure 8.5: Multiplicity map across the 48 parcel × lag × term tests: teal cells survive Benjamini–Yekutieli FDR control across the family; orange cells pass unadjusted p <= .05 only.



Choice point — Split-wise mixed_by() vs. joint medusa_multilag_infer(), and disk streaming: Choose mixed_by() when testing specific planned lags, complex random-effects structures, or trial-by-trait interactions; for large whole-cortex cohorts, pass a Hive-partitioned Parquet directory directly to mixed_by(data = ..., split_filter = ...) so Arrow streams one split at a time with minimal RAM. Choose medusa_multilag_infer() (Substep 5.3) when your primary question concerns the full peri-event waveform, simultaneous epoch bands, or window contrasts.



5.3 Model multi-lag trajectories jointly with medusa_multilag_infer()
Because neighboring lags share both deconvolution smoothness (\(R_{\text{lag}}\)) and correlated observation noise (\(C_{\text{lag}}\)), modeling the lag vector \(\widehat{b} = (\widehat{b}_1, \dots, \widehat{b}_L)^\top\) jointly is substantially more informative than treating lags as unrelated splits:

Joint within-run regression and available-case lag pooling: medusa_multilag_infer() fits all supplied time-varying covariates together within each run (routing any participant-constant trait covariates to between-participant weighted least squares with leverage-adjusted HC2 standard errors) and pools participant slopes across lags using available cases—retaining participants at interior lags even if boundary censoring removed an edge lag.
Cross-lag sharpening and uncertainty-aware spline smoothing: Under trajectory_mode = "auto" (with upstream demix_within_trial = FALSE), medusa_multilag_infer() first gently inverts the known cross-lag blurring matrix \(R_{\text{lag}}\) (regularized spectral deblurring; "deblur", Figure 8.6) and then fits a smooth penalized spline ("deblur_pspline"), folding uncertainty from the smoothing penalty itself into \(\Sigma_{\text{multilag}}\) (Marra–Wood posterior covariance; Marra & Wood, 2012) rather than treating the smooth curve as bias-free.
Finite-sample cross-lag calibration (n_perm draws): Because the \(L \times L\) cross-lag covariance is estimated from a finite cohort of participants, medusa_multilag_infer() simulates null covariance draws that propagate that finite-sample covariance uncertainty (studentized Wishart draws). From those joint draws it computes simultaneous Max-|T| bands (p_maxT, conf.low.sim, conf.high.sim), threshold-free cluster enhancement (p_tfce, accumulating contiguous same-sign deflections without an arbitrary cutoff), and a multivariate departure test across the whole epoch (omnibus_p, Mahalanobis test; Figure 8.7, Figure 8.8).







Figure 8.6: Spectral cross-lag deblurring on a deterministic coefficient curve spread by C_blur: the deblurred trajectory recovers the underlying phasic width.









Figure 8.7: Raw lag estimates, pointwise 95% intervals, simultaneous 95% Max-|T| band, and smoothed P-spline trajectory on the simulated Phasic parcel.









Figure 8.8: Epoch-level significance summaries (min_p_maxT, min_p_tfce, omnibus_p) across Phasic value, Sustained entropy, and Null entropy trajectories (4,000 Wishart draws).



In Figure 8.8, both generated effects hit the 4,000-draw floor (min_p_maxT = 0.0002, omnibus_p = 0.0005), while the null trajectory stays well above .05 (omnibus_p = 0.269). Custom first-stage participant slope tables can also enter directly via the coefficient-table interface:


Show optional custom participant slope-table call
partial_trajectory <- medusa_multilag_infer(
  subject_slopes,
  lag_resolution  = resolution_by_parcel,
  lag_error_cor   = error_cor_by_parcel,
  trajectory_mode = "deblur",
  n_perm          = 4000L,
  seed            = 6205L
)


Choice point — Trajectory mode (trajectory_mode) and multiplicity: Use trajectory_mode = "auto" as the standard setting (or "none" when inspecting raw unsmoothed lag averages). Within one (parcel, term) curve, p_maxT and p_tfce already control familywise error across lags; when testing multiple parcels or covariates, adjust latency$omnibus_p across the planned parcel–term family using Holm or BY.



5.4 Evaluate planned window contrasts, continuous latency, and volumetric NIfTI maps
To compare early vs. late epoch activity (contrasts = list(late_minus_early = list(early = c(0, 1), late = c(3, 4)))), medusa_multilag_infer() evaluates \(c^\top \widehat{b}_*\) with cross-lag SE \(\sqrt{c^\top \Sigma_* c}\):



contrast_source
Curve evaluated
Recommended use




"unsmoothed" (default)
Spectrally deblurred curve prior to P-spline smoothing
Standard inferential choice: retains resolution recovery without spline curvature shrinkage between windows.


"raw"
Raw group lag estimates
Direct test of raw lag window averages without cross-lag deblurring.


"multilag"
Deblurred + P-spline smoothed curve
Descriptive contrast matching the plotted smooth curve (worked comparison).



On our simulated panel, late_minus_early distinguishes the decaying phasic value response (estimate = -0.177, \(t_{23} = -7.49\), \(p = 1.3e-07\)) from the sustained entropy response (estimate = 0.082, \(t_{23} = 4.26\), \(p = 0.0003\)), while $latency summarizes natural-spline peak_lag (1.02 s, 95% CI [0.92, 1.11] s for Phasic) and center-of-mass / FWHM (com_lag = 2.45 s, fwhm = 3.94 s for Sustained) on trajectories that pass omnibus gating.
Finally, parcel-level group tables from either mixed_by() or medusa_multilag_infer() map directly onto 3D or 4D NIfTI volumes via backproject_medusa(..., brain_mask = decon, fill = NA_real_) (see recipe below and Spatial Graph Pooling).

Recommended Settings

Pathway A: Split-wise mixed models (mixed_by()) & NIfTI backprojection

library(medusa)

group_formula <- decon_demixed ~ value_within + value_mean + entropy_within +
  (1 + value_within + entropy_within || id) + (1 | id:run)

group_models <- mixed_by(
  group_panel,
  model_formulae = list(trial_effects = group_formula),
  split_on       = c("parcel", "evt_time"),
  weights        = "precision_weight_cohort",
  calculate      = "parameter_estimates_reml",
  padjust_by     = NULL,
  tidy_args      = list(effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE),
  return_models  = TRUE
)

focal_tests <- subset(
  group_models$coef_df_reml,
  term %in% c("value_within", "entropy_within")
)
focal_tests$p_by <- p.adjust(focal_tests$p.value, method = "BY")

Practical Diagnostics, Interpretation Conventions, and Scope

Auditing split-level convergence and residual dependence: Inspect participant counts, lme4::isSingular() flags, and within-run lag-1 conditional residual correlations across splits (Figure 8.9):



Show split-level model audit code
fits <- lapply(group_models$models$model, function(entry) entry$reml)
group_models$models[, .(
  parcel, evt_time,
  trials       = vapply(fits, nobs, numeric(1)),
  participants = vapply(fits, function(fit) nlevels(model.frame(fit)$id), integer(1)),
  singular     = vapply(fits, lme4::isSingular, logical(1))
)]








Figure 8.9: Lag-1 correlations of scaled conditional residuals per participant and run in the focal mixed model.




Matched coordinates when using ZCA-whitened panels (use_whitened = TRUE): In rapid-ISI designs where conditional residuals retain serial correlation, set whiten_panel = TRUE in Step 4 and pair decon_demixed_whitened with *_whitened predictors from the same (parcel, evt_time) split (forming any within-run interaction columns before Step 4 whitening, since \(T(x \odot z) \neq (Tx) \odot (Tz)\)).
Interpreting between-person effects: Because Step 2 centers BOLD within each run, tonic run-constant baselines are removed; person-mean predictors (x_mean) test differences in average event-locked phasic deflections across people (or cross-level x_within * trait moderation), scaled in physical BOLD units under Step 1’s HRF normalization (normalize = "positive_lobe").
Scope transition to Step 6: Step 5 treats neural activity as the dependent outcome predicted by error-free task or behavioral covariates (for visual diagnostics of uncentered predictors and omitted random slopes, see the Visual QC Gallery). Whenever a deconvolved neural readout moves to the right-hand side to predict another brain region (Target ~ Seed * Task) or behavior (Behavior ~ Seed), proceed to Step 6 (decon_connectivity_repair()) to correct predictor measurement error and shared regional noise.
