title: Step 6: Trial-Level Connectivity and PPI
text:
Overview
Whereas Step 5 places deconvolved neural activity on the left-hand side as an outcome (Neural ~ Behavior), Step 6 moves a deconvolved parcel readout onto the right-hand side (Target ~ Seed + Task + Seed:Task or Behavior ~ Seed) to test trial-to-trial functional connectivity and psychophysiological interaction (PPI).
When an estimated quantity with trial-level sampling error is used as a regression predictor, two measurement properties directly affect structural slopes (Fuller, 1987; Vig & Hallquist, 2026): predictor measurement error inflates the observed design variance \(X^\top X\) (attenuating both main connectivity and PPI interaction slopes toward zero), and any shared scanner or physiological noise between seed and target shifts the cross-product \(X^\top Y\). Step 6 (decon_connectivity_repair(), backed by medusa_fit_mmom()) subtracts Step 4’s analytical per-trial error variances (se_demixed^2) and task-free cross-parcel noise correlations (unit_error_cor / shared_noise_loading) from each participant’s sample cross-products while guarding against unstable small denominators in noisy scans (Modified Method of Moments with Step-up Regularization, M-MOMS), and then aggregates participant slopes across the cohort using finite-sample random-effects \(t\)-intervals scaled by observed between-participant slope dispersion (Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman, HKSJ pooling).
library(medusa)

ppi <- decon_connectivity_repair(
  panel_dt             = subject_epochs,
  seed_region          = "Seed",
  target_region        = "Target",
  seed_lag             = 0,
  target_lag           = 0,
  covariates           = "x_within",
  test_ppi             = TRUE,
  orthogonalize_seed_x = FALSE,
  shared_error         = "auto",
  method               = "mmoms"
)
The walkthrough below develops Step 6 in four substeps directly paralleling the REPAIR two-step moment framework: specifying the latent structural equation (6.1), constructing the trial-specific error covariance matrices (6.2), estimating participant slopes via regularized M-MOMS (6.3), and pooling across participants (6.4).

title: Step 6: Trial-Level Connectivity and PPI
section: Goals, Inputs, and Outputs
text:
Goals, Inputs, and Outputs

Goals of Step 6

Disattenuate noisy neural predictors and PPI product terms: Construct per-trial predictor measurement-error covariance blocks \(\Psi_i\)—capturing both heteroskedastic interaction error \(x_i^2 s_i^2\) and off-diagonal seed–interaction error covariance \(x_i s_i^2\)—and subtract them from observed design moments.
Account for stationary cross-parcel shared measurement error: Subtract expected seed–target error covariance \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i)\) (shared_error = "auto") estimated from Step 4’s task-free noise_innovations.
Support clear direct and residualized-seed PPI parameterizations: Allow analysts to choose explicitly between unresidualized seed coupling (orthogonalize_seed_x = FALSE) and task-residualized seed coupling with exact error-covariance projection (orthogonalize_seed_x = TRUE).
Pool participant connectivity estimates with calibrated random-effects uncertainty: Aggregate participant M-MOMS slopes at the group level via leverage-guarded HKSJ random-effects inference.



Inputs: What Step 6 Receives and Why



Input
Structure
Why Step 6 Uses It

Named subject_epochs list (preferred) or stacked group_panel (data.table / .rds / Parquet)
Pairs seed and target trial readouts by (id, run, trial) while supplying se_demixed and Step 4’s cross-parcel noise correlations ($unit_error_cor on subject_epochs, or $panel$shared_noise_loading on stacked panels).

Parcel names and peri-event lags (e.g., seed_lag = 0, target_lag = 0 or lagged seed_lag = 0, target_lag = 1)
Select the paired seed readout \(\widehat{z}_{S,i}\) and target readout \(\widehat{z}_{T,i}\) along with their trial-specific measurement SEs.

Character vector of centered task covariates; logical test_ppi
When test_ppi = TRUE, the first element of covariates defines the error-free psychological modulator \(x_i\) forming seed:x, while any additional covariates enter as additive controls.

shared_error = c("auto", "supplied", "zero"); method = c("mmoms", "mmom", "naive_unweighted")
Govern cross-parcel error subtraction and moment-matrix conditioning.

title: Step 6: Trial-Level Connectivity and PPI
section: Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points
text:
Step-by-Step Walkthrough: Substeps and Choice Points

6.1 Specify the latent trial connectivity or PPI structural equation
Within a participant (after centering seed, target, and task covariates within each run), let \(\theta_{S,i}\) denote true latent seed amplitude at seed_lag, \(\theta_{T,i}\) denote latent target amplitude at target_lag, and \(x_i\) denote an error-free centered task modulator on trial \(i\):
\[
\theta_{T,i} = \beta_S \theta_{S,i} + \beta_x x_i + \beta_P (\theta_{S,i} x_i) + \varepsilon_i.
\]
Each coefficient answers a distinct biological question: \(\beta_S\) is baseline trial-to-trial seed–target coupling at the mean of \(x_i\) (\(x_i = 0\)), \(\beta_x\) absorbs direct task activation in the target parcel so shared main-effect responses are not mistaken for coupling, and \(\beta_P\) is the PPI slope—how much seed–target coupling changes per unit change in \(x_i\) (for \(x_i \in \{-1, +1\}\), \(2\beta_P\) is the slope difference between task conditions).
Choice point — Seed parameterization (orthogonalize_seed_x) and lagged control (control_target_seed_lag):

Direct vs. residualized seed (orthogonalize_seed_x): Setting orthogonalize_seed_x = FALSE (recommended when testing the direct structural equation above) enters centered \(\theta_{S,i}\) and \(x_i\) symmetrically without altering quadratic task structure. Setting orthogonalize_seed_x = TRUE first residualizes the seed against covariates (projecting diag(se_demixed^2) through \(P D_u P^\top\)) to isolate pure task-orthogonal seed fluctuations; note that when the seed responds linearly to \(x_i\), residualizing shifts the product column by a term proportional to \(x_i^2\).
Concurrent vs. lagged Granger-style coupling (control_target_seed_lag): When target_lag > seed_lag, setting control_target_seed_lag = TRUE includes target activity at seed_lag as an additional error-corrected neural predictor so \(\beta_S\) and \(\beta_P\) test whether seed activity predicts subsequent change in the target parcel.




6.2 Construct trial-specific predictor and shared-error covariance matrices
In practice, Step 4 provides de-mixed additive-error readouts \(\widehat{z}_{S,i} = \theta_{S,i} + u_i\) and \(\widehat{z}_{T,i} = \theta_{T,i} + v_i\) rather than latent \((\theta_{S,i}, \theta_{T,i})\), with known conditional sampling variances \(s_{S,i}^2 = \texttt{se\_demixed}_{S,i}^2\) and \(s_{T,i}^2 = \texttt{se\_demixed}_{T,i}^2\). Forming the observed predictor row \(X_i = [\widehat{z}_{S,i},\, x_i,\, \widehat{z}_{S,i} x_i]^\top\) and observed outcome \(Y_i = \widehat{z}_{T,i}\) induces predictor error \(e_{X,i} = [u_i,\, 0,\, x_i u_i]^\top\).
Notice that even though \(u_i\) is a scalar on trial \(i\), both the seed column (\(\widehat{z}_{S,i}\)) and the ppi column (\(\widehat{z}_{S,i} x_i\)) contain the same noise draw \(u_i\), producing a structured \(3 \times 3\) predictor measurement-error covariance block on trial \(i\):
\[
\Psi_i = \operatorname{Cov}(e_{X,i} \mid x_i) = s_{S,i}^2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & x_i \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ x_i & 0 & x_i^2 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Two properties follow immediately from \(\Psi_i\): interaction error variance scales heteroskedastically with \(x_i^2 s_{S,i}^2\), and whenever \(x_i \neq 0\), the predictor and interaction errors covary with signed entry \(x_i s_{S,i}^2\).
At the same time, scanner drift, physiological pulsatility, and vascular proximity can induce correlated observation error \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i) = c_i\) between seed and target parcels, shifting the observed cross-moment \(X_i Y_i\) by \([c_i,\, 0,\, x_i c_i]^\top\). Under shared_error = "auto", Step 6 estimates stationary per-trial cross-error covariance \(c_i = \widehat{r}_{ST}\, s_{S,i} s_{T,i}\) automatically from Step 4’s task-free innovation correlation \(\widehat{r}_{ST}\) (unit_error_cor, or the inner product of shared_noise_loading vectors, combined with cross-lag error correlation when seed_lag != target_lag).
Choice point — Cross-parcel shared error (shared_error): Use shared_error = "auto" as the standard setting, and compare against shared_error = "zero" to see how much stationary background noise correlation contributed to the raw coupling estimate.



6.3 Estimate participant slopes via regularized Modified Method of Moments (M-MOMS)
Given observed trial vectors \((X_i, Y_i)\) and error moments \((\Psi_i, c_i)\), medusa_fit_mmom() estimates each participant’s structural coefficients in three non-iterative moment steps (Fuller, 1987; Vig & Hallquist, 2026):

Error-corrected preliminary normal equations: Subtracts predictor error covariances from \(X^\top X\) and shared seed–target error covariances from \(X^\top Y\): \[
\left(X^\top X - c(\hat{\lambda}_1, \alpha_1)\sum_{i=1}^n \Psi_i\right) \widehat{\beta}^{(1)}
= X^\top Y - c(\hat{\lambda}_1, \alpha_1)\sum_{i=1}^n \begin{pmatrix} c_i \\ 0 \\ x_i c_i \end{pmatrix},
\] where Fuller’s generalized-eigenvalue factor \(c(\hat{\lambda}, \alpha)\) prevents subtracting more error variance than the sample design matrix supports.
Structural disturbance variance & composite trial weights: Uses \(\widehat{\beta}^{(1)}\) to estimate measurement-error-corrected structural disturbance variance \(\hat{\sigma}_\varepsilon^2\) and forms per-trial composite residual variances \(\hat{w}_i = \hat{\sigma}_\varepsilon^2 + s_{T,i}^2 - 2\widehat{\beta}^{(1)\top}\psi_{XY,i} + \widehat{\beta}^{(1)\top}\Psi_i\widehat{\beta}^{(1)}\).
Weighted M-MOMS update & conditioning guard: Re-estimates \(\widehat{\beta}\) and sandwich standard errors using inverse composite weights \(\hat{w}_i^{-1}\). Under method = "mmoms", an adaptive step-up search selects the smallest regularization constant \(\alpha \ge p + 1\) that keeps the corrected predictor block well-conditioned—preventing small-denominator outliers in low-reliability participants while matching unmodified M-MOM whenever signal reliability is moderate to high.

Choice point — Moment estimator (method): Use method = "mmoms" as the primary estimator, and fit method = "naive_unweighted" in the same coordinates (use_whitened = FALSE) alongside it so the magnitude of measurement-error disattenuation is directly visible.



6.4 Pool participant slopes and compare against naive regression
Across independent participants, decon_connectivity_repair() pools participant slopes \(\widehat{\beta}_s\) and standard errors using dispersion-scaled finite-sample random-effects \(t\)-intervals (Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman, HKSJ meta-regression, with leverage protection against extreme precision weights), anchoring group degrees of freedom to the number of participants \(S\).
To see how M-MOMS behaves when disattenuating genuine trial-level PPI (Genuine PPI scenario in simulate.R: 120 simulated cohorts of \(S = 16\) participants, 2 runs × 60 trials, true population interaction \(\beta_P = 0.35\), seed and target measurement error SDs \(= 0.70\), independent errors), compare the top three rows of the benchmark table and left panel of Figure 9.1:

Naive regression is attenuated by roughly one-third (0.230 vs. true 0.350), yielding 0.0% 95% CI coverage because tight group SEs center around the attenuated value.
M-MOMS removes the attenuation (0.343), cuts population RMSE more than threefold (from 0.123 to 0.039), and restores nominal 95.0% confidence-interval coverage.

Figure 9.1: Population PPI estimates across 120 simulated cohorts per scenario (dashed line marks generating truth). Left: M-MOMS recovers the true 0.35 interaction under independent errors. Right: under a condition-flipped shared-error null, disattenuation alone amplifies the artifact unless condition-specific cross-error moments are subtracted.

title: Step 6: Trial-Level Connectivity and PPI
section: Practical Diagnostics, Shared-Error Sensitivity, and Scope
text:
Practical Diagnostics, Shared-Error Sensitivity, and Scope

Evaluating sensitivity to condition-dependent shared noise
Stationary shared_error = "auto" subtracts baseline cross-parcel noise correlation \(\operatorname{Cov}(u, v) = r_0 \sigma_S \sigma_T\), which protects main-effect seed connectivity. What if physiological or motion noise correlation between two regions changes sign or magnitude with task condition—for instance, condition-locked breath-holding or head motion during \(x_i = +1\) trials (Shared-error null in Figure 9.1, right: \(\beta_P = 0\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i) = 0.65 x_i \sigma^2\), zero run-wide average correlation)?
Because \(\mathbb{E}[x_i u_i v_i] = r \sigma^2 \neq 0\), naive regression already shows a positive artifact (0.214), and dividing by the disattenuated denominator \(X^\top X - \sum \Psi_i\) without knowing the condition-flipped cross-error magnifies it (0.322), returning to zero (-0.018) once the condition-specific cross-error moment is supplied. Plotting the implied M-MOMS slope across plausible condition-modulated cross-error correlations \(r(x)\) (Figure 9.2)—paired with physiological/motion nuisance modeling in Steps 1–2 and a negative-control reference parcel—makes it transparent how large a condition-locked artifact would need to be to account for an observed PPI.






Figure 9.2: Sensitivity curve in the shared-error null scenario: implied population PPI slope as a function of hypothesized condition-dependent cross-error correlation amplitude (crossing zero at the generating value 0.65).





Reporting checklist and scope boundaries

Report circuit, lag, and estimand choices: Document seed_region, target_region, seed_lag, target_lag, orthogonalize_seed_x, control_target_seed_lag, and multiplicity adjustment across region pairs.
Present naive and M-MOMS side by side: Include "naive_unweighted" alongside "mmoms" and summarize ppi$subjects (r_shared_error, alpha_final, lambda_final, participant/trial counts, and convergence; see the Visual QC Gallery for side-by-side participant connectivity distributions under intact vs. stripped shared_error metadata).
Scope boundaries: Just as in Vig & Hallquist (2026), Step 6 treats first-stage error variances (se_demixed^2) and selected regularization constants as fixed plug-in quantities, requires full-rank within-person predictor designs with adequate seed reliability, and corrects within-trial second moments rather than asymmetric cross-parcel resolution differences (\(K_S \neq K_T\)). For mathematical derivations and full-covariance extensions, see From BOLD noise to M-MOM error variances and Measurement-error models and REPAIR.

title: Visual QC and Troubleshooting Gallery
text:
Overview
When an end-to-end single-trial fMRI analysis yields unexpectedly weak slopes, implausibly shifted peri-event peaks, or inflated connectivity estimates, identifying which pipeline stage introduced the distortion is much faster when you know the visual signature each failure mode leaves behind. Because MEDuSA preserves explicit diagnostic summaries, operator resolution metrics, and propagated standard errors at every stage (see the end-to-end data-flow schematic), most upstream mis-specifications can be localized in a few lines of R before fitting group models across hundreds of parcels.
The snippet below collects the six fastest pre-flight checks across a completed or pilot participant workflow:
# 1. Step 0: Check motion censoring share, dummy frames, and event clock bounds (in seconds)
print(sub01$confounds$summary[, c("run", "n_volumes", "pct_censored", "n_non_steady_state")])
lapply(split(sub01$events$onset, sub01$events$run), range)

# 2. Step 1: Check out-of-sample HRF task relevance and AR(p) rho stationarity ceiling (0.90)
lapply(hrf_fit$selections, function(s) summary(s$selected_task_p))
lapply(hrf_fit$noise, function(n) quantile(n$rho[, 1], probs = c(0.5, 0.9, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE))

# 3. Step 2: Check deconvolution conditional self-gain and attenuation
diagnose_crossrun_recovery(decon, events = sub01$events)$summary

# 4. Step 3 & 4: Audit trial-level SE distribution and BOLD-coverage NA gating
summary(epochs$panel$se_demixed)
mean(is.na(epochs$panel$decon_demixed))

# 5. Step 5: Verify predictor centering (run/person mean ~ 0) and random-effect singularity
tapply(group_panel$rpe_within, group_panel$id, mean, na.rm = TRUE) |> summary()

# 6. Step 6: Inspect M-MOMS attenuation factor (alpha_final) and shared cross-parcel error
summary(ppi$subjects[, c("estimate", "r_shared_error", "alpha_final", "converged")])

title: Visual QC and Troubleshooting Gallery
section: Visual Diagnostic Pairs Across the Pipeline
text:
Visual Diagnostic Pairs Across the Pipeline

1. Steps 0 & 1: Event-Clock Shifts, Onset-Unit Errors, and AR(1) Ceiling Pile-Ups






Figure 10.1: Healthy versus mis-specified diagnostics in Steps 0 and 1. A: True feedback RPE slope (0.60 at lag 0 s, TR = 2.0 s) recovered cleanly when initial dummy volumes are masked via valid_rows (blue), versus physically dropping 3 dummy volumes without setting time_offset = 6 (solid red, shifting the recovered peak backward to -6 s) or supplying events$onset in TR indices rather than seconds (dashed amber, compressing all events into the first half of the scan and destroying the association). B: Parcel-level hrf_fit$noise$run1$rho across 36 parcels (true \(\rho \in [0.30, 0.62]\)) on detrended BOLD (blue) versus BOLD contaminated by an unmodeled mid-run shim step and low-frequency drift (red, pinning 100% of parcels against the 0.90 stationarity ceiling).



What to look for in Figure 10.1:

Event-clock shifts (Panel A, solid red): If an external script slices \(k\) initial dummy volumes out of the 4D NIfTI file (Y <- Y[-c(1:k), ]) while events.tsv remains referenced to the first scanner trigger (time_offset = 0), row 1 of the matrix is actually acquired at \(t = k \cdot \text{TR}\) rather than \(t = 0\). Every neural response then appears in the BOLD record \(k \cdot \text{TR}\) seconds earlier than the event table expects—producing an unmistakable “pre-stimulus” peak at \(-k \cdot \text{TR}\) (-6 s here for 3 dropped 2.0 s volumes) and near-zero effect at 0 s.
Onset-unit mismatches (Panel A, dashed amber): Passing 0-based or 1-based volume indices instead of seconds when \(\text{TR} \ne 1.0\text{ s}\) rescales the entire task timeline by \(1 / \text{TR}\). Step 1’s cross-run HRF selector finds almost no out-of-sample variance explained (selected_task_p shifts toward uniform noise), and Step 3 lag profiles flatten to zero.
Stationarity ceiling pile-ups (Panel B, red): Step 1 bounds REML \(\text{AR}(p)\) roots inside a causal, stationary region (rho <= 0.90 for \(\text{AR}(1)\)) so prewhitening stays invertible. A natural physiological distribution spans roughly 0.25–0.70 depending on \(\text{TR}\). When a large share of parcels stacks directly on 0.90, the noise model is absorbing deterministic low-frequency drift, coil/shim jumps, or unmasked motion bursts rather than stationary innovations.


# Diagnostic check & remedy for Steps 0-1
stopifnot(max(sub01$events$onset) <= max(sub01$confounds$summary$n_volumes) * sub01$tr)
mean(hrf_fit$noise$run1$rho[, 1] >= 0.89, na.rm = TRUE)  # healthy: typically < 0.05

# Remedy: keep intact 4D runs + valid_rows, and ensure drift + FD censoring are active
sub01   <- read_fmriprep_subject(..., strategy = "24p", fd_threshold = 0.5, include_non_steady_state = TRUE)
hrf_fit <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(sub01, kernel_grid = candidates, drift_order = 2L, pooling = "parcel")

For full walkthroughs of clock-preserving ingestion and prewhitening choices, see Step 0 and Step 1.



2. Step 2: Over-Smoothing Gain Collapse and Uncensored Spike Ringing






Figure 10.2: Healthy versus mis-specified continuous deconvolution in Step 2. A: Continuous restored activity trace \(\widehat{a}_r(t)\) across 67–117 s of Run 1 containing two true neural events (76 s and 108 s, green dotted lines) and a framewise motion artifact at 91 s (red dashed line). Healthy deconvolution with valid_rows censoring and automatic \(\lambda_v\) / RWLS recovers crisp phasic peaks at 76 s and 108 s while suppressing 91 s (blue). Fixing lambda = 8.0 flattens true neural peaks nearly to zero (amber), whereas leaving the 91 s spike uncensored with rwls = "none" produces strong positive and negative deconvolution ringing lobes across 82–96 s (red). B: diagnose_crossrun_recovery() immediately flags over-smoothing via collapsed mean_gain (0.043 vs. 0.317), whereas uncensored spike artifacts leave deterministic operator mean_gain almost unchanged (0.300) and therefore require inspecting censoring masks or RWLS weights.



What to look for in Figure 10.2:

Gain collapse from over-regularization (amber): Because continuous deconvolution trades variance reduction against temporal shrinkage via the resolution matrix \(D_r H_r\), setting lambda manually to a large value crushes the diagonal self-gain of diagnose_crossrun_recovery() below 0.05. Notice that deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() scales penalties cleanly when scaling = "noise_sd" and lambda = NULL; manual lambda overrides are rarely needed outside sensitivity analyses.
Why spike ringing requires both operator and residual/weight checks (red): Look closely at Panel B: the uncensored spike run (rwls = "none", no valid_rows mask) still reports a healthy-looking mean_gain = 0.300 in diagnose_crossrun_recovery(). That is because mean_gain audits the linear operator \(D_r H_r\), which depends on the HRF, run schedule, and \(\lambda_v\)—not on an isolated BOLD outlier in \(y_r\). An unmasked motion spike acts like a delta impulse that does not follow the slow hemodynamic shape \(h_r\); inverting \(H_r\) therefore surrounds the spike with alternating positive and negative side-lobes across neighboring timepoints. Masking high-FD frames via valid_rows (Step 0) and keeping rwls = "auto" (Step 2) prevents these artifacts from contaminating nearby trials.


# Check both operator gain AND adaptive RWLS outlier downweighting
rec <- diagnose_crossrun_recovery(decon, events = sub01$events)
print(rec$summary[, c("run", "mean_gain", "mean_abs_gain_error", "mean_abs_excess_leakage")])

# Inspect minimum RWLS observation weights per run (weights << 1 indicate downweighted residual spikes)
lapply(decon$rwls_weights, function(w) quantile(w, probs = c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.5), na.rm = TRUE))

For details on Sobolev versus ridge penalties, scaling = "noise_sd", and rwls = "auto", see Step 2.



3. Steps 3 & 4: Motion-Scrubbing Shadows in Trial SEs and Shrunken Outcome Misuse






Figure 10.3: Healthy versus mis-specified trial epoching and panel assembly in Steps 3 and 4. A: Propagated trial-level standard error (se_demixed) across 16 feedback trials in Run 1. In an uncensored run (blue), interior trials share uniform precision (se_demixed \(\approx 0.062\)) with an expected uptick only on Trial 16 (215.5 s, whose causal HRF tail is truncated by scanner shutoff at 220 s). When 3 frames on Trial 7’s HRF peak are motion-scrubbed (red), se_demixed spikes selectively at Trial 7 (0.076) so downstream precision weights downweight it automatically; when 10 frames covering Trial 11’s HRF are scrubbed, min_bold_coverage gates Trial 11 cleanly to NA (red dashed line). B: Entering decon_demixed + precision_weight_cohort in mixed_by() across 16 participants recovers the generating slope (0.454 vs. truth 0.50, blue), whereas mistakenly entering empirical-Bayes shrunken decon_eb as the outcome shrinks the estimated population slope nearly in half (0.231, red).



What to look for in Figure 10.3:

Protective se_demixed spikes vs. run-wide degradation (Panel A): Seeing isolated spikes in panel$se_demixed (like Trial 7) or run-boundary upticks (like Trial 16) is not a software bug—it is the propagated sandwich covariance \(\Omega_{r,\tau}\) faithfully recording where censored frames or run-end truncation reduced effective BOLD observations inside that event’s hemodynamic window. When precision_weight_cohort is passed to mixed_by(), Trial 7 receives lower inverse-variance weight automatically, and Trial 11 (NA) is omitted without shifting event_index. Intervention is only warranted when a run has so many censored frames that most trials sit at elevated se_demixed or NA.
Outcome vs. predictor column roles in Step 4 panels (Panel B): Step 4 exports both unshrunken decon_demixed (\(\widehat{z}_{ri} = \theta_{ri} + e_{ri}\)) and empirical-Bayes shrunken decon_eb (\(\tilde{z}_{ri} \approx \bar{z} + \kappa_{ri}(\widehat{z}_{ri} - \bar{z})\), where \(\kappa_{ri} = \widehat{\tau}^2 / (\widehat{\tau}^2 + s_{ri}^2) < 1\)). Entering decon_eb on the left-hand side of mixed_by() multiplies the true fixed-effect slope by \(\bar{\kappa} < 1\) (0.231 vs. 0.454 here), biasing population inference toward zero.


# Audit per-run NA gating rate and high-SE tail in Step 3/4 panels
panel_dt <- data.table::as.data.table(epochs$panel)
panel_dt[, .(
  pct_gated_na = 100 * mean(is.na(decon_demixed)),
  median_se    = median(se_demixed, na.rm = TRUE),
  p95_se       = quantile(se_demixed, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)
), by = run]

# Always pair decon_demixed + precision_weight_cohort when neural activity is the outcome
group_models <- mixed_by(group_panel, outcomes = "decon_demixed",
                         rhs_model_formulae = ~ rpe_within + (1 + rpe_within || id) + (1 | id:run),
                         split_on = c("parcel", "evt_time"), weights = "precision_weight_cohort")

For full guidance on min_bold_coverage, (T, O) de-mixing, and column-role assignment, see Step 3 and Step 4.



4. Steps 5 & 6: Multilevel Centering/Random-Slope Pitfalls and Connectivity Shared Noise






Figure 10.4: Healthy versus mis-specified group inference (Step 5) and trial-level connectivity (Step 6). A: Across 36 participants (16 target trials/person) where true within-person trial coupling is +0.45 but between-person trait coupling is -0.35 with participant slope SD 0.42, decomposing x_within + x_mean with (1 + x_within || id) recovers +0.434 (df = 35, blue). Entering uncentered x_raw conflates within- and between-person variance and flips the estimated slope to -0.258 (red), while omitting the random slope (1 | id) understates uncertainty with pooled-trial degrees of freedom (df = 573, amber). B: Participant connectivity slopes (ppi$subjects, term == "seed_c") across 16 participants where true seed-to-target neural coupling is 0.35 and shared cross-parcel measurement error is \(r_{ST} = 0.55\). M-MOMS with shared_error = "auto" recovers 0.295 (blue); stripping unit_error_cor / shared_noise_loading (shared_error = "zero") disattenuates shared noise up to 0.751 (red); naive OLS without measurement-error repair attenuates down to 0.178 (amber).



What to look for in Figure 10.4:

Within/between conflation and inflated degrees of freedom in Step 5 (Panel A): Any predictor that varies both across trials within a person (e.g., trial-by-trial RT, value, arousal) and in mean level across people (fast vs. slow responders, high vs. low baseline value) carries two distinct biological associations. Entering raw x_raw forces lmer() to estimate a precision-weighted blend of \(\beta_{\text{within}}\) and \(\beta_{\text{between}}\)—which can attenuate or even reverse the sign of the trial effect (-0.258 vs. +0.45). Equally important, inspect the df column of coef_df_reml: a within-person fixed effect tested across \(S = 36\) participants should have Satterthwaite df near \(S - 1\) (35), never in the hundreds (573), which signals that the random slope (1 + x_within || id) was omitted or collapsed to zero.
Asymmetric bias modes in Step 6 connectivity (Panel B): When deconvolved seed activity moves to the right-hand side as a noisy predictor (Target ~ Seed * Task), two opposing biases act simultaneously: seed estimation variance \(s_{S,i}^2\) attenuates naive OLS toward zero (0.178), while correlated scanner/physiological noise shared across parcels (\(r_{ST} > 0\)) inflates coupling. If you export panel to a plain .csv file without shared_noise_loading or the participant unit_error_cor matrix (forcing shared_error = "zero"), M-MOMS subtracts seed error variance in the denominator without subtracting shared error covariance in the numerator—magnifying shared noise (0.751). Passing the intact subject_epochs list (or preserving shared_noise_loading in tabular exports) allows shared_error = "auto" to correct both terms simultaneously (0.295).


# Step 5 audit: check Satterthwaite df on within-person terms (should scale with N_subjects, not N_trials)
subset(group_models$coef_df_reml, term == "rpe_within")[, c("parcel", "evt_time", "estimate", "std.error", "df")]

# Step 6 audit: confirm r_shared_error is non-zero when expected and check convergence
ppi <- decon_connectivity_repair(
  subject_epochs, seed_region = "Seed", target_region = "Target",
  covariates = "x_within", shared_error = "auto", method = "mmoms"
)
summary(ppi$subjects[, c("r_shared_error", "alpha_final", "converged")])

For complete coverage of group trajectory modeling and M-MOMS connectivity repair, see Step 5 and Step 6.


Simulation Details & Reproduction

All four healthy-versus-pathological figure pairs and Table 10.1 are generated from live medusa calls (estimate_crossrun_hrf(), deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(), diagnose_crossrun_recovery(), decon_epoch_regression(), mixed_by(), and decon_connectivity_repair()) with fixed seed 20261116:

Pair 1 (Steps 0 & 1): 3 runs \(\times\) 140 volumes at TR = 2.0 s, 16 jittered feedback events/run with true lag-0 RPE slope 0.60; compares valid_rows dummy masking (1:3) against physical truncation (Y[-c(1:3), ] with time_offset = 0) and onset-unit mis-specification (on_sec / tr_slow). Step 1 rho check simulates 36 parcels (true rho uniform on [0.30, 0.62]) with and without an unmodeled mid-run shim step + 0.008 Hz drift.
Pair 2 (Step 2): 3 runs \(\times\) 180 volumes at TR = 1.0 s; compares valid_rows censoring + automatic GCV \(\lambda_v\) + rwls = "auto" against lambda = 8.0 and an uncensored 91 s spike with rwls = "none".
Pair 3 (Steps 3 & 4): 3 runs \(\times\) 220 volumes (16 trials/run, Trial 16 at 215.5 s), comparing uncensored se_demixed against partial peak scrubbing on Trial 7 (3 frames) and full HRF scrubbing on Trial 11 (10 frames); plus a 16-participant cohort comparing decon_demixed + precision_weight_cohort against shrunken decon_eb as outcome in mixed_by() (true slope 0.50).
Pair 4 (Steps 5 & 6): Step 5 simulates \(S = 36\) participants (16 target trials/person, \(\beta_{\text{within}} = +0.45\), \(\beta_{\text{between}} = -0.35\), random slope SD 0.42). Step 6 simulates \(S = 16\) participants (80 trials/person, true seed-target slope 0.35, shared cross-parcel error correlation \(r_{ST} = 0.55\), trial SE 0.75).

title: Spatial Graph Pooling: Voxelwise and Parcel-Wise NIfTI Workflows
text:
Overview
Volumetric fMRI analysis faces a classic spatial dilemma whenever trial-by-trial dynamics are estimated across the cortex:
MEDuSA resolves this trade-off by pooling estimation evidence and variance parameters over a sparse, anatomically and functionally adaptive graph—without ever smoothing raw BOLD or deconvolved neural time series. Starting from a single NIfTI/atlas bundle (read_nifti_ts() or read_fmriprep_subject()), the spatial pooling architecture supports both full-resolution voxelwise mapping and precision-weighted parcel-panel modeling seamlessly:
Notice the synergy in Pathway B: even when your final group hypothesis in Step 5 or Step 6 is parcel-wise, running Step 1 with pooling = "graph" (parcel_boundary = "soft") and Step 2 with lambda_mode = "auto" before aggregating into parcels in Step 4 lets interior gray-matter and pial-rim voxels retain their distinct whiteners and HRF strata while Step 4’s exact multi-stratum operator (\(\sum_v u_v D_v F_v\)) combines them cleanly.

title: Spatial Graph Pooling: Voxelwise and Parcel-Wise NIfTI Workflows
text:
Pure single-voxel estimation preserves fine spatial specificity, but single 2 mm voxels have low per-trial signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Unpooled voxelwise fits suffer from noisy HRF latency selection in Step 1, unstable \(\text{AR}(p)\) autocorrelation estimates, oversmoothed global cross-validation (GCV) penalties in Step 2, and severe zero-collapse (\(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2 = 0\)) when estimating biological trial-to-trial variance in Step 3.
Rigid group-atlas parcel pooling boosts SNR dramatically when a participant’s functional organization aligns with nominal parcel borders. Yet individual functional boundaries routinely shift by 4–10 mm relative to group templates (such as Schaefer-200), sub-parcel focal hotspots can occupy \(< 15\%\) of a large parcel, and exterior pial-vein voxels carry much stronger physiological autocorrelation than interior gray matter inside the same parcel.
Traditional isotropic Gaussian BOLD smoothing avoids atlas rigidity only by blurring raw time series across sulcal CSF spaces, opposing gyral banks, and functional borders—destroying spatial resolution and inducing unmodeled spatial noise covariance.








NoteTwo Complementary Spatial Pathways from One NIfTI Bundle




Pathway A — Voxelwise Graph-Pooled Mapping (write_nifti_ts): read_nifti_ts(..., mask, atlas) \(\longrightarrow\) estimate_crossrun_hrf(..., pooling = "graph") \(\longrightarrow\) deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., lambda_mode = "auto") \(\longrightarrow\) decon_epoch_regression(..., tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb") \(\longrightarrow\) write_nifti_ts(..., reference = decon) \(\longrightarrow\) ggbrain
Pathway B — Parcel-Wise Multi-Stratum Panel (backproject_medusa): read_nifti_ts(..., mask, atlas) \(\longrightarrow\) estimate_crossrun_hrf(..., pooling = "graph") (preserving intra-parcel HRF & rim-noise heterogeneity) \(\longrightarrow\) deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., lambda_mode = "auto") \(\longrightarrow\) decon_epoch_regression(..., parcel_groups = ts$parcel_ids, restore_scale = TRUE, whiten_panel = TRUE, return_panel = TRUE) \(\longrightarrow\) mixed_by(..., weights = "precision_weight_cohort") \(\longrightarrow\) backproject_medusa(..., brain_mask = decon) \(\longrightarrow\) ggbrain

section: End-to-End Code Recipes with ggbrain
text:
End-to-End Code Recipes with ggbrain

Shared Step 0: Ingest 4D NIfTIs + Ribbon Mask + Atlas & Inspect Graph Topology
Whether your inputs come from fMRIPrep (read_fmriprep_subject(..., atlas = atlas_nii)) or preprocessed 4D NIfTI runs (read_nifti_ts()), MEDuSA validates grid/affine alignment up front and attaches voxel_map (i, j, k, x, y, z, linear_index, atlas_value), parcel_ids, and NIfTI geometry to the returned "medusa_nifti_ts" object.

library(medusa)
library(ggbrain)

# 1. Stream in-mask cortical ribbon time series + Schaefer parcel labels into memory
ts <- read_nifti_ts(
  niftis    = c("sub-01_run-01_bold.nii.gz",
                "sub-01_run-02_bold.nii.gz",
                "sub-01_run-03_bold.nii.gz"),
  mask      = "sub-01_space-MNI152NLin2009cAsym_desc-ribbon_mask.nii.gz",
  atlas     = "Schaefer2018_200Parcels_7Networks_2009c_2mm.nii.gz",
  tr        = 1.0,
  run_names = c("run1", "run2", "run3")
)

# Optional: build and inspect the cortical-sheet neighborhood graph explicitly
# (estimate_crossrun_hrf(..., pooling = "graph") builds this automatically when omitted)
g_geo <- build_spatial_graph(
  ts,
  spatial_fwhm    = 6,         # 6 mm cortical-sheet Gaussian kernel along 26-connected lattice
  parcel_boundary = "soft",    # soft cross-parcel relaxation when profiles agree
  metric          = "geodesic" # stops at out-of-mask CSF sulci and fissures
)



Pathway A: Voxelwise Graph-Pooled Analysis & ggbrain Visualization

# Step 1: Out-of-sample cortical-sheet HRF & REML AR(1) noise estimation
hrf_fit <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(
  bold            = ts,
  events          = events,
  kernel_grid     = hrf_library(tr = ts$tr, preset = "medusa"),
  pooling         = "graph",
  spatial_graph   = g_geo,
  parcel_boundary = "soft",
  amplitude_model = "trial",
  selection_mode  = "soft_average"
)

# Step 2: Event-informed continuous deconvolution with SNR-stratified smoothing
decon <- deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(
  bold        = ts,
  hrf_fit     = hrf_fit,
  scaling     = "noise_sd",
  lambda_mode = "auto"         # task-SNR tiers with monotone non-increasing smoothing
)

# Optional: export the realized per-voxel log10(lambda) SNR-tier map in 1 line
write_nifti_ts(
  log10(decon$settings$lambda_by_voxel),
  "sub-01_log10_lambda.nii.gz",
  reference = decon,
  fill      = NA_real_
)

# Step 3 (Voxelwise): Epoch de-mixing + edge-preserving neighborhood variance pooling
ep_vox <- decon_epoch_regression(
  deconvolution    = decon,
  covariates       = covariates,       # e.g., list(run1 = data.frame(rpe = ...), ...)
  events           = events,
  target_condition = "feedback",
  lags             = -1:3,
  restore_scale    = TRUE,
  tau2_shrinkage   = "graph_eb"        # pre-truncation neighborhood shrinkage + hotspot guard
)

# Export lag = 0 s voxelwise GLS t-map directly using decon's carried NIfTI geometry
lag0_vox <- subset(ep_vox$coefficients, lag == 0 & term == "rpe")
t_vec    <- stats::setNames(lag0_vox$t_gls, lag0_vox$voxel)
write_nifti_ts(t_vec, "sub-01_feedback_rpe_t_lag0.nii.gz", reference = decon, fill = NA_real_)

# Render axial brain map with Schaefer parcel outlines in ggbrain
t1_nii    <- system.file("extdata", "mni_template_2009c_2mm.nii.gz", package = "ggbrain")
atlas_nii <- system.file("extdata", "Schaefer_200_7networks_2009c_2mm.nii.gz", package = "ggbrain")

gg_vox <- ggbrain(bg_color = "white") +
  images(c(underlay = t1_nii, atlas = atlas_nii, tmap = "sub-01_feedback_rpe_t_lag0.nii.gz")) +
  slices(c("z = 6", "z = 8", "z = 10")) +
  geom_brain("underlay[underlay > 8]",
             fill_scale = ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(low = "#30363D", high = "#E6ECF0"),
             show_legend = FALSE) +
  geom_brain("tmap[abs(tmap) > 2.0]",
             fill_scale = scale_fill_bisided(name = "GLS t", symmetric = TRUE)) +
  geom_outline("atlas[atlas > 0]", mapping = ggplot2::aes(group = value),
               outline = "#1F2933", size = 1, alpha = 0.35, show_legend = FALSE)
plot(gg_vox)



Pathway B: Parcel-Wise Multi-Stratum Panel, Cohort mixed_by(), & ggbrain Map

# Step 4 (inside decon_epoch_regression): Exact multi-stratum parcel pooling
# Reuses the exact same graph-pooled `decon` object from Step 2
ep_parcel <- decon_epoch_regression(
  deconvolution    = decon,
  covariates       = covariates,
  events           = events,
  target_condition = "feedback",
  lags             = -1:3,
  parcel_groups    = ts$parcel_ids,    # triggers Step 4 continuous parcel aggregation
  restore_scale    = TRUE,
  whiten_panel     = TRUE,
  return_panel     = TRUE
)

# Attach participant ID and stack across subjects for Step 5 mixed_by()
panel_sub <- data.table::as.data.table(ep_parcel$panel)
panel_sub[, id := "sub-01"]
# ... repeat across cohort into `group_panel <- data.table::rbindlist(subject_panels)` ...

group_fit <- mixed_by(
  data               = group_panel,
  outcomes           = "decon_demixed",
  rhs_model_formulae = ~ rpe + (1 + rpe || id),
  split_on           = c("parcel", "evt_time"),
  weights            = "precision_weight_cohort",
  padjust_by         = "term",
  padjust_method     = "BY"
)

# Backproject Schaefer parcels directly onto 3D NIfTI via decon's carried map
# (`parcel` character IDs and `evt_time` are auto-detected and matched to `atlas_value`)
coef_lag0 <- subset(group_fit$coef_df_reml, term == "rpe" & evt_time == 0)

nii_paths <- backproject_medusa(
  coef_df    = coef_lag0,
  brain_mask = decon,                  # uses carried voxel_map$atlas_value & geometry directly
  plot_cols  = c("estimate", "statistic"),
  output_dir = "group_maps",
  fill       = NA_real_
)

# Plot group parcel statistic map in ggbrain
gg_par <- ggbrain(bg_color = "white") +
  images(c(underlay = t1_nii, atlas = atlas_nii, gstat = "group_maps/statistic_rpe.nii.gz")) +
  slices("z = 8", title = "Cohort feedback RPE t-map (lag = 0 s)") +
  geom_brain("underlay[underlay > 8]",
             fill_scale = ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient(low = "#30363D", high = "#E6ECF0"),
             show_legend = FALSE) +
  geom_brain("gstat[!is.na(gstat)]",
             fill_scale = scale_fill_bisided(name = "Group t", symmetric = TRUE)) +
  geom_outline("atlas[atlas > 0]", mapping = ggplot2::aes(group = value),
               outline = "#1F2933", size = 1, alpha = 0.4, show_legend = FALSE)
plot(gg_par)

section: Volumetric Benchmark on the MNI152 Cortical Ribbon
text:
Volumetric Benchmark on the MNI152 Cortical Ribbon
To evaluate every component of the spatial and parcel pooling pipeline against known ground truth on genuine human cortical folding, simulate_spatial_pooling.R constructs a 3-slice cortical gray-matter ribbon slab (\(z = 6, 8, 10\text{ mm}\), V = 6,655 voxels across 61 Schaefer-200 parcels) from mni_template_2009c_2mm.nii.gz and Schaefer_200_7networks_2009c_2mm.nii.gz. Three 4D NIfTI runs (TR = 1.0 s, 170 TRs/run, 22 jittered cue + feedback trials per run = 66 total target trials with a unit-variance signed rpe covariate) are written to disk and ingested via read_nifti_ts().
Four realistic anatomical and physiological testbeds are embedded simultaneously on the cortical sheet:

Cross-fissure barrier + parcel-aligned active cortex (Parcels 10 & 89 vs. 109 & 194): Left Calcarine (Parcel 10, fast 2.8 s HRF peak, \(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = +0.55\)) and Left Superior Medial PFC (Parcel 89, slow 6.8 s HRF peak, \(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = +0.50\)) are homogeneously active across their entire parcel boundaries, while their homologous right-hemisphere neighbors across the 2–4 mm interhemispheric CSF gap (Parcels 109 & 194, canonical 5.1 s HRF peak) are purely null for feedback RPE (\(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = 0, \tau_{\text{bio}} = 0\)).
Shifted individual functional/vascular border (Parcels 78 & 79, Left Posterior Temporal Cortex): While the group Schaefer boundary between Parcel 79 and Parcel 78 sits near \(y = -55\text{ mm}\) on \(z = 8\text{ mm}\), this participant’s true neurovascular and computational transition sits anteriorly at \(y = -43\text{ mm}\)—splitting Parcel 78 cleanly into a posterior slow-HRF negative-RPE zone (\(y \le -43\text{ mm}\), 6.8 s HRF peak, \(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = -0.62\)) and an anterior fast-HRF positive-RPE zone (\(y > -43\text{ mm}\), 2.8 s HRF peak, \(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = +0.62\)).
Sub-parcel focal hotspot (Parcel 155, Right Insula): A compact 30-voxel spherical nucleus (\(r \le 4.6\text{ mm}\) around \((42, 6, 8)\), occupying \(13.3\%\) of Parcel 155’s 225 voxels) exhibits strong positive RPE coding (\(\beta_{\text{RPE}} = +0.92, \tau_{\text{bio}} = 0.78\)) surrounded by 195 quiet insular voxels.
Whole-ribbon pial-vein vs. gray-matter noise heterogeneity: Exterior cortical rim voxels bordering CSF (23.0% of the mask) generate high temporal autocorrelation (\(\rho = 0.76, \sigma = 0.38\)) compared to interior gray matter (\(\rho = 0.28, \sigma = 0.21\)), driven by spatially correlated \(\text{AR}(1)\) innovations along the geodesic sheet.



1. Cortical-Sheet (Geodesic) Neighborhoods vs. 3D Euclidean Shortcuts (build_spatial_graph())
On folded cortex, two gyral banks separated by a dark CSF sulcus or longitudinal fissure are often only 2–5 mm apart in 3D Euclidean space while lying centimeters apart along the cortical sheet. When build_spatial_graph() receives a volumetric "medusa_nifti_ts" object (or 3D mask/voxel_map carrying integer lattice indices i, j, k), metric = "auto" measures shortest-path step distances strictly through connected in-mask gray-matter voxels (metric = "geodesic", computed on the 26-neighbor lattice via Dijkstra’s algorithm in physical millimeter world coordinates: \(2\text{ mm}\) face, \(2\sqrt{2}\text{ mm}\) edge-diagonal, \(2\sqrt{3}\text{ mm}\) corner-diagonal).






Figure 11.1: Geodesic lattice topology vs. 3D Euclidean cross-fissure shortcuts on the MNI152 cortical ribbon (z = 8 mm).



In our slab, an unconstrained 6 mm Euclidean graph (metric = "euclidean") creates 8,051 directed shortcut edges that jump across out-of-mask CSF gaps (547 in-plane pairs on \(z = 8\text{ mm}\) alone; orange segments in Figure 11.1, right). Along the posterior midline, those shortcuts bleed Left Calcarine’s fast HRF across the interhemispheric CSF cleft onto Right Calcarine’s medial rim (Parcel 109 rim HRF MAE = 0.828 s vs. 0.617 s under geodesic pooling).



2. Step 1 Edge-Preserving HRF Pooling & Soft Parcel Relaxation
Geodesic distance alone prevents cross-CSF shortcuts where the mask resolves the sulcus, yet two challenges remain: (a) at 2 mm resolution, narrow sulci are sometimes bridged by partial-volumed voxels, and (b) functional transitions occur inside continuous gyri where group parcel boundaries are misregistered. estimate_crossrun_hrf(..., pooling = "graph") addresses both by weighting nearby cortical neighbors by both anatomical sheet proximity and out-of-sample functional similarity (an edge-preserving bilateral graph filter):

Strict target-run exclusion: For held-out target run \(r\), training score profiles, noise \((\hat{\rho}^{(-r)}, \log\hat{\sigma}^{(-r)})\), and spatial noise correlations are computed exclusively from runs \(s \neq r\).
Concordance weighting & anti-correlation stopping: Neighbor \(v\)’s influence on focal voxel \(u\) combines cortical-sheet Gaussian proximity with the noise-disattenuated cross-run correlation between their candidate HRF score profiles (\(\tilde{c}_{uv}\)). Negative concordance triggers a sharp brake \(\exp(-3.5\gamma c_-^2)\), halting pooling across opposite-tuned or distinct vascular borders even on a continuous gyral ribbon.
Soft cross-parcel relaxation (parcel_boundary = "soft", parcel_cross_weight = 0.35): Cross-parcel edges start downweighted at 0.35 when task signal is ambiguous, but smoothly relax toward \(1.0\) when neighboring voxels across a nominal atlas line share strong positive out-of-sample candidate concordance.
Spatial noise calibration & stratum grouping: Combined cross-run evidence is scaled to account for shared local scanner noise between neighbors so correlated background noise never triggers false HRF switches in null cortex, and soft-averaged kernels are grouped into at most max_hrf_strata = 48L representative waveforms so Step 2 operator evaluation stays fast.







Figure 11.2: Step 1 HRF peak-latency recovery across single-voxel, group-parcel, and bilateral geodesic graph pooling.

As shown in Figure 11.2 and Table 11.1, single-voxel selection (pooling = "voxel") is unbiased on average but noisy (Active MAE = 1.085 s). Group-parcel pooling (pooling = "parcel") denoises aligned parcels (10 and 89) well, but averages the fast (2.8 s) and slow (6.8 s) domains inside Parcel 78 into a flat intermediate plateau (Shifted Parcel 78 MAE = 2.062 s). Bilateral geodesic graph pooling with parcel_boundary = "soft" achieves the lowest error globally (0.334 s) and inside shifted Parcel 78 (0.430 s), tracking the participant’s true \(y = -43\text{ mm}\) transition cleanly.



3. Bilateral REML Noise Smoothing at Pial-Vein Borders
In Step 1, temporal autocorrelation (\(\rho\)) and marginal innovation scale (\(\log\hat{\sigma}\)) vary sharply at tissue boundaries: pial surface veins and CSF-adjacent voxels exhibit strong physiological pulsation (\(\rho = 0.76\)), whereas interior gray matter is much whiter (\(\rho = 0.28\)). Pooling noise uniformly across whole Schaefer parcels contaminates interior gray matter with pial-rim autocorrelation (Figure 11.3, orange violins).
Under pooling = "graph", Step 1 applies an edge-preserving (bilateral) noise filter that multiplies cortical-sheet proximity weights by similarity in pilot autocorrelation and log noise scale \((\Delta\hat{\rho}, \Delta\log\hat{\sigma})\) before grouping voxels into up to max_noise_strata = 10L noise strata. High-\(\rho\) rim voxels borrow strength along the pial rim while deep gray-matter voxels pool with interior gray matter, cutting single-voxel \(\hat{\rho}\) RMSE nearly in half in both compartments without blurring the tissue boundary (Table 11.1).






Figure 11.3: Bilateral REML noise smoothing preserves the sharp boundary between pial-vein/CSF rim autocorrelation and interior gray matter.






4. Step 2 SNR-Stratified Deconvolution (lambda_mode = "auto")
In volumetric fMRI, most gray-matter voxels exhibit weak or zero task modulation for any specific contrast while focal task-engaged regions carry high out-of-sample task \(R^2\). A single global deconvolution penalty (lambda_mode = "global") is forced into an awkward compromise: low enough to avoid crushing active peaks, yet leaving high-frequency inverse-filter noise across thousands of silent background voxels.
deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., lambda_mode = "auto") addresses this by stratifying voxels into task-SNR tiers and enforcing that smoothing never increases as task SNR rises:

Cross-run significance gate: Out-of-sample Step 1 run \(p\)-values are combined via Fisher’s method and adjusted across voxels via Benjamini–Hochberg FDR. On pure-null maps (no voxels passing \(q \le 0.10\)), "auto" collapses safely to 1 global stratum.
Edge-preserving task-\(R^2\) tiers: When task signal is present, Step 1 task \(R^2\) is stabilized locally over the cortical graph, separating a quiet background tier (\(q > 0.20\), \(R^2_{\text{stab}} < 0.025\)) from ascending active task-SNR quantiles (max_lambda_strata = 4L).
Monotone smoothing across tiers: Each tier tunes \(\lambda\) on its relevant cross-validation objective (pure prewhitened GCV + background level stability in the quiet tier; modulation-transfer-guarded GCV in active tiers), and a monotone ordering constraint (weighted pool-adjacent-violators, PAVA) enforces \(\lambda_{\text{quiet}} \ge \lambda_{\text{low-SNR}} \ge \dots \ge \lambda_{\text{high-SNR}}\). Crucially, each voxel’s exact \(\lambda_v\) is carried forward into Steps 3 and 4.







Figure 11.4: Step 2 SNR-stratified GCV tuning assigns strong noise suppression to quiet cortex while preserving sharp phasic impulses in focal active cortex.

Stratified tuning suppresses continuous background standard deviation in null voxels from 2.786 (global \(\lambda\)) down to 0.930 while maintaining crisp neural spike recovery in the 30-voxel Right Insula hotspot (\(r =\) 0.247 with generating continuous impulses; Figure 11.4).



5. Step 3 Voxelwise Bilateral Graph-EB (tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb")
In Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()), GLS precision weights and ZCA trial whitening depend on partitioning total trial-to-trial variance into propagated observation-noise variance \(s_{\text{obs},u}^2\) (known analytically from the Step 1–2 operator) and latent biological trial-to-trial variance \(\tau_{\text{bio},u}^2\). At the single-voxel level with 50–80 trials, raw method-of-moments estimation \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{raw},u}^2 = \hat{\sigma}_{\text{tot},u}^2 - s_{\text{obs},u}^2\) has wide sampling variance, creating two simultaneous distortions when truncated at zero (\(\max(0, \hat{\tau}_{\text{raw},u}^2)\)):

Active-cortex zero-collapse: 34.2% of genuinely active voxels randomly draw \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{raw},u}^2 \le 0\) and collapse to \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2 = 0\), reducing trial weights to pure inverse-measurement-error weights.
Null-cortex truncation bias: Nearly half of true \(\tau_{\text{bio}}^2 = 0\) voxels draw positive noise fluctuations, inflating average null \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) above zero (0.156).
Meanwhile, global Empirical Bayes (tau2_shrinkage = "eb") pools all 6,655 voxels toward one whole-slab prior dominated by the 85% null background—leaving 35.1% active zero-collapse unaddressed while pulling the 30-voxel Right Insula hotspot downward relative to local bilateral pooling (hotspot mean \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2 =\) 0.602 vs. 0.800 under Graph-EB).

tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb" (the automatic setting under tau2_shrinkage = "auto" whenever deconvolution carries a spatial graph or voxel_map coordinates in voxelwise mode) addresses all three issues:

Pre-truncation scale-free pooling: Shrinks the untruncated dimensionless ratio \(\hat{\theta}_u = \hat{\tau}_{\text{raw},u}^2 / s_{\text{obs},u}^2\) across concordant cortical neighbors before applying \(\max(0, \cdot)\)—allowing positive and negative estimation errors in null cortex to cancel symmetrically around zero while reducing active zero-collapse to 21.7%.
Discounting shared scanner noise between neighbors: Because adjacent voxels share correlated scanner innovations (noise_innovations), their squared trial errors also covary (\(\operatorname{Corr}(Z_u^2, Z_v^2) = \rho_{uv}^2\) under Gaussian errors, by Isserlis’ identity); discounting for \(\rho_{uv}^2\) prevents shared noise from being mistaken for independent spatial replication.
Edge-preserving border stopping & focal hotspot protection: Downweights neighbors whose pilot variance ratios or trial-residual patterns disagree across a functional border, and caps how far any individual voxel can be pulled toward its neighborhood prior at \(2.5\sigma_u\) (Efron–Morris limited-translation shrinkage) so isolated focal hotspots retain their true biological variance (0.800 in the Right Insula core; Figure 11.5). Residual error scales ([scale_unw, scale_pw, scale_gls]) are similarly stabilized across concordant neighbors (Empirical-Bayes variance moderation; Smyth, 2004) to boost \(t\)-statistic degrees of freedom without ever smoothing trial slopes \(\hat{\beta}_u\).

The results crystallize the practical modeling guidance:

When functional anatomy aligns with the parcellation (Parcels 10 & 89): Step 4 parcel aggregation pools continuous deconvolved time series across 154–341 voxels using cross-run precision weights while propagating spatial innovation correlation accurately—cutting slope RMSE more than \(3\times\) relative to single voxels and achieving 100% detection power, with clean cohort-level inference in Step 5 (mixed_by() + BY control; bold black parcel outlines in Figure 11.6, Panel 4).
When individual functional boundaries shift across a parcel (Parcel 78): Averaging the posterior negative-RPE sub-domain (\(\beta = -0.62\)) and anterior positive-RPE sub-domain (\(\beta = +0.62\)) inside Parcel 78 cancels the parcel slope to nearly zero. Voxelwise Graph-EB resolves both sub-domains cleanly on the cortical ribbon without blurring across the \(y = -43\text{ mm}\) border.
When an effect is restricted to a sub-parcel focal nucleus (Right Insula Parcel 155 core): Averaging 30 active hotspot voxels with 195 silent surround voxels dilutes the parcel slope by nearly \(85\%\). Voxelwise Graph-EB—protected by SNR-stratified Step 2 \(\lambda\) and Efron–Morris limited translation—preserves the focal hotspot amplitude and detects it reliably while keeping false positives controlled across the 55 null parcels.



Practical Defaults for Atlas-Free, Atlas-Carrying, and Dense Parcellations

Default pooling = "voxel" on atlas-free vs. atlas-carrying NIfTIs: On atlas-free NIfTI inputs (read_nifti_ts(..., atlas = NULL)), estimate_crossrun_hrf(ts, ...) keeps pooling = "voxel" as a single-voxel fit unless you opt into pooling = "graph", whereas Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression(..., tau2_shrinkage = "auto")) still builds the 26-connected cortical neighborhood graph automatically from decon$voxel_map to stabilize voxelwise trial variances ("graph_eb"). On atlas-carrying NIfTI inputs, default pooling = "voxel" retains individual HRFs for task-supported voxels (spatial_strength = 0), pools AR(\(p\)) noise within parcels, and uses the parcel HRF as a "fallback_parcel" reference on low-SNR voxels; setting pooling = "graph" upgrades both HRF evidence and REML noise to edge-preserving cortical-sheet pooling across all voxels.
Parcel-level Graph-EB across dense parcellations (Schaefer-400 / 1000): When aggregate_by_parcel = TRUE (parcel_groups = ...) and no parcel-level spatial_graph is supplied, tau2_shrinkage = "auto" resolves to "none" because standard coarse parcels already have high multi-voxel SNR. For fine-grained parcellations with many small parcels, set tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb" explicitly so decon_epoch_regression() constructs a precision-weighted 3D parcel-centroid Euclidean graph from decon$voxel_map (or supply cortical-surface geodesic parcel distances via build_spatial_graph(parcel_dist_mat)).

title: Spatial Graph Pooling: Voxelwise and Parcel-Wise NIfTI Workflows
section: Mathematical Details
text:
Mathematical Details


Show mathematical formulation of bilateral geodesic graph pooling, SNR-stratified PAVA, and pre-truncation Graph-EB


1. Sparse Geodesic CSR Graph and Bilateral Step 1 Weights
Let \(G = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})\) denote the sparse compressed-sparse-row (CSR) neighborhood graph built by build_spatial_graph() with Gaussian bandwidth \(\sigma_d = \text{FWHM} / \sqrt{8 \ln 2}\) and cutoff radius \(r_{\max} = 2\sigma_d\) (capped at \(k_{\max} = 32\) nearest in-mask neighbors via 26-connected lattice Dijkstra distances \(d_{\text{geo}}(u, v)\)).
For held-out target run \(r\), let \(S_u^{(-r)} \in \mathbb{R}^K\) denote voxel \(u\)’s out-of-sample adjusted partial-\(R^2\) profile across the \(K\)-kernel physiological HRF manifold, and let \((\hat{\rho}_u^{(-r)}, \log\hat{\sigma}_u^{(-r)})\) denote its target-excluded pilot \(\text{AR}(1)\) parameters. Neighbor \(v \in \mathcal{N}(u)\) receives bilateral HRF pooling weight: \[
w_{uv}^{(-r)} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{d_{\text{geo}}(u,v)^2}{2\sigma_d^2}\right) \cdot \pi_{uv} \cdot \exp\!\left(-3.5\,\gamma\,\max(0, -\tilde{c}_{uv})^2\right)
\] where \(\tilde{c}_{uv} \in [-1, 1]\) is the Spearman-disattenuated cross-run candidate-profile correlation between \(u\) and \(v\), and the parcel boundary factor \(\pi_{uv}\) equals \(1\) when \(g_u = g_v\), \(0\) under parcel_boundary = "hard", and smoothly interpolates from parcel_cross_weight (\(w_{\times} = 0.35\)) toward \(1\) as positive concordance \(c_+ = \max(0, \tilde{c}_{uv})\) increases under parcel_boundary = "soft": \[
\pi_{uv}^{\text{soft}} = w_{\times} + (1 - w_{\times})\, c_+^2 \quad (g_u \neq g_v).
\] To calibrate out-of-sample signal gating against spatially correlated scanner innovations \(Z^{(-r)}\), csr_quad_cor_cpp() evaluates the exact quadratic spatial correlation inflation factor on the normalized graph weights \(\tilde{w}_{uv} = w_{uv}^{(-r)} / \sum_{v'} w_{uv'}^{(-r)}\) in \(O(m k_{\max}^2 V)\) time: \[
v_{\text{quad}, u}^{(-r)} = \sum_{a \in \mathcal{N}(u) \cup \{u\}} \sum_{b \in \mathcal{N}(u) \cup \{u\}} \tilde{w}_{ua}\,\tilde{w}_{ub}\,\widehat{\operatorname{Corr}}\!\left(z_a^{(-r)}, z_b^{(-r)}\right)^2,
\] scaling Stouffer–Cauchy combined run evidence by \((v_{\text{quad}, u}^{(-r)})^{-1/2}\).


2. Step 2 SNR-Stratified Regularization with Weighted PAVA
Let \(\tilde{R}_u^2\) be the graph-stabilized out-of-sample Step 1 task \(R^2\) and \(q_u\) the Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted Fisher combination \(p\)-value across runs. When \(\min_u q_u \le 0.10\), voxels are partitioned into a quiet background tier (\(q_u > 0.20\) and \(\tilde{R}_u^2 < 0.025\)) and up to \(M - 1\) ascending active SNR quantiles with unconstrained tier penalties \((\hat{\lambda}_1, \dots, \hat{\lambda}_M)\). Monotone non-increasing smoothness penalties \(\lambda_1^\star \ge \lambda_2^\star \ge \dots \ge \lambda_M^\star\) are obtained via weighted pool-adjacent-violators: \[
\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\star = \arg\min_{\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_M} \sum_{m=1}^M n_m \left(\log \lambda_m - \log \hat{\lambda}_m\right)^2.
\]


3. Step 3 Pre-Truncation Bilateral Graph-EB with Isserlis Discount & Efron–Morris Guard
At lag \(\tau\), let \(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{tot}, u}^2\) be voxel \(u\)’s residual trial variance across \(N\) target trials (with effective residual degrees of freedom \(\nu_u\)) and \(s_{\text{obs}, u}^2\) its operator-propagated measurement-error variance. Define the untruncated dimensionless biological-to-measurement variance ratio: \[
\hat{\theta}_u = \frac{\hat{\tau}_{\text{raw}, u}^2}{s_{\text{obs}, u}^2} = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_{\text{tot}, u}^2 - s_{\text{obs}, u}^2}{s_{\text{obs}, u}^2}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}_u) \approx v_u = \frac{2}{\nu_u}\bigl(1 + \max(0, \tilde{\theta}_u)\bigr)^2.
\] For bilateral edge weights \(\alpha_{uv}\) (combining geodesic Gaussian kernel, Cauchy pilot-jump factor \([1 + (\tilde{\theta}_u - \tilde{\theta}_v)^2 / s_0^2]^{-1}\), and orthogonalized trial-residual sign concordance), Gaussian innovations with spatial correlation \(\rho_{ab}\) obey Isserlis’ identity \(\operatorname{Corr}(Z_a^2, Z_b^2) = \rho_{ab}^2\). Accounting for self-weight \(\alpha_{uu}\) and neighbor error correlation yields the local prior mean \(\mu_{\text{loc}, u}\), prior variance \(\tau_{\text{prior}, u}^2\), shrinkage factor \(B_u = v_u / (v_u + \tau_{\text{prior}, u}^2)\), and Efron–Morris limited-translation posterior estimate (\(M_{\text{EM}} = 2.5\)): \[
\theta_u^{\text{raw-EB}} = (1 - B_u)\,\hat{\theta}_u + B_u\,\mu_{\text{loc}, u}, \qquad
\theta_u^{\text{EM}} = \hat{\theta}_u + \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\theta_u^{\text{raw-EB}} - \hat{\theta}_u,\; -M_{\text{EM}}\sqrt{v_u},\; +M_{\text{EM}}\sqrt{v_u}\right),
\] followed only at the end by non-negativity truncation \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}, u}^2 = s_{\text{obs}, u}^2 \max(0, \theta_u^{\text{EM}})\).
Compiled C++ and internal R kernels (src/spatial_graph_kernels.cpp, R/spatial_graph.R, R/crossrun_hrf.R): csr_hrf_graph_pool_cpp(), csr_bilateral_noise_smooth_cpp() (called by hrf_estimate_noise()), csr_quad_cor_cpp(), smooth_scalar_csr_cpp(), hrf_pava_nonincreasing(), graph_eb_tau2_csr_cpp(), and moderate_scale_csr_cpp().

title: From BOLD Noise to M-MOM Error Variances
text:
1. Estimate the BOLD noise
MEDuSA estimates how much observation noise enters each recovered trial activity estimate. When deconvolved neural activity becomes a predictor in Step 6 (Target ~ Seed * Task or Behavior ~ Neural), Method-of-Moments measurement-error correction (medusa_fit_mmom() / decon_connectivity_repair()) needs its measurement-error variance, typically se_demixed^2, expressed in the exact same units as the predictor. This trial-level measurement variance is distinct from the standard error of a fitted group regression coefficient.
\[
\underbrace{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\varepsilon_r)}_{\text{BOLD noise (Step 1)}}
\ \longrightarrow\
\underbrace{\widehat\Omega_{r,\tau}}_{\text{trial error covariance (Steps 3–4)}}
\ \longrightarrow\
\underbrace{s_{ri}=\sqrt{[\widehat\Omega_{r,\tau}]_{ii}}}_{\text{trial SE (`se_demixed`)}}
\ \longrightarrow\
\underbrace{\Psi_i}_{\text{M-MOM error block (Step 6)}}.
\]
For one run \(r\) and voxel, write \(y_r = H_r a_r + Z_r\gamma_r + \varepsilon_r\), with
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_r) = \sigma_{\rm obs}^2 \Sigma_{\rm cor}.
\]
Here \(H\) applies the selected HRF and \(Z\) contains nuisance terms. Step 1’s pooled AR(1) profile REML and shrunk residual AR(\(q\)) correction define a cascaded AR(\(p\)) temporal correlation model \(\Sigma_{\rm cor}\) (evaluated at the exact retained acquisition indices \(\Gamma_N[\text{rows}, \text{rows}]\) when frames are censored). The amplitude \(\sigma_{\rm obs}\) is the marginal observation-noise SD, not the white-noise innovation SD.
In deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., scaling = "noise_sd"), MEDuSA estimates \(\sigma_{\rm obs}\) primarily from outlier-trimmed, leverage-adjusted task-free GLS residuals (Winsorized GLS residuals) after conditioning on Step 1’s cross-fitted HRF and post-selection AR(\(p\)) correlation model, converting white-noise innovation scale to stationary marginal observation scale. As a standalone estimator for single-run deconvolve_reglin(), omitted-event safeguard, and low-degrees-of-freedom fallback, MEDuSA estimates marginal noise amplitude from second differences \(d_t = y_t - 2y_{t-1} + y_{t-2}\), which suppress smooth BOLD signal (combining sample SD with outlier-resistant median absolute deviation, \(\operatorname{MAD}_0\)):
\[
\widehat\sigma_{\rm obs}
=\frac{0.5\,\operatorname{SD}(d)+0.5\,\operatorname{MAD}_0(d)}
       {\sqrt{6-8\widehat r_1+2\widehat r_2}}.
\]
The normal-consistent MAD is centered at zero, and the denominator adjusts analytically for lag-1 and lag-2 autocorrelation. Crucially, BOLD noise is estimated prior to downstream behavioral or connectivity regressions.

title: From BOLD Noise to M-MOM Error Variances
section: 2. Propagate noise through the linear inverse and epoch operators
text:
2. Propagate noise through the linear inverse and epoch operators
With HRF, regularization penalty, frame weights, nuisance projection, and noise parameters held fixed, deconvolution is a linear map \(\widehat{a}_r = D_r \tilde{y}_{r,o}\). Event interpolation, gain restoration, and Step 3’s cross-event and within-trial demixing combine with \(D_r\) into a composite linear trial-readout operator \(B_{r,\tau}\). Therefore, conditional on the learned operators,
\[
\Omega_{r,\tau,\rm raw}
=\sigma_{\rm eff}^2\,\widetilde B_{r,\tau}\Sigma_{\rm cor}\widetilde B_{r,\tau}^\top,
\]
where \(\widetilde B_{r,\tau}\) incorporates input run-centering and inverse nuisance/whitening projections. In our independent numerical verification (worked/mmom-check.R), MEDuSA’s operator-propagated cascade covariance matches an explicit stationary AR(3) Toeplitz reference to 1.11e-16.
Run-centered finite-sample calibration. Because downstream within-run regressions center trial series within each run, decon_epoch_regression() centers the propagated \(m \times m\) trial error covariance (\(m > 1\) valid trials) and applies a finite-sample degrees-of-freedom factor \((1 - 1/m)^{-1}\) (analogous to Bessel’s sample-variance correction):
\[
Q_m = I_m - \frac{\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top}{m},\qquad
\widehat\Omega_{r,\tau} = \frac{Q_m\Omega_{r,\tau,\rm raw}Q_m}{1-1/m},
\] \[
\boxed{\texttt{se\_demixed}_{ri} = \sqrt{\max(0, [\widehat\Omega_{r,\tau}]_{ii})}}.
\]
Thus se_demixed represents a run-centered, finite-sample-calibrated trial measurement SE. The full off-diagonal \(\widehat\Omega_{r,\tau}\) is used internally for biological variance estimation (tau2_bio) and optional ZCA panel whitening, while the panel exports diagonal se_demixed and adjacent-trial error autocorrelation error_ac1.

Keep units and spatial aggregation consistent
If \(d\) is the Step 2 scaling divisor, restore_scale = FALSE uses \(\sigma_{\rm eff} = \widehat\sigma_{\rm obs} / d\), whereas restore_scale = TRUE restores \(\sigma_{\rm eff} = \widehat\sigma_{\rm obs}\) so activity and se_demixed scale together. Rescaling a predictor by \(c\) requires rescaling its SE by \(|c|\) and its error variance by \(c^2\).
In Step 4, parcel aggregation forms precision-weighted parcel series using task-free Step 2 whitened noise_innovations to estimate both within-parcel spatial noise covariance (propagated through exact operator strata) and low-rank cross-parcel shared_noise_loading vectors that survive rbindlist() stacking.

title: From BOLD Noise to M-MOM Error Variances
section: 3. Supply measurement-error moments to M-MOM
text:
3. Supply measurement-error moments to M-MOM
For an observed de-mixed trial predictor \(\widehat{z}_{S,i} = \theta_{S,i} + u_i\), set \(\psi_i = \operatorname{Var}(u_i) = \texttt{se\_demixed}_{S,i}^2\). A single noisy neural predictor uses \(\Psi_i = [\psi_i]\). For a PPI design \((\widehat{z}_{S,i},\, x_i,\, \widehat{z}_{S,i} x_i)\) with error-free modulator \(x_i\),
\[
\Psi_i = \psi_i
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & x_i\\
0 & 0 & 0\\
x_i & 0 & x_i^2
\end{bmatrix}.
\]



Exported quantity
Role in downstream modeling




se_demixed^2
Predictor measurement-error variance (\(\psi_i\)) for decon_demixed in M-MOM / M-MOMS


se_whitened^2
Transformed trial error variance for decon_demixed_whitened


shared_noise_loading / unit_error_cor
Task-free cross-parcel noise innovation basis used by shared_error = "auto" to estimate \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i)\) (err_xy)


tau2_bio
Estimated latent biological trial-to-trial variance (not measurement error)


precision_weight / precision_weight_cohort
Inverse total trial variance \((\widehat\tau_{\rm eff}^2 + s_i^2)^{-1}\) for Step 5 outcome weighting (never substitute for \(\Psi_i\))


fit$coefficients$se
Standard error of an estimated M-MOM regression slope




Minimal applied interface (medusa_fit_mmom())
When decon_connectivity_repair() handles parcel-to-parcel connectivity and PPI automatically, it calls medusa_fit_mmom() under the hood. You can also call medusa_fit_mmom() directly when predicting a behavioral outcome (rt, choice log-odds score, pupillometry) from one or more deconvolved parcel readouts within a participant:


Show supporting code
library(medusa)
set.seed(20261110)
n <- 300L
latent <- rnorm(n)
task <- rnorm(n)
se <- runif(n, 0.3, 0.7)
d <- data.frame(
  decon_demixed = latent + rnorm(n, sd = se),
  se_demixed = se,
  task = task,
  outcome = 0.6 * latent + 0.25 * task + rnorm(n, sd = 0.8)
)



stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.matrix(d))), all(d$se_demixed >= 0))
X <- cbind(neural = d$decon_demixed, task = d$task) # intercept handled internally
Psi <- array(0, dim = c(ncol(X), ncol(X), nrow(X)))
Psi[1, 1, ] <- d$se_demixed^2

fit <- medusa_fit_mmom(
  outcome = d$outcome,
  predictors = X,
  err_x = Psi,                 # q x q x N predictor error covariance blocks
  err_y = rep(0, nrow(d)),     # outcome measurement error variance (0 for error-free behavior)
  regularization = "step_up"   # M-MOMS positive-definiteness safeguard

title: From BOLD Noise to M-MOM Error Variances
section: 4. Distributional assumptions and scope conditions
text:
4. Distributional assumptions and scope conditions

Operator covariance propagation is distribution-free up to second moments: \(\operatorname{Cov}(B\varepsilon) = B\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)B^\top\) requires finite second moments and an accurate temporal/spatial noise correlation model, not Gaussianity—though Winsorized/MAD scale factors calibrate to Gaussian efficiency.
Single-subject M-MOM SEs are conditional model-based estimates: Within-subject SEs from repair::fit_mmom() / medusa_fit_mmom() use a normal-error variance formula conditional on first-stage error moments. Across multiple participants, decon_connectivity_repair() pools participant slopes using dispersion-scaled finite-sample random-effects \(t\)-intervals (Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman, HKSJ pooling) so group \(p\)-values rely on between-participant replication rather than single-subject row independence.
Zero-mean measurement error vs. regularization bias: Propagating se_demixed^2 quantifies observation-noise variance \(B_{r,\tau}\Sigma_r B_{r,\tau}^\top\), not residual resolution distortion \((K - I)\theta\) from strong regularization or HRF mismatch. When seed and target parcels experience substantially different effective trial resolution (\(K_S \neq K_T\)), disattenuating variance alone does not undo unequal resolution; see Measurement-Error Models and REPAIR for resolution-aware extensions.



Implementation locations and reproduction

Core implementation files in medusa: - R/crossrun_hrf.R (hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd, hrf_ar_cascade_info, fit_crossrun_decon) - R/deconvolve_reglin.R (estimate_decon_noise_sd, deconvolve_reglin) - R/hrf_noise_evidence.R (hrf_inverse_operator) - R/diagnose_crossrun_recovery.R (compute_ar1_operator_cov, decon_epoch_regression) - R/medusa_connectivity.R / R/diagnose_crossrun_recovery.R (medusa_fit_mmom, decon_connectivity_repair, medusa_between_subject_repair)
To regenerate the numerical cascade covariance check (worked/mmom-check.rds):
cd worked && Rscript mmom-check.R
