title: Measurement-Error Models and REPAIR
text:
Summary of Findings
Attaching diagonal trial SEs to ordinary M-MOMS disattenuates independent white measurement noise, but full latent connectivity inference faces three deeper structural requirements: unbiased source resolution, cross-parcel/cross-trial shared-error moments, and participant-cluster uncertainty calibration.

title: Measurement-Error Models and REPAIR
text:
Recover an unbiased source mean (or model resolution explicitly): Regularized continuous deconvolution yields \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat{z}_{g} \mid \theta_g] = K_g \theta_g\) with \(K_g \neq I\). In our controlled unequal-resolution experiment (\(K_S \neq K_T\)), full noise-moment subtraction alone estimated connectivity as 0.767 when truth was 0.550. Inverting known, well-conditioned resolution operators restored recovery to 0.551.
Propagate shared errors and cluster at the participant level: Under unbiased source measurements with strong serial (\(0.55\)) and shared cross-parcel (\(0.45\)) Gaussian noise, the full cross-trial corrected-score estimator recovered 0.546. Participant-cluster intervals covered truth in 94.8% of repetitions, whereas row-based intervals covered only 86.0%.
Respect finite-participant limits: With only 12 participants, asymptotic cluster sandwich intervals undercovered (91.8% connectivity coverage)—motivating the dispersion-scaled finite-sample \(t\)-interval (HKSJ) pooling used in medusa::decon_connectivity_repair().

title: Measurement-Error Models and REPAIR
section: 1. Define the neural relationship and the measurement relationship
text:
1. Define the neural relationship and the measurement relationship
For participant \(s \in \{1, \dots, S\}\) and trial \(i\), define a centered task modulator \(x_{si}\) and latent seed/target trial amplitudes \((\theta_{S,si}, \theta_{T,si})\) matching Step 6:
\[
\theta_{T,si}=\alpha_s+\beta_S \theta_{S,si}+\beta_x x_{si}
               +\beta_P (x_{si}\theta_{S,si})+\eta_{si}.
\]
\(\beta_S\) is the seed–target association at \(x=0\); \(\beta_P\) is its task modulation (PPI). Across all trials of participant \(s\), the linear trial-readout measurement interface is:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}\widehat{z}_{S,s}\\\widehat{z}_{T,s}\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}K_{S,s}&0\\0&K_{T,s}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\theta_{S,s}\\\theta_{T,s}\end{bmatrix}
+\begin{bmatrix}u_s\\v_s\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\!\begin{pmatrix}u_s\\v_s\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}\Omega_{SS,s}&\Omega_{ST,s}\\
\Omega_{ST,s}^{\top}&\Omega_{TT,s}\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Classical additive measurement-error correction assumes \(K_S = K_T = I\). In addition, PPI products and trial smoothing do not commute:
\[
K\,\operatorname{diag}(x)\theta_S \ne \operatorname{diag}(x)K \theta_S.
\]
Multiplying a smoothed or within-run decorrelated (ZCA-whitened) seed by the task modulator \(x\) afterward does not match smoothing the latent interaction—which is why decon_connectivity_repair() defaults to use_whitened = FALSE.

title: Measurement-Error Models and REPAIR
section: 2. Three workable measurement models
text:
2. Three workable measurement models

A. Likelihood-only coefficients in a modest source basis
Represent each parcel \(g\)’s BOLD run series using a prespecified, low-dimensional neural event basis passed through its learned HRF:
\[
y_g=G_g \theta_g+Z_g\gamma_g+\varepsilon_g,
\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_g)=\Sigma_g.
\]
When \(G_g\) has full column rank (e.g., well-spaced trial impulses or low-dimensional epoch bases) and is fit via unpenalized GLS in whitened coordinates,
\[
\widehat{z}_g=B_g y_g,\qquad B_g G_g=I,
\qquad \mathbb{E}(\widehat{z}_g\mid \theta_g)=\theta_g,
\qquad \Omega_{gg}=B_g\Sigma_g B_g^{\top},
\qquad \Omega_{ST}=B_S\Sigma_{\varepsilon_S,\varepsilon_T}B_T^{\top}.
\]
This provides an exact unbiased additive measurement-error model (\(K_g = I\)), closely paralleling likelihood-only coefficient reconstruction in REPAIR (Abdulrahman & Henson, 2016). In likelihood_only_bridge.R (16 source amplitudes, 180 BOLD volumes, distinct regional HRFs, shared/serial AR noise), trial operators satisfy \(BG = I\) to 8.88e-16, and a 10,000-draw Monte Carlo check matches analytical source SDs within 1.5%. Its trade-off is design conditioning: rapid jittered event schedules or omitted sustained activity can make unpenalized \(G_g\) collinear or misspecified.


B. De-penalize only identifiable contrasts
For a linear Gaussian posterior with precision \(C_{\rm post}^{-1} = J + P_{\rm prior}\), likelihood information \(J\) is recoverable only on subspaces where \(J\) is well-conditioned. In likelihood_only_bridge.R, the full 180-column continuous convolution matrix has numerical rank 178, confirming why continuous TR-grid deconvolution cannot simply drop its penalty globally without projecting onto identifiable trial/window contrasts first.


C. Retain resolution \(K_S, K_T\) inside a joint latent Gaussian model
When unshrinking is ill-conditioned, \(K_S\) and \(K_T\) can be retained explicitly inside a joint Gaussian marginal likelihood over \((\widehat{z}_{S,s}, \widehat{z}_{T,s}) \mid x_s\). In joint_gaussian_demo.R (known unequal \(K_S \neq K_T\) and known \(\Omega\)), maximum likelihood recovered connectivity 0.507 (truth 0.550) and PPI 0.336 (truth 0.350) with a positive-definite Hessian, trading stronger distributional assumptions and computation for exact handling of non-identity resolution.


Gaussian conditional-mean calibration variant

Let \(m_S = \mathbb{E}(\theta_S \mid \widehat{z}_S, x)\) under a Gaussian seed prior. With independent regional errors, \[
\mathbb{E}(\widehat{z}_T \mid \widehat{z}_S, x) = K_T\{Z\gamma + \beta_S m_S + \beta_P\operatorname{diag}(x)m_S\},
\] requiring design columns \(K_T m_S\) and \(K_T \operatorname{diag}(x) m_S\) rather than multiplying \(m_S\) by \(x\) after applying \(K_T\), plus an explicit shared-noise regression term \(\Omega_{TS}(K_S V_S K_S^\top + \Omega_{SS})^{-1}(\widehat{z}_S - K_S \mu_S)\) whenever \(\Omega_{TS} \neq 0\).

title: Measurement-Error Models and REPAIR
section: 3. Full cross-trial corrected-score estimating equations
text:
3. Full cross-trial corrected-score estimating equations
For unbiased trial readouts (\(K_S = K_T = I\)), form participant \(s\)’s centered trial design \(\widehat{X}_s = X_s + U_s\) for columns \([\theta_S,\, x,\, \theta_S x]\) and define full cross-trial error moments \(\Psi_s = \mathbb{E}(U_s^\top U_s)\) and \(c_s = \mathbb{E}(U_s^\top v_s)\) (including run-centering projections applied consistently to both data and \(\Omega_{SS}, \Omega_{ST}\)). Solving the summed participant corrected score (Nakamura, 1990; Buonaccorsi, 1996):
\[
q_s(\beta)=\widehat{X}_s^{\top}\widehat{z}_{T,s}-c_s
       -(\widehat{X}_s^{\top}\widehat{X}_s-\Psi_s)\beta,
\qquad \sum_{s=1}^S q_s(\widehat\beta)=0,
\]
yields an unbiased estimating equation \(\mathbb{E}[q_s(\beta_0)] = 0\) with participant-cluster sandwich variance:
\[
\widehat V=H^{-1}\left[\frac{S}{S-1}\sum_{s=1}^S
q_s(\widehat\beta)q_s(\widehat\beta)^{\top}\right]H^{-\top},
\quad
H=\sum_{s=1}^S(\widehat{X}_s^{\top}\widehat{X}_s-\Psi_s).
\]


Prototype interface (measurement_error_models.R)

source("measurement_error_models.R")
fit <- fit_corrected(blocks, mode = "full")
stopifnot(fit$ok)
fit$estimate  # neural association, task main effect, PPI
fit$se        # participant-cluster score SEs
The prototype refuses indefinite corrected information matrices rather than silently regularizing unidentified designs.

title: Measurement-Error Models and REPAIR
section: 4. Conditional simulation benchmarks (400 repetitions per scenario)
text:
4. Conditional simulation benchmarks (400 repetitions per scenario)
Each scenario simulates 400 repetitions of \(S = 60\) participants (Few participants uses \(S = 12\)) with 24 trials per participant, true connectivity \(\beta_S = 0.55\), task main effect \(\beta_x = 0.25\), and PPI \(\beta_P = 0.35\) (Null sets \(\beta_S = \beta_P = 0\)), under serial trial error correlation \(0.55\) and shared cross-region error correlation \(0.45\).






Figure 13.1: Mean coefficient bias across three stress scenarios. Bars show plus/minus 1.96 Monte Carlo SE; horizontal scales differ across columns. The oracle uses true neural amplitudes. Empty Undo K rows mean that method was only evaluated in the unequal-resolution scenario.









Figure 13.2: Coverage of nominal 95% normal intervals. Bars are exact binomial 95% intervals for the Monte Carlo coverage probability, not individual-model confidence intervals. The dashed reference is 95%; all horizontal axes span 0–100%. Full + row SE and Full + cluster SE have the same point estimate.

Three practical lessons bridge these benchmarks back to empirical medusa analyses:

Omitting shared cross-parcel error creates severe false connectivity: Under Null serial + shared, ignoring \(\Omega_{ST}\) (Zero shared covariance) falsely rejects in 95.0% of repetitions, whereas subtracting \(\Omega_{ST}\) drops connectivity false positives to 5.0%—directly motivating shared_error = "auto" in Step 6.
Unequal source resolution requires matched HRF/inverse scales: When two parcels have markedly different effective smoothing (\(K_S \neq K_T\)), naive attenuation and resolution distortion can partially cancel (0.579) while variance-only disattenuation overshoots (0.767). Keep regularization policies matched across seed and target parcels and control shared task main effects carefully (Cole et al., 2019).
Small-\(S\) cohorts require finite-sample \(t\)/HKSJ adjustments: Normal asymptotic cluster SEs undercover at \(S = 12\) (MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb, 2022), which is why decon_connectivity_repair() uses HKSJ \(t\)-intervals over participant slopes rather than normal row or unadjusted cluster \(z\)-intervals.

title: Validation and the Limits of the Evidence
text:
Designing a Study-Specific Calibration Check
The standalone medusa package is evaluated through two complementary layers of evidence:
Keeping the scope of each test distinct is essential: an algebraic check verifies that operator covariance propagation is exact conditional on a fitted noise model, whereas a Monte Carlo study measures bias and interval coverage under its specific data-generating process.
Before making high-stakes inferential claims on a novel task schedule—especially rapid event-related designs with variable-duration phases or trial-level PPI—run a compact synthetic calibration tailored to your exact study geometry:
crumbs: 14  Validation and the Limits of the Evidence

title: Validation and the Limits of the Evidence
text:
Lock the estimand and multiplicity family upfront: Prespecify the target parcels, peri-event lag grid, behavioral covariates, planned time windows, and study-wide adjustment rule ("holm" or "BY") before inspecting empirical \(p\)-values.
Use your actual empirical event schedule and censor masks: Simulate BOLD on the exact empirical onset times, reaction-time durations, run lengths, and framewise-displacement censor masks (valid_rows) from your cohort so collinearity and edge truncation match your real data.
Simulate both active signals and realistic structured nulls: Include voxelwise HRF variation across the physiological manifold, AR(\(p\)) temporal noise, spatially correlated parcel innovations, and—for Step 6 PPI—a stress null where shared physiological/motion noise varies across task conditions while true neural modulation is zero.
Refit the complete pipeline inside every Monte Carlo replicate: Keep Step 1 HRF/noise learning, Step 2 lambda and rwls = "auto" estimation, Step 3/4 epoch demixing and parcel weighting, and Step 5/6 inference inside the loop rather than freezing oracle operators.
Report bias, 95% CI coverage, null rejection, and convergence health together: Track missing edge-lag participants, isSingular() rates in mixed_by(), step-up regularization triggers in decon_connectivity_repair(), and binomial Monte Carlo intervals around empirical rejection and coverage rates.
crumbs: 14  Validation and the Limits of the Evidence

title: Calibration of Multi-Lag Trajectory Inference
text:
Simulation Design
Step 5 introduced medusa_multilag_infer() for joint peri-event trajectory estimation, simultaneous confidence bands, 1D TFCE, epoch omnibus testing, and planned window contrasts. This chapter evaluates the empirical Type I error and 95% confidence-band coverage of medusa::medusa_multilag_infer() across 180 independent synthetic cohorts per scenario, separating two distinct error-rate targets:
Each Monte Carlo replication simulates 20 participants, 2 runs per participant, 6 peri-event lags (0 to 5 s), 1 active parcel, and 2 null parcels (Null A and Null B):
Note what this benchmark isolates: it starts at the participant trial panel to test group pooling, available-case edge support, finite-sample cross-lag covariance calibration (Wishart draws), and study-wide Holm adjustment under known lag covariance and serial trial dependence. End-to-end HRF/deconvolution estimation is evaluated separately in the 14-study validation suite.
crumbs: 15  Calibration of Multi-Lag Trajectory Inference

title: Calibration of Multi-Lag Trajectory Inference
text:
Realistic heteroskedasticity and cross-lag/cross-parcel dependence: Inter-trial intervals jitter between 3 and 9 seconds; Run 2 has \(1.6\times\) the residual SD of Run 1; residuals share common cross-parcel noise and positive cross-lag autocorrelation; and true participant slopes vary randomly around the population trajectory in every parcel.
Two benchmark regimes (180 replications each):

Complete / independent trials: Complete lag support for all 20 participants and independent trial innovations within each run.
Gaps / serially dependent trials: Adds serial autocorrelation in both behavioral predictor and neural trial residuals, drops random subsets of trials within runs, and censors the final edge lag entirely in 3 of the 20 participants. Under medusa_multilag_infer()’s available-case cross-lag pooling, all 20 participants are retained at supported lags (0–4 s) while the 17 uncensored participants inform lag 5 s.

Inference settings: Each replication runs the panel pathway of medusa_multilag_infer() with trajectory_mode = "none", contrast_source = "unsmoothed", 799 finite-sample-calibrated cross-lag covariance draws per trajectory (studentized Wishart null draws), and a planned late_minus_early contrast ([3, 4] s minus [0, 1] s).

Parentheses report exact Clopper–Pearson 95% binomial intervals for Monte Carlo uncertainty (\(N = 180\) replications). Single-trajectory null metrics evaluate the prespecified Null A parcel in every replication; study-family metrics count rejecting either Null A or Null B when testing all three parcels (Active, Null A, Null B).






Figure 15.1: Rejection rates for a prespecified null trajectory and for the three-parcel study family. Bars show 95% Monte Carlo intervals.




Key findings from the rejection and coverage benchmarks

Calibrated within-trajectory Type I error (Max-|T|, TFCE, Omnibus): Accounting for finite-participant covariance uncertainty via studentized Wishart draws keeps single-trajectory null false-positive rates squarely around the 5% target in the complete design (3.9% for Max-|T|, 5.0% for TFCE, and 2.8% for Omnibus), and remains well controlled under serial trial dependence and edge-lag missingness (7.2%, 6.1%, and 2.8%; all 95% Monte Carlo intervals contain 5%).
Study-wide multiplicity control via Holm: Applying Holm across the 3-parcel family (Active, Null A, Null B) holds familywise false-discovery rates to 1.7% and 1.7%—scaling cleanly to larger parcel parcellations where unadjusted epoch tests would accumulate false positives across dozens of regions.







Figure 15.2: Coverage of the raw Max-|T| band over all lags and of the planned window interval. The reference line is 95%. Bars show 95% Monte Carlo intervals.




Simultaneous 95% confidence bands and window contrasts achieve nominal coverage: Across all 6 lags simultaneously, the raw Max-|T| band covers the entire true curve in 96.1% (null) and 95.0% (active) of complete replications, and 92.8% (null) and 96.7% (active) under gapped/serial stress. The planned late_minus_early window contrast (contrast_source = "unsmoothed") covers the true population difference in 95.6% and 97.8% of replications, with negligible mean bias (+0.005 and +0.002 slope units).

title: Temporal Autocorrelation and Noise Calibration
text:
1. What Woolrich et al. (2001) demonstrate
Woolrich, Ripley, Brady, and Smith (2001), Temporal Autocorrelation in Univariate Linear Modeling of FMRI Data (NeuroImage 14, 1370–1386, DOI 10.1006/nimg.2001.0931), highlights three principles that directly shape Step 1 of medusa: (1) separating task mean-model mismatch from residual autocorrelation, (2) regularizing temporal covariance across neighboring voxels without pooling signed BOLD responses, and (3) estimating noise correlation and marginal noise scale coherently so propagated readout covariance \(B_{r,\tau}\Sigma_r B_{r,\tau}^\top\) is well calibrated. At the same time, our diagnostic benchmarks show why replacing MEDuSA’s REML AR(\(p\)) cascade with a raw-residual Tukey lag taper is not advantageous under high-rank event-related mean models.
Woolrich et al. (2001) compare temporal autocorrelation estimators for univariate task-activation GLMs. Their FILM procedure estimates residual autocorrelation, stabilizes long-lag estimates with a Tukey cosine lag taper:
\[
\widehat r_T(\ell)=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12\{1+\cos(\pi\ell/M)\}\widehat r(\ell),&0\le\ell<M,\\
0,&\ell\ge M,
\end{cases}
\]
borrows information locally within tissue types (SUSAN), and prewhitens both data and design. Two nuances matter when translating their findings to modern fast-TR event-related deconvolution:
crumbs: 16  Temporal Autocorrelation and Noise Calibration

title: Temporal Autocorrelation and Noise Calibration
text:
Bandwidth scales with TR, not volume count: Fifteen lags spans 45 s at \(\text{TR} = 3\text{ s}\) (Woolrich’s primary acquisition) but only 9.75 s at \(\text{TR} = 0.65\text{ s}\).
Projection distortion grows with design rank: After projecting out an \(m\)-column event/nuisance design \(X\) (\(M_X = I - P_X\)), raw OLS residuals have covariance \(\operatorname{Cov}(r) = M_X \Sigma M_X^\top \neq \Sigma\). In rapid trial-wise designs where \(X\) carries dozens of free event columns, raw-residual sample autocorrelations acquire substantial negative projection bias that simple lag tapering does not undo.
crumbs: 16  Temporal Autocorrelation and Noise Calibration

title: Temporal Autocorrelation and Noise Calibration
section: 2. How medusa implements and extends these principles
text:
2. How medusa implements and extends these principles



Principle
Implementation in estimate_crossrun_hrf() & deconvolve_crossrun_hrf()
Methodological role




Separate HRF shape mismatch from noise autocorrelation
Two-pass target-excluding REML noise refit: Pass 1 estimates initial noise under a canonical fallback HRF + free event amplitudes + temporal derivatives; once cross-run HRFs are selected out of sample, Pass 2 refits each run’s AR(\(p\)) noise model using the selected HRF while keeping HRF selection strictly frozen
Prevents unmodeled fast/slow vascular dispersion from spilling into residuals and pushing \(\widehat\rho\) to the upper boundary (0.90).


Regularize temporal covariance without projection bias
Pooled AR(1) profile REML on the exact residual subspace \(M_X\) + shrunk residual AR(\(q\)) Yule–Walker correction with projection-bias adjustment
Achieves low-variance spectral regularization while accounting analytically for degrees-of-freedom and projection loss from \(M_X\).


Borrow spatially without cancelling opposing task signals
Pools REML log-likelihood profiles across voxels within each parcel (pooling = "parcel") or across concordant tissue neighbors (pooling = "graph") rather than averaging raw BOLD time series
Voxels with positive, negative, or null task responses contribute coherently to shared physiological noise estimation.


Estimate correlation and marginal scale coherently
deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(..., scaling = "noise_sd") computes outlier-trimmed, leverage-adjusted GLS residual scale (Winsorized GLS residuals) under the post-selection HRF and AR(\(p\)) cascade, converting innovation SD to stationary marginal noise_sd
Eliminates mismatch between temporal whitening correlation \(\Sigma_{\rm cor}\) and marginal amplitude \(\sigma_{\rm obs}\) in propagated covariance \(\Omega = \sigma_{\rm obs}^2 B \Sigma_{\rm cor} B^\top\).

title: Temporal Autocorrelation and Noise Calibration
section: 3. Benchmark 1: Separating HRF mismatch from temporal autocorrelation
text:
3. Benchmark 1: Separating HRF mismatch from temporal autocorrelation
Using the Step 1 simulation (3 runs, \(\text{TR} = 0.65\text{ s}\), 360 volumes, 24 jittered events/run, 8 voxels each in Fast, Slow, and Null parcels, true noise parameters \(\rho = 0.65, \psi_1 = 0.20, \psi_2 = -0.30\)), we compare:

Single-pass canonical HRF (Canonical_HRF): Single-pass AR(\(p\)) noise estimation locked to a fixed canonical HRF (no post-selection refit).
Two-pass MEDuSA refit (Current_MEDuSA): estimate_crossrun_hrf() with its 2-pass post-selection REML AR(\(p\)) refit (using the out-of-sample cross-run selected HRF, zero target-run leakage).
Oracle HRF (Oracle_true_HRF): Noise fit conditioned on the exact data-generating HRF.
Tukey lag-taper comparators (Tukey10/15/28): Pooled raw-residual Tukey lag tapers (\(M \in \{10, 15, 28\}\)) under either canonical or selected-HRF mean models.

Run 1 implied noise autocorrelation functions across parcels. Current MEDuSA (2-pass post-selection REML refit) overlaps the true generating ACF and Oracle HRF fit, whereas locking the mean model to a misspecified Canonical HRF inflates long-lag correlation, and raw-residual Tukey tapers exhibit projection distortion.


Two results stand out clearly:

Post-selection noise refitting eliminates HRF-induced autocorrelation inflation: Under the single-pass canonical HRF fit, unmodeled vascular shape residuals drive \(\widehat\rho\) to its upper bound in both active parcels (acf_RMSE_1_24 = 0.260 in Fast, 0.314 in Slow). MEDuSA’s target-excluding 2-pass refit drops ACF RMSE to 0.006 (Fast) and 0.008 (Slow)—matching the oracle-HRF fit (0.006 and 0.008) without touching target-run HRF selection.
REML subspace likelihood outperforms raw-residual lag tapering: Even when given the selected HRF (Tukey15_selected), raw-residual Tukey tapering retains 0.090–0.100 ACF RMSE—even on the pure Null parcel (0.100 vs. 0.011 for MEDuSA’s 2-pass REML fit)—because projecting 24 free trial predictors + drift terms out of 360 volumes distorts sample residual autocorrelations (\(\operatorname{Cov}(r) = M_X \Sigma M_X^\top\)).

4. Benchmark 2: Coherent marginal scale and propagated readout covariance
What ultimately matters for Step 3–6 inference is not the ACF plot in isolation, but the accuracy of the propagated trial readout covariance \(\Omega_{r,\tau} = \sigma_{\rm obs}^2 B_{r,\tau} \Sigma_{\rm cor} B_{r,\tau}^\top\). Evaluating a frozen linear inverse (\(\lambda = 0.01\), second-difference penalty) at event onsets, we compare the single-pass canonical HRF model against MEDuSA’s two-pass refit under both a standalone second-difference noise scale (d2) and MEDuSA’s covariance-consistent GLS residual scale (gls, scaling = "noise_sd"). title: Temporal Autocorrelation and Noise Calibration
section: 5. Practical takeaways
text:
5. Practical takeaways

Keep noise pooling groups tissue-homogeneous: Under pooling = "parcel", spatial_groups defines both HRF evidence pooling and AR(\(p\)) noise pooling. When volumetric parcels span both high-pulsatility pial/CSF-border voxels and quieter interior gray matter, use pooling = "graph" (Spatial Graph Pooling), which weights noise smoothing by local autocorrelation similarity so pial-rim pulsatility does not bleed into deep gray matter (Parlak et al., 2023; Olszowy et al., 2019).
Match ar_order to acquisition TR: Default ar_order = "auto" (up to cascaded AR(3)) works well for standard and moderate multiband TRs (\(0.65\text{–}2.0\text{ s}\)); ultra-fast TRs (\(< 0.5\text{ s}\)) with unmodeled cardiac/respiratory aliases should pair physiological regressors (nuisance) with residual ACF inspection.
Remember what temporal prewhitening does not identify: Temporal whitening within each parcel calibrates \(\Omega_{gg}\), not cross-parcel shared noise \(\Omega_{ST}\)—which is why deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() also retains task-free noise_innovations so Step 4 and Step 6 (shared_error = "auto") can estimate spatial noise covariance directly.



Internal R helpers & benchmark scripts

Inside R/crossrun_hrf.R and R/deconvolve_reglin.R, the two-pass noise refit and GLS marginal scale are implemented by fit_crossrun_decon(), hrf_estimate_noise(), and hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd(), while standalone second-difference scaling is implemented by estimate_decon_noise_sd().

Relationship to the medusa R Package
This Quarto book lives in the book/ directory of the standalone medusa R package (0.1.0, excluded from CRAN/tarball builds via .Rbuildignore). Every simulation, figure, and diagnostic table in the active chapters was executed directly against library(medusa)—incorporating the complete modern pipeline architecture:
(Under the hood, computationally intensive 3D/4D NIfTI streaming, cortical-sheet graph filters, batched Cholesky deconvolution solves, and peri-event alignment run in compiled Rcpp/RcppArmadillo kernels while exposing clean R S3 objects.)
For NIfTI matrix and file-backed workflows (read_nifti_ts(), write_nifti_ts(), build_spatial_graph(), align_medusa_ts(), voxelwise_deconvolution(), and evt_align_decon_files()), see the package vignettes (vignettes/medusa-workflows.Rmd and vignettes/medusa-docs.md) and function reference (?read_nifti_ts, ?build_spatial_graph, ?estimate_crossrun_hrf, ?deconvolve_crossrun_hrf, ?align_medusa_ts, ?decon_epoch_regression, ?medusa_multilag_infer, ?decon_connectivity_repair).

Pipeline component
Core medusa functions
Key methodological features




Step 0 · Task design & BIDS/fMRIPrep ingestion
read_fmriprep_subject(), read_bids_events(), read_fmriprep_confounds(), read_fmriprep_aroma(), apply_aroma(), read_nifti_ts()
Multi-run & inter-phase jitter feasibility benchmarks, direct 4D NIfTI ↔︎ T × V matrix extraction with pre-flight geometry checks, BIDS/fMRIPrep/BrainGnomes ingestion with clock-preserving valid_rows, non-aggressive ICA-AROMA partial regression, explicit missed_feedback nuisance event retention, and event_index-keyed trial joins.


Step 1 · Spatial Graph, Cross-Run HRF & AR(\(p\)) noise
build_spatial_graph(), hrf_library(), estimate_crossrun_hrf()
Zero-phase respiratory motion filtering (motion_bandstop_bpm / motion_lowpass_hz), 3D physiological HRF manifold (preset = "medusa"), out-of-sample parcel and edge-preserving cortical-sheet pooling (pooling = "graph"), and 2-pass target-excluding REML AR(\(p\)) noise refit.


Step 2 · Event-informed continuous deconvolution
deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(), diagnose_crossrun_recovery(), write_nifti_ts(), deconvolve_reglin(), deconvolve_nlreg()
Continuous neural source recovery with monotone SNR-stratified lambda tuning (lambda_mode = "auto", PAVA), task-guarded rwls = "auto" glitch downweighting, outlier-trimmed GLS marginal "noise_sd" scaling, task-free noise_innovations, explicit hrf_inverse_operator() strata, and 3D/4D NIfTI export (deconvolve_nlreg() retained as blind Bush & Cisler, 2013 comparator).


Step 3 · Trial-epoch readout, alignment & demixing
decon_epoch_regression(), align_medusa_ts(), evt_align_decon_files()
Local time-averaging (kernel quadrature) onto peri-event lag grids, collateral non-target removal (demix_other_events), ridge-stabilized target demixing (demix_target_trials), within-trial lag demixing (demix_within_trial), duration "rate" vs. "integral" readout, edge-preserving neighborhood trial-variance shrinkage (tau2_shrinkage = "graph_eb"), exact stationary error propagation (se_demixed), and descriptive peri-event alignment (align_medusa_ts()).


Step 4 · Parcel panels & cohort weights
decon_epoch_regression(..., parcel_groups = ...)
Multi-stratum inverse-variance parcel pooling using task-free noise_innovations, shared_noise_loading & unit_error_cor export, precision_weight & precision_weight_cohort, and paired within-run trial decorrelation (whiten_panel, ZCA).


Step 5 · Group & trajectory inference
mixed_by(), medusa_multilag_infer(), backproject_medusa()
Cohort-weighted split-wise REML mixed models (lmerTest, supporting disk-backed Parquet/.rds/CSV streaming and split_filter pushdown), joint multi-lag trajectories with available-case pooling, cross-lag deblurring, uncertainty-aware penalized splines (Marra–Wood), finite-sample covariance draws (studentized Wishart) for Max-|T| / 1D TFCE / omnibus tests, "unsmoothed" window contrasts, and NIfTI map backprojection.


Step 6 · Trial connectivity & PPI
decon_connectivity_repair(), medusa_fit_mmom(), medusa_between_subject_repair()
Within-trial predictor disattenuation with conditioning protection (M-MOMS), automatic cross-parcel shared_error = "auto" subtraction, exact residualized-seed covariance projection, and finite-sample random-effects \(t\)-interval pooling (HKSJ).
